nodes.title: (g, R^{k−1}_{2−k}f)^{reg} via constant terms (Bruinier–Ono–Rhoades Theorem 4.1, corrected)
nodes.statement: Let Γ ≤ SL₂(ℤ) have finite index, k ≥ 2, g ∈ M_k(Γ), f ∈ H_{2−k}^+(Γ). Then (g, R^{k−1}_{2−k}f)^{reg} = ((−1)^k(k−2)!/[SL₂(ℤ) : Γ])·Σ_{κ ∈ Γ\ℙ¹(ℚ)} w_κ·c_g(0, κ)·\overline{c⁺_f(0, κ)}, where c_g(0, κ), c⁺_f(0, κ) are the constant terms at the cusp κ and w_κ its width. BOR print the formula without the factor (k−2)! (sourceIssue E408). In particular (g, D^{k−1}f)^{reg} = 0 for cusp forms g (Bruinier–Ono–Rhoades Cor. 4.2).
hypotheses: k ≥ 2; h := R^{k−1}_{2−k}f = (−4π)^{k−1}D^{k−1}f ∈ M^!_k has vanishing constant terms (coefficients a⁺(n)(−4πn)^{k−1}), so the truncated product is defined.
proofSteps: Put H := v^{k−2}\overline{R^{k−2}_{2−k}f}; then h = R^{k−1}_{2−k}f = v^{−k}\overline{L_{2−k}H} (BOR Remark 7), so g\overline{h}v^k dμ = g·L_{2−k}H dμ = −d(Hg dτ) (g holomorphic).

Stokes on F_T(Γ) (QM.3/truncated-fundamental-domain-stokes summed over cosets; sides and arcs cancel) leaves the top edges: the integral tends to the constant terms of H·g at the cusps, weighted by the widths.

Constant term of H: from R^{k−2}_{2−k}(c) = (−1)^k(k−2)!·c·v^{2−k} for constants (induction: R^j_{2−k}(1) = (2−k)(3−k)⋯(1−k+j)v^{−j}) and BOR's expansion H = (−1)^kΣ_n\overline{c⁺(n)}Γ(k−1, 4πnv)e(−nτ) + (−1)^k(k−2)!²Σ_{n<0}\overline{c⁻(n)}e(−nτ), whose n = 0 term is (−1)^k\overline{c⁺(0)}Γ(k−1, 0) = (−1)^k(k−2)!\overline{c⁺(0)}; the other terms of Hg have no constant term or tend to 0 as T → ∞.
acceptance: For g ∈ S_k(Γ): (g, D^{k−1}f)^{reg} = 0 (BOR Cor. 4.2).
For k = 2 the factor (k−2)! = 1 and BOR's formula is correct as printed.

sources.match: The statement as printed (missing (k−2)!, E408).

nodes.title: The image of D^{k−1} on H_{2−k}^+ (Bruinier–Ono–Rhoades Theorem 1.2 / Corollary 4.3)
nodes.statement: Let Γ ≤ SL₂(ℤ) have finite index and k ≥ 2. The image of D^{k−1} : H_{2−k}^+(Γ) → M^!_k(Γ) consists exactly of those h ∈ M^!_k(Γ) with vanishing constant term at every cusp and (g, h)^{reg} = 0 for all g ∈ S_k(Γ).
hypotheses: k ≥ 2; Γ of finite index.
proofSteps: ⊆: D^{k−1}f has zero constant terms (coefficients a⁺(n)(n/h_κ)^{k−1}) and is orthogonal to cusp forms by QM.3/regularized-pairing-with-bol-image.

⊇: given h, choose f ∈ H_{2−k}^+ whose principal parts at all cusps match those of D^{1−k}h up to constants (QM.3/harmonic-maass-form-prescribed-principal-parts, applied to the negative-index coefficients divided by (n/h_κ)^{k−1} at a cusp of strict period h_κ); then h − D^{k−1}f ∈ S_k(Γ) (constant terms both zero) and is orthogonal to S_k(Γ), hence 0.

nodes.title: The non-holomorphic Eisenstein series E₂*
nodes.statement: E₂*(τ) := E₂(τ) − 3/(πv), with Mathlib's E₂ = EisensteinSeries.E2 (= 1 − 24Σσ₁(n)q^n). It is SL₂(ℤ)-invariant of weight 2, harmonic (Δ_2(v^{−1}) = 0), of moderate growth, hence E₂* ∈ H_2(SL₂(ℤ)), and ξ_2E₂* = 3/π. Since 3/π is not a cusp form, E₂* ∉ H_2^+(SL₂(ℤ)).
hypotheses: Level one, weight 2 (the case k ≥ 2 of the first exact sequence, where ξ_2 maps onto M^!_0).
proofSteps: Transformation: E₂|_2γ = E₂ − (3/π²)·2πic/(cτ + d) (Mathlib EisensteinSeries.E2_slash_action, 1/(2ζ(2)) = 3/π²), and (v^{−1})|_2γ = v^{−1} − 2ic/(cτ + d); so (3/(πv))|_2γ = 3/(πv) − 6ic/(π(cτ + d)) and the defects cancel.
Harmonic: E₂ holomorphic (E2_mdifferentiable) and Δ_2(v^{−1}) = (−1)(1 − 2 + 1)v^{−1} = 0 (hyperbolicLaplacian_im_rpow).
Growth: bounded at ∞ (E₂ → 1, 3/(πv) → 0); one cusp.
ξ_2E₂* = ξ_2(−(3/π)v^{−1}) = (−3/π)(1 − 2) = 3/π (xiOperator_im_rpow_one_sub).
acceptance: E₂*(i) = E₂(i) − 3/π = 0 (from the S-invariance of E₂* at the fixed point i: E₂*(i) = i^{−2}E₂*(i)).

sources.match: E₂* is the basic example with a non-zero v^{1−k} term (k = 2), i.e. an element of H_2 \ H_2^+.

E is odd, increasing, E(x) → ±1 as x → ±∞, E′(x) = 2e^{−πx²}, and E(x) = Σ_{n≥0}(−π)^n x^{2n+1}/(n!(n + 1/2)) (Zwegers Def. 1.6). Zwegers defines E as an entire function of z ∈ ℂ, but every use in the thesis (R, R_{m,l}, ρ^c) evaluates it at real arguments, so the real function is the object built here.
hypotheses: Real variable only; the entire extension is not needed by any node.

nodes.title: Zwegers' function β(x)
nodes.statement: For x ≥ 0, β(x) := ∫_x^∞ u^{−1/2}e^{−πu}du = erfc(√(πx)); for x>0 also β(x)=π^{−1/2}Γ(1/2, πx) (Zwegers Lemma 1.7), with Γ(s, x) the upper incomplete gamma function (QM.3/upper-incomplete-gamma). It satisfies β(0) = 1, 0 ≤ β(x) ≤ e^{−πx}, β decreasing, β′(x) = −x^{−1/2}e^{−πx} for x > 0.
hypotheses: x ≥ 0 (β(0) = 1 via Γ(1/2) = √π); totalised by β(x) := 1 for x < 0 is not used.
QM.3 totalizes upperIncompleteGamma(s,0) to 0. Thus the identity with upperIncompleteGamma is restricted to x>0; β(0)=1 uses the complete Gamma value or erfc(0), not that totalized value.
proofSteps: For x>0, substitute t=πu to obtain β(x)=π^{−1/2}Γ(1/2,πx)=erfc(√(πx)) by upperIncompleteGamma_half_sq. At x=0 use the complete Gamma or erfc value separately, since the roadmap’s totalized upper incomplete Gamma is zero there.
β(0) = π^{−1/2}Γ(1/2) = 1 (Mathlib Real.Gamma_one_half_eq).
acceptance: β(0) = 1 and β(x) ≤ e^{−πx}, the two facts used in every convergence proof of Zwegers Ch. 1–4.

nodes.statement: For every real x: E(x) = sgn(x)·(1 − β(x²)).

nodes.title: The Mordell integral h(z; τ)

Holomorphy in (z, τ): differentiation under the integral with this dominating function.

nodes.title: Convergence and real-analyticity of R (Zwegers Lemma 1.8, first part)

Real analyticity requires normal convergence on complex neighbourhoods, not just uniform convergence of real-analytic terms or their derivatives. Near a real coordinate point with y>0, complexify the four real coordinates of (u,τ), choose the local branch of √(2y), and use the entire extension E(w)=2∫_0^w exp(−πt²)dt. For Re w>0, 1−E(w)=2∫_0^∞ exp(−π(w+t)²)dt gives |1−E(w)|≤C exp(−π Re(w²))/Re w; use oddness for ν<0. On a sufficiently small complex polydisc, the quadratic exponent after multiplying by exp(−πiν²τ−2πiνu) still has real part ≤−cν²+C|ν|. nodes.title: Modular transformation of μ̃ (Zwegers Thm 1.11(2))
nodes.statement: For γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ): μ̃(u/(cτ + d), v/(cτ + d); (aτ + b)/(cτ + d)) = v(γ)^{−3}(cτ + d)^{1/2}e^{−πic(u−v)²/(cτ+d)}μ̃(u, v; τ), where v(γ) = η(γτ)/((cτ + d)^{1/2}η(τ)) is the eta multiplier.
hypotheses: Branch of (cτ + d)^{1/2} as in the eta multiplier system of QM.1 (the product v(γ)^{−3}(cτ+d)^{1/2} is independent of the branch choice).
proofSteps: From Prop. 1.5, 1.10: μ̃(u, v; τ + 1) = e^{−πi/4}μ̃ and μ̃(u/τ, v/τ; −1/τ) = −√(−iτ)e^{−πi(u−v)²/τ}μ̃ (the Mordell integrals cancel).
m(u, v; τ) := ϑ(u − v; τ)μ̃(u, v; τ) satisfies m(·; τ + 1) = m and m(u/τ, v/τ; −1/τ) = τm, hence m transforms with weight 1 under all of SL₂(ℤ) (generated by S, T).
ϑ(z/(cτ+d); γτ) = χ(γ)(cτ + d)^{1/2}e^{πicz²/(cτ+d)}ϑ(z; τ) with χ(γ)⁸ = 1; differentiating at z = 0 and using ϑ′(0) = −2πη³ gives χ(γ) = v(γ)³.

Divide: μ̃ transforms with v(γ)^{−3}(cτ + d)^{1/2}e^{−πic(u−v)²/(cτ+d)}. First divide where ϑ(u−v;τ)≠0; extend to the permitted points with u−v∈ℤτ+ℤ by continuity, since μ̃ is smooth there when u and v themselves avoid the lattice.
acceptance: For γ = T: v(T) = e^{πi/12} (η(τ + 1) = e^{πi/12}η(τ)), so v(T)^{−3} = e^{−πi/4}, consistent with Prop. 1.5(1).
A real-analytic Jacobi form of weight 1/2: the acceptance criterion of QM.4 (completion with a transformation proof).

nodes.title: The weight-3/2 unary theta function g_{a,b}
nodes.statement: For a, b ∈ ℝ and τ ∈ ℍ: g_{a,b}(τ) := Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ} ν e^{πiν²τ + 2πiνb} (Zwegers Def. 1.14). It is holomorphic in τ; for rational a, b it is a modular form of weight 3/2 on a congruence subgroup (Zwegers, after Prop. 1.15). In Mathlib's terms g_{a,b}(τ) = e^{πia²τ + 2πiab}·[a·jacobiTheta₂(aτ+b,τ)+(2πi)^{−1}jacobiTheta₂′(aτ+b,τ)].
hypotheses: a, b real; the modularity for rational a, b is stated through Prop. 1.15(4), (5) (the precise congruence subgroup is not needed by any node).
proofSteps: Absolute, locally uniform convergence from |νe^{πiν²τ}| = |ν|e^{−πν²y}.
(1)–(3) of Prop. 1.15: reindex ν ↦ ν + 1, factor e^{2πia}, ν ↦ −ν.
acceptance: g_{1/2,1/2}(τ) relates to η³: Σ_{ν∈1/2+ℤ}ν e^{πiν²τ+πiν} is a multiple of η(τ)³.

nodes.title: ∫ e^{πiτw²}/(w + ir) dw as a period integral (Zwegers Lemma 1.18)
nodes.statement: For r ∈ ℝ, r ≠ 0, τ ∈ ℍ: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} e^{πiτw²}/(w + ir) dw = −πr∫_0^{i∞} e^{πir²z}/√(−i(z + τ)) dz.
hypotheses: r ≠ 0; principal branch; the z-integral along the imaginary axis.
proofSteps: Both sides are holomorphic in τ; prove for τ = it: both solve (−∂_t + πr²)f(t) = −πir/√t and tend to 0 as t → ∞, hence coincide (ODE uniqueness).
acceptance: Used for Thm 1.16(2).

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Partial fractions for e^{2πbz}/cosh πz (Zwegers Lemma 1.19)
nodes.statement: For b ∈ (−1/2, 1/2) and z ∈ ℂ, z ∉ (1/2 + ℤ)i: −e^{2πbz}/cosh(πz) = (1/π)Σ_{ν∈1/2+ℤ} e^{2πiν(b+1/2)}/(z − iν), the series converging (conditionally, as a symmetric limit; the source proves convergence by partial summation).
proofSteps: Use the existing classical residue theorem for closed null-homologous piecewise-C1 curves from Completed/ContourIntegration Layer 3. For integer N>|z|+1 integrate F(w)=exp(2πbw)/(cosh(πw)(w−z)) around the counterclockwise rectangle with vertices ±N±iN. An open rectangle with sides at ±(N+1/4) contains the curve, is convex, and contains just the listed finitely many poles; the curve avoids all poles and has winding number one around each pole in its interior.

At w=z the residue is exp(2πbz)/cosh(πz). At w=iν, ν∈1/2+ℤ and |ν|<N, use πsinh(πiν)=πi sin(πν) to obtain residue exp(2πiν(b+1/2))/(π(z−iν)). All these poles are simple and meromorphic on the chosen open rectangle.
For each horizontal side, |cosh(π(x±iN))|=cosh(πx) and |x±iN−z|≥N−|z|. Its integral is bounded by C_b/(N−|z|), where C_b=∫_ℝ exp(2πbx)/cosh(πx) dx<∞ because |b|<1/2.
For each vertical side, |cosh(π(±N+iy))|≥sinh(πN) and |±N+iy−z|≥N−|z|. Its integral is at most 2N exp(2π|b|N)/((N−|z|)sinh(πN)), which tends to zero.

The boundary integral therefore tends to zero. The residue identity gives the stated limit of the sums over |ν|<N. This proves the symmetric conditional limit directly, without invoking an absolute Fourier-series HasSum theorem. Bounded geometric partial sums also give one-sided conditional convergence by summation by parts.
acceptance: At z = 0: Σ_{ν∈1/2+ℤ} e^{2πiν(b+1/2)}/ν = πi (symmetric summation), used at the end of the proof of Thm 1.16(2).

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: R as a period integral of a unary theta function (Zwegers Thm 1.16(1))
hypotheses: |a| < 1/2 (so sgn(ν + a) = sgn(ν) on 1/2 + ℤ); the path from −τ̄ vertically to i∞; principal branch.
proofSteps: Substitute z = iu − τ with u ∈ [2y, ∞): at u = 2y the path starts at −τ̄ and −i(z + τ) = u. The integral becomes i∫_{2y}^∞ g(iu − τ)u^{−1/2}du. Equivalently parameterise z = −τ̄ + it, t ≥ 0, with denominator √(2y+t), as in the suggested file.
Interchange sum and integral (absolute convergence) and use ∫_{2y}^∞ u^{−1/2}e^{−πν²u}du = |ν|^{−1}β(2ν²y) and β = 1 − E·sgn (Lemma 1.7), then reindex ν ↦ ν + a.
acceptance: This is the statement 'the shadow of μ̃ is a weight-3/2 unary theta function'.

nodes.title: Integral quadratic forms of type (r − 1, 1) with a chosen negative component
nodes.statement: Data (Zwegers §2.2): r ≥ 1, a symmetric matrix A ∈ M_r(ℤ) with det A ≠ 0, Q(x) := ½⟨x, Ax⟩ and B(x, y) := ⟨x, Ay⟩ = Q(x + y) − Q(x) − Q(y) on ℝ^r (and ℂ^r), of type (r − 1, 1) — the largest subspace on which Q is negative definite has dimension 1 — together with a vector c₀ ∈ ℝ^r with Q(c₀) < 0 selecting one of the two components of {Q < 0}. Pinned encoding: the structure records A, symmetry, det A ≠ 0, c₀ with Q(c₀) < 0, and positivity of Q on the B-orthogonal complement of c₀ (equivalent to type (r − 1, 1) given Q(c₀) < 0).
hypotheses: A integral, symmetric, non-degenerate; A need not be even (Prop. 2.7(6) treats odd diagonals).
proofSteps: Define the structure; Q, B from A.

Type (r − 1, 1) ⟺ (∃c₀, Q(c₀) < 0 and Q|_{c₀^⊥} positive definite): Sylvester's law of inertia (Mathlib QuadraticForm diagonalisation) or directly: a 2-dimensional negative definite subspace would meet c₀^⊥ non-trivially.

Decompose c₂ = t c₁ + v with B(c₁,v)=0; positivity on c₁⊥ and Q(c₂)<0 imply t ≠ 0 and B(c₁,c₂)=2tQ(c₁) ≠ 0. The sign of t distinguishes the two negative components. If c₁,c₂ are independent their span has type (1,1); if collinear handle c₂=t c₁ directly.
acceptance: A = (1 0; 0 1) admits no c₀.

nodes.title: The negative cone C_Q and its primitive cusp augmentation C̄_Q
nodes.statement: For a form of type (r − 1, 1) with chosen c₀: C_Q := {c ∈ ℝ^r : Q(c) < 0, B(c, c₀) < 0}; S_Q := {c ∈ ℤ^r primitive : Q(c) = 0, B(c, c₀) < 0} (representatives of the cusps of C_Q/ℝ₊); C̄_Q := C_Q ∪ S_Q (Zwegers §2.2).
hypotheses: Primitive: gcd of the coordinates is 1.
proofSteps: Define the three sets.
C_Q is an open convex cone (Q(c) < 0 on the component is preserved by positive combinations of vectors with pairwise negative B).
For c₁ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q, c₃ ∈ C_Q and t > 0: c₂ + tc₃ ∈ C_Q (Zwegers proof of Prop. 2.7(5): Q(c₂ + tc₃) = tB(c₂, c₃) + t²Q(c₃) < 0).
acceptance: S_Q = ∅ for A = (1 0; 0 −3) (x² − 3y² = 0 has no non-zero integral solution).

nodes.title: The weight function ρ^{c₁,c₂}(ν; τ)
nodes.statement: For c ∈ C̄_Q, ν ∈ ℝ^r, τ ∈ ℍ with y = Im τ: ρ^c(ν; τ) := E(B(c, ν)y^{1/2}/√(−Q(c))) if c ∈ C_Q and ρ^c(ν; τ) := sgn(B(c, ν)) if c ∈ S_Q; ρ^{c₁,c₂} := ρ^{c₁} − ρ^{c₂} (Zwegers Def. 2.1). ρ depends on τ only through y; replacing c by λc (λ > 0) does not change ρ^c (Remark 2.2).
hypotheses: E = QM.4/zwegers-error-function; sgn(0) = 0.
proofSteps: Define by cases on membership in C_Q (decidable classically).
Decomposition (Lemma 1.7): for c ∈ C_Q, ρ^c(ν) = sgn(B(c, ν))(1 − β(−B(c, ν)²y/Q(c))).
acceptance: ρ^{c,c} = 0; ρ^{c₁,c₂} = −ρ^{c₂,c₁}; ρ^{c₁,c₂} + ρ^{c₂,c₃} + ρ^{c₃,c₁} = 0.

nodes.statement: For c₁, c₂ ∈ C̄_Q, a ∈ R(c₁) ∩ R(c₂), b ∈ ℝ^r: ϑ_{a,b}(τ) = ϑ^{c₁,c₂}_{a,b}(τ) := Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r} ρ^{c₁,c₂}(ν; τ)e^{2πiQ(ν)τ + 2πiB(ν,b)}, and for (z, τ) ∈ D(c₁) ∩ D(c₂), with z = aτ + b: ϑ(z; τ) = ϑ^{c₁,c₂}_A(z; τ) := e^{−2πiQ(a)τ − 2πiB(a,b)}ϑ_{a,b}(τ) = Σ_{n∈ℤ^r} ρ(n + a; τ)e^{2πiQ(n)τ + 2πiB(n, z)} (Zwegers Def. 2.1). nodes.title: Q_c is positive definite and dominates Q_{c₀} (Zwegers Lemma 2.5)
nodes.statement: For c ∈ C_Q the form Q_c(ν) := Q(ν) − B(c, ν)²/(2Q(c)) is positive definite, and Q_c(ν) ≥ λ_{c,c₀}Q_{c₀}(ν) with λ_{c,c₀} = (B(c,c₀)² − 2Q(c)Q(c₀) − |B(c,c₀)|√(B(c,c₀)² − 4Q(c)Q(c₀)))/(2Q(c)Q(c₀)) > 0; λ_{c,c₀} depends continuously on c.
hypotheses: c ∈ C_Q.
proofSteps: On span{c, ν} (ν ∉ ℝc) Q has type (1, 1), so 4Q(ν)Q(c) − B(c, ν)² < 0, giving Q_c(ν) > −B(c,ν)²/(4Q(c)) ≥ 0; for ν = λc, Q_c = −Q(c)λ² > 0.
Minimise Q_c on the ellipsoid {Q_{c₀} = 1} by Lagrange multipliers: the multiplier satisfies Q(c)Q(c₀)(λ + 1)² = λB(c, c₀)² or equals 1, and the minimum is λ₋ = λ_{c,c₀}.
acceptance: For c = c₀: λ_{c₀,c₀} = 1.

nodes.title: Q⁺ is positive definite (Zwegers Lemma 2.6)
nodes.statement: For linearly independent c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q, Q⁺(ν) := Q(ν) + B(c₁,c₂)/(4Q(c₁)Q(c₂) − B(c₁,c₂)²)·B(c₁,ν)B(c₂,ν) is positive definite.
hypotheses: c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q linearly independent.
proofSteps: For ν ∉ span{c₁, c₂}: Q has type (2, 1) on span{c₁, c₂, ν}, so the 3 × 3 Gram determinant is negative, which rewrites to Q⁺(ν) > (Q(c₂)B(c₁,ν)² + Q(c₁)B(c₂,ν)²)/(4Q(c₁)Q(c₂) − B(c₁,c₂)²) ≥ 0.
On span{c₁, c₂} equality holds and Q⁺(ν) = 0 forces B(c₁, ν) = B(c₂, ν) = 0, i.e. ν = 0.
acceptance: Bounds the sign-difference part of ρ: |sgn B(c₁,ν) − sgn B(c₂,ν)||e^{2πiQ(ν)τ}| ≤ 2e^{−2πQ⁺(ν)y}.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Convergence of the β-series (Zwegers, proof of Prop. 2.4, (2.10))
nodes.statement: For c ∈ ℝ^r with Q(c) < 0, a, b ∈ ℝ^r, τ ∈ ℍ: Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r} sgn(B(c,ν))β(−B(c,ν)²y/Q(c))e^{2πiQ(ν)τ+2πiB(ν,b)} converges absolutely, locally uniformly in (c, τ).
proofSteps: β(x) ≤ e^{−πx} bounds the ν-term by e^{−2πQ_c(ν)y} (2.12); Q_c is positive definite (Lemma 2.5, with c or −c in C_Q), so Σ e^{−2πQ_c(ν)y} converges; local uniformity from the continuity of λ_{c,c₀}.
acceptance: Also gives continuity in c (Prop. 2.7(4)).

sources.match: The step.

nodes.title: Convergence of the sign-difference series (Zwegers, proof of Prop. 2.4, (2.11))
nodes.statement: For c₁, c₂ ∈ C̄_Q, a ∈ R(c₁) ∩ R(c₂), b ∈ ℝ^r, τ ∈ ℍ: Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r}{sgn(B(c₁,ν)) − sgn(B(c₂,ν))}e^{2πiQ(ν)τ + 2πiB(ν,b)} converges absolutely.
hypotheses: a admissible for the cusp vectors among c₁, c₂.
proofSteps: If c₁ and c₂ lie on the same positive ray, the sign difference vanishes identically. Apply Lemma 2.6 only in the remaining linearly independent interior case.
Case c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q: non-zero terms have B(c₁,ν)B(c₂,ν) ≤ 0, where Q(ν) ≥ Q⁺(ν) (Lemma 2.6), bounded by 2e^{−2πQ⁺(ν)y}.

Case c₁ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q: reduce to c₁ integral; write ν = μ + nc₂ with B(c₁,μ)/B(c₁,c₂) ∈ [0,1), sum the geometric series in n (possible since B(c₂, μ) is bounded away from 0 on a + ℤ^r by admissibility), leaving a positive definite theta series over ⟨c₁⟩^⊥_ℤ with bounded coefficients.
Cases c₁ ∈ S_Q, c₂ ∈ C_Q and c₁, c₂ ∈ S_Q: by antisymmetry and the cocycle relation with an auxiliary c₃ ∈ C_Q.
acceptance: For c₁, c₂ ∈ S_Q the resulting holomorphic series are Göttsche–Zagier's.

sources.match: The step, with its four cases.

nodes.title: Absolute convergence of ϑ^{c₁,c₂} (Zwegers Prop. 2.4)
nodes.statement: For c₁, c₂ ∈ C̄_Q and (z, τ) ∈ D(c₁) ∩ D(c₂), the series defining ϑ^{c₁,c₂}(z; τ) (and ϑ_{a,b}(τ)) converges absolutely.
hypotheses: As stated.
proofSteps: Write ρ^{c₁,c₂} as the sum of (2.7), (2.8), (2.9) (Lemma 1.7 applied to ρ^{c_i} for c_i ∈ C_Q); (2.7), (2.8) are β-series (QM.4/indefinite-theta-beta-series-convergence) and (2.9) the sign-difference series (QM.4/indefinite-theta-sign-series-convergence).
acceptance: Makes Def. 2.1 meaningful despite Q being indefinite.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Cocycle relations (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(1))
nodes.statement: ϑ^{c₁,c₂} + ϑ^{c₂,c₁} = 0 and ϑ^{c₁,c₂} + ϑ^{c₂,c₃} + ϑ^{c₃,c₁} = 0 on D(c₁) ∩ D(c₂) ∩ D(c₃).
hypotheses: c₁, c₂, c₃ ∈ C̄_Q.
proofSteps: From the corresponding identities for ρ and absolute convergence.
acceptance: Reduces cusp cases to cone cases.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Elliptic transformation (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(2))
nodes.statement: ϑ(z + λτ + μ; τ) = e^{−2πiQ(λ)τ − 2πiB(z,λ)}ϑ(z; τ) for λ ∈ ℤ^r, μ ∈ A^{−1}ℤ^r.
hypotheses: (z, τ) ∈ D(c₁) ∩ D(c₂).
proofSteps: μ: B(n, μ) ∈ ℤ for n ∈ ℤ^r; λ: replace n by n + λ (a ↦ a + λ).
acceptance: Index-type transformation of a Jacobi form of matrix index.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: ϑ(−z) = −ϑ(z) (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(3))
proofSteps: Replace n by −n; E and sgn are odd.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Continuity in (c₁, c₂) (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(4))
nodes.statement: (c₁, c₂) ↦ ϑ^{c₁,c₂}(z; τ) is continuous on C_Q × C_Q.
proofSteps: For distinct rays c₁,c₂ use a neighbourhood of the pair where the positive-definite Q⁺ comparison stays bounded below, together with the locally uniform β-series bounds. Apply continuity to the combined ρ-summand (E is continuous), since the separate sign and β pieces can jump and cancel.

For collinear c₁,c₂ choose an auxiliary c₃∈C_Q on a different ray and use the theta cocycle to reduce both terms to independent pairs. In rank one all negative vectors are on the same ray, so ρ^{c₁,c₂}=0 identically.
acceptance: Needed for the limit argument of Prop. 2.7(5).

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: The sign part tends to 0 at a cusp (Zwegers (2.17))
nodes.statement: For c₁ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q, c(t) = c₂ + tc₁ and (z, τ) ∈ D(c₂): lim_{t↓0}Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r}{sgn(B(c₂,ν)) − sgn(B(c(t),ν))}e^{2πiQ(ν)τ+2πiB(ν,b)} = 0.
hypotheses: As stated (one may take c₃ = c₁).
proofSteps: |sgn(B(c₂,ν)) − sgn(B(c(t),ν))| ≤ |sgn(B(c₁,ν)) − sgn(B(c₂,ν))| for all t > 0, a t-independent summable majorant (Case 2 of Prop. 2.4); termwise limit 0 since B(c₂, ν) ≠ 0 on a + ℤ^r.

sources.match: The majorant for (2.17).

nodes.title: The β part tends to 0 at a cusp (Zwegers (2.18))
nodes.statement: In the situation of the previous node: lim_{t↓0}Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r} sgn(B(c(t),ν))β(−B(c(t),ν)²y/Q(c(t)))e^{2πiQ(ν)τ+2πiB(ν,b)} = 0.
hypotheses: As before.
proofSteps: Split a + ℤ^r into P₁, P₂, P₃ (sign conditions on B(c₁, ν), B(c₂, ν) and B(c₁,c₂)B(c₁,ν) − 2Q(c₁)B(c₂,ν)).

Majorants independent of t: on P₁ e^{−2πQ(ν)y} (summable by Case 2); on P₂ e^{−2πQ_{c₁}(ν)y} (Lemma 2.5); on P₃ e^{−2πQ̃(ν)y} with the auxiliary form Q̃ of type (r − 1, 1) (2.20) and the Case-2 convergence for (Q̃, c̃₁, c̃₂).

The auxiliary real form Q̃ need not have integral matrix. Extend Case 2 to a real Lorentz form with integral isotropic c̃₂ and discrete B̃(c̃₂, ℤ^r): choose an integral covector in the open dual negative cone (scale a rational approximation), and take its inverse-form vector c′₁. Then B̃(c′₁, ℤ^r) is discrete and B̃(c′₁,c̃₂) is a nonzero integer. The same finite-slab decomposition along the primitive c̃₂ and the positive definite kernel-lattice Gaussian bound proves the required majorant convergence. Here B̃(c̃₂,ν)=−B(c₂,ν), so admissibility and discreteness transfer from the original integral form.
Termwise the argument −B(c(t),ν)²y/Q(c(t)) → ∞ as t ↓ 0 and β(x) → 0.
acceptance: The longest estimate of Chapter 2 (source pp. 34–38).

sources.match: The start of the three-set majorant argument for (2.18).

nodes.title: Limit to a cusp vector (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(5))
nodes.statement: Let c₁, c₃ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q, (z, τ) ∈ D(c₂), c(t) := c₂ + tc₃. Then c(t) ∈ C_Q for t > 0 and lim_{t↓0}ϑ^{c₁,c(t)}(z; τ) = ϑ^{c₁,c₂}(z; τ).
hypotheses: As stated.
proofSteps: Reduce to c₃ = c₁ by the cocycle relation; c(t) ∈ C_Q (QM.4/negative-cone API).
ϑ^{c₁,c(t)} − ϑ^{c₁,c₂} = ϑ^{c₂,c(t)}, decompose via (2.7)–(2.9) and apply (2.17), (2.18).
acceptance: Used to transfer Prop. 2.7(7) from cone vectors to cusp vectors.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: ϑ(z; τ + 1) (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(6))
nodes.statement: ϑ(z; τ + 1) = ϑ(z + ½A^{−1}A*; τ), where A* = (A₁₁, …, A_rr)^T; in particular ϑ(z; τ + 2) = ϑ(z; τ), and ϑ(z; τ + 1) = ϑ(z; τ) if A is even.
proofSteps: ρ(a; τ) depends only on Im τ; e^{2πiQ(n)} = e^{πiΣA_ll n_l²} = e^{2πiB(½A^{−1}A*, n)} since n_l² ≡ n_l mod 2.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Gaussian integrals for a positive definite matrix and τ ∈ ℍ
nodes.statement: For a positive definite symmetric M ∈ M_n(ℝ), τ ∈ ℍ and α ∈ ℂ^n: ∫_{ℝ^n} e^{πi⟨a, Ma⟩τ + 2πi⟨a, Mα⟩}da = (−iτ)^{−n/2}(det M)^{−1/2}e^{−πi⟨α, Mα⟩/τ}.
hypotheses: Principal branch of (−iτ)^{−n/2} (as the n-th power of (−iτ)^{−1/2}).
proofSteps: Change variables a = M^{−1/2}w (Jacobian (det M)^{−1/2}) to reduce to M = I; then Mathlib's GaussianFourier.integral_cexp_neg_mul_sq_norm_add on Euclidean space with b = −πiτ (Re b = πy > 0).
acceptance: n = 1, M = (1): ∫e^{πiτa² + 2πiaα}da = (−iτ)^{−1/2}e^{−πiα²/τ}.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: a ↦ ρ(a; τ)e^{2πiQ(a)τ} is essentially its own Fourier transform (Zwegers Lemma 2.8)
nodes.statement: For c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q, all α ∈ ℝ^r and τ ∈ ℍ: the function a ↦ ρ(a; τ)e^{2πiQ(a)τ + 2πiB(a,α)} is integrable (indeed a Schwartz function of a), and ∫_{ℝ^r}ρ(a; τ)e^{2πiQ(a)τ+2πiB(a,α)}da = (i/√(−det A))(−iτ)^{−r/2}ρ(α; −1/τ)e^{−2πiQ(α)/τ}.
hypotheses: c₁, c₂ in the open cone (the cusp case follows by Prop. 2.7(5)).
proofSteps: Integrability and rapid decay with all derivatives: decomposition (2.7)–(2.9) with the bounds of Lemmas 2.5, 2.6 (derivatives of E are Gaussians).
∂/∂α_l of e^{2πiQ(α)/τ}·(integral) equals −(1/τ)∫(∂ρ/∂a_l)e^{2πiQ(aτ+α)/τ}da (integration by parts), and ∂ρ/∂a_l is a combination of E′-terms (2.23).

Each E′-integral is computed by splitting ℝ^r = ℝc ⊕ c^⊥ (Q positive definite on c^⊥) and QM.4/multivariate-gaussian-integral twice. Use the Lebesgue Jacobian |det(c C)|, or choose an oriented basis C with det(c C)>0. Then (det(c C))² det A = 2Q(c)det(CᵀAC) gives the positive factor 1/√(−det A). In the generic c derivative the denominator is √(−Q(c)), not √(−Q(c₁)); see E508; the source already includes the absolute Jacobian (E509 rejected).
So the difference of both sides has zero gradient in α; both sides are odd in α, hence equal.
acceptance: The mechanism behind the modularity of the non-holomorphic theta function (Zwegers: 'the main point – and the reason for the deﬁnition of the function ρ').

sources.match: Exactly the statement (proved there for c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q).

nodes.title: Modular S-transformation of ϑ^{c₁,c₂} (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(7))
nodes.statement: Let D′(c) := {(z, τ) ∈ D(c) : (z/τ, −1/τ) ∈ D(c)} (for c ∈ S_Q: z = aτ + b with B(c, a), B(c, b) ∉ ℤ; for c ∈ C_Q: all (z, τ)). For (z, τ) ∈ D′(c₁) ∩ D′(c₂): ϑ(z/τ; −1/τ) = (i/√(−det A))(−iτ)^{r/2}Σ_{p∈A^{−1}ℤ^r/ℤ^r} e^{2πiQ(z + pτ)/τ}ϑ(z + pτ; τ).
hypotheses: Principal branches; D′(c) as corrected in sourceIssue E504.
proofSteps: Case c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q: Poisson summation over ℤ^r for the Schwartz function of Lemma 2.8 (dual lattice of ℤ^r for B is A^{−1}ℤ^r) gives (2.24) for ϑ_{a,b}; substitute ϑ_{a,b} = e^{2πiQ(a)τ+2πiB(a,b)}ϑ(aτ + b; τ).
Case c₁ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q: take lim_{t↓0} along c(t) (Prop. 2.7(5)) on both sides.
Remaining cases by the cocycle relations.
acceptance: Example 2.16: ϑ_{e/6,e/6}(−1/τ) = −iτϑ_{e/6,e/6}(τ), the weight-1 law of η².
The 'modularity theorem' of the indefinite theta function (with Prop. 2.7(6)).

sources.match: The statement (the displayed description of D′(c) is correct for c ∈ S_Q only, E504).

nodes.title: ϑ_{a,b} under shifts of a, b (Zwegers Cor. 2.9(1)–(3))

proofSteps: Reindex ν ↦ ν + λ; B(ν, μ) ≡ B(a, μ) mod ℤ for ν ∈ a + ℤ^r; ν ↦ −ν with oddness of ρ.
acceptance: Used to reduce the characteristic vectors in §4.3–4.4.

nodes.title: ϑ_{a,b}(−1/τ) (Zwegers Cor. 2.9(5))
nodes.statement: If a, b ∈ R(c₁) ∩ R(c₂) then ϑ_{a,b}(−1/τ) = (i/√(−det A))(−iτ)^{r/2}e^{2πiB(a,b)}Σ_{p∈A^{−1}ℤ^r mod ℤ^r} ϑ_{b+p,−a}(τ).

nodes.title: The group O_A^+(ℤ)
nodes.statement: O_A^+(ℝ) := {C ∈ GL_r(ℝ) : CᵀAC = A, B(Cc, c) < 0 for all c ∈ C_Q} (the index-2 subgroup of O_A(ℝ) preserving C_Q) and O_A^+(ℤ) := O_A^+(ℝ) ∩ GL_r(ℤ) (Zwegers Def. 2.10).
proofSteps: Subgroup: CᵀAC = A is preserved by products and inverses; preserving the component C_Q likewise.
det C = ±1 from CᵀAC = A (Remark 2.11).

nodes.title: An indefinite theta function equal to 2e^{πi/3}η² (Zwegers Example 2.16)
proofSteps: T- and S-transformations from Cor. 2.9: ϑ(τ + 1) = e^{πi/6}ϑ(τ), ϑ(−1/τ) = −iτϑ(τ).
The β-parts (2.7), (2.8) vanish by an O_A^+(ℤ) symmetry fixing c₁ (resp. c₂) and changing the sign of the characteristic (C = (1 0; −4 −1), resp. (−1 −4; 0 1)).

So ϑ_{a,b} is the holomorphic sign sum (2.29), a modular form of weight 1 with the multiplier of η² (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier); the quotient by η² is a holomorphic modular function on the compactified X(1), hence constant; compare the first coefficients.

nodes.title: The elliptic and modular laws (E), (M) of index m and weight k
nodes.statement: For ϕ : ℂ × ℍ → ℂ (meromorphic in z, with junk value 0 at its poles), m ∈ ℤ_{>0} and k ∈ ℤ, put ϕ̂(τ, z) := ϕ(z; τ). ϕ satisfies (E) of index m if ϕ̂|_m[λ, μ] = ϕ̂ for all (λ, μ) ∈ ℤ² (QM.1/jacobi-elliptic-slash), i.e. ϕ(z + λτ + μ; τ) = e^{−2πim(λ²τ + 2λz)}ϕ(z; τ); and (M) of weight k and index m if ϕ̂|_{k,m}γ = ϕ̂ for all γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) (QM.1/jacobi-modular-slash), i.e. ϕ(z/(cτ+d); (aτ+b)/(cτ+d)) = (cτ + d)^k e^{2πimcz²/(cτ+d)}ϕ(z; τ) (Zwegers §3.1). Jacobi forms of weight k and index m (QM.1/jacobi-form) are the holomorphic ϕ satisfying (E), (M) and a growth condition; here neither holomorphy nor growth is assumed, which is what Zwegers' Chapter 3 needs (ϕ has poles in z).
hypotheses: Two predicates on functions. The pole set of a ϕ satisfying the laws is invariant under the actions, so with the junk value 0 at poles the equalities hold everywhere.
proofSteps: Define the predicates as invariance under QM.1's two slash actions, with the arguments swapped to Zwegers' order (z; τ).
Compatibility: a Jacobi form of QM.1/jacobi-form is invariant under both slashes by definition (trivial multiplier and character).
acceptance: φ_{−2,1} := −ϑ(z; τ)²/η(τ)⁶ satisfies (E) with m = 1 and (M) with k = −2.
(E) and (M) for m, k are preserved by multiplication by modular forms of weight k′ (index unchanged).

nodes.statement: Let c ∈ C_Q ∩ ℤ^r be primitive. Then there is a finite set P₀ ⊂ a + ℤ^r with {μ ∈ a + ℤ^r : B(c,μ)/(2Q(c)) ∈ [0, 1)} = ⊔_{μ₀∈P₀}(μ₀ + ⟨c⟩^⊥_ℤ) such that Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r} sgn(B(c,ν))β(−B(c,ν)²y/Q(c))e^{2πiQ(ν)τ+2πiB(ν,b)} = −Σ_{μ₀∈P₀} R_{B(c,μ₀)/2Q(c), −B(c,b)}(−2Q(c)τ)·Σ_{ξ∈μ₀^⊥+⟨c⟩^⊥_ℤ} e^{2πiQ(ξ)τ+2πiB(ξ, b^⊥)}, where μ₀^⊥ = μ₀ − B(c,μ₀)c/(2Q(c)), b^⊥ = b − B(c,b)c/(2Q(c)) and ⟨c⟩^⊥_ℤ = {ξ ∈ ℤ^r : B(c, ξ) = 0}.
hypotheses: c integral primitive in C_Q; the inner sums are positive definite theta series of rank r − 1 (Remark 4.4).
proofSteps: Write ν = μ₀ + ξ + nc and ν = (n + B(c,μ₀)/2Q(c))c + μ₀^⊥ + ξ; Q and B split orthogonally; the n-sum is R_{B(c,μ₀)/2Q(c), −B(c,b)}(−2Q(c)τ) (note −2Q(c) > 0).

nodes.title: The seventh-order mock theta functions F₀, F₁, F₂ and the vector F₇
nodes.statement: Following Zwegers §4.3 (Hickerson's identities used as definitions): (q)_∞F₀(q) := (Σ_{r,s≥0} − Σ_{r,s<0})(−1)^{r+s}q^{3r²/2+4rs+3s²/2+r/2+s/2}, (q)_∞F₁(q) := (Σ_{r,s≥0} − Σ_{r,s<0})(−1)^{r+s}q^{3r²/2+4rs+3s²/2+5r/2+5s/2+1}, (q)_∞F₂(q) := (Σ_{r,s≥0} − Σ_{r,s<0})(−1)^{r+s}q^{3r²/2+4rs+3s²/2+3r/2+3s/2}, with (q)_∞ = ∏(1 − q^n) and q = e(τ); and F₇(τ) := (q^{−1/168}F₀(q), q^{47/168}F₂(q), q^{−25/168}F₁(q)) (fractional powers e(sτ)).
hypotheses: The identification with Ramanujan's Eulerian series (e.g. F₀(q) = Σ_{n≥0}q^{n²}/(q^{n+1}; q)_n) is Hickerson's theorem, which Zwegers takes as the definition; it is recorded as a gap, not used.
proofSteps: The double series converge absolutely for |q| < 1 (the exponent 3r²/2 + 4rs + 3s²/2 is positive on the summation cones r, s ≥ 0 and r, s < 0); (q)_∞ ≠ 0 on the unit disc (Mathlib ModularForm.eta_ne_zero), so F_j are holomorphic functions of τ ∈ ℍ.
acceptance: F₀(q) = 1 + q + q³ + q⁴ + q⁵ + 2q⁷ + q⁸ + 2q⁹ + O(q^{10}), equal to Ramanujan's Σq^{n²}/(q^{n+1}; q)_n to this order (numerically checked).
F₇ is holomorphic on ℍ and 1-periodic up to the diagonal multiplier.

proofSteps: Split ρ^{c₁,c₂} into (2.7) + (2.8) + (2.9) for each component of ϑ in H₇: the sign part (2.9) gives 2ζ₁₄η·F-component by QM.4/seventh-order-indefinite-theta-identities.

The β-parts (2.7), (2.8) are evaluated by Prop. 4.3 with P₀ = {−13e/14, −27e/14, −41e/14} and ⟨c⟩^⊥_ℤ = {(0, ξ₂)}: the unary sums Σ_{μ₂∈−13/6+ℤ}e^{3πiμ₂²τ+πiμ₂} and Σ_{μ₂∈−41/6+ℤ}(…) equal ζ₁₂^{−1}η(τ) and ζ₁₂η(τ) by Euler's pentagonal number theorem (Mathlib eulerFunction_eq_tsum_pentagonal, eulerFunction_eq_tprod), and the sum over μ₂ ∈ −27/6 + ℤ = 1/2 + ℤ vanishes (μ₂ ↔ −μ₂ with e^{πiμ₂} + e^{−πiμ₂} = 0); this gives η(τ)(ζ₁₂^{−1}R_{13/42,−1/2}(21τ) + ζ₁₂R_{41/42,−1/2}(21τ)) and similarly for the other components.

nodes.title: Radial limits at rational points and at roots of unity
nodes.statement: For a function G : ℂ → ℂ (only its values on the upper half-plane ℍ matter), a real number x and L ∈ ℂ, G has radial limit L at x, written HasRadialLimit G x L, if G(x + it/(2π)) → L as t → 0 through positive reals. With q = e^{2πiτ} and G(τ) = g(q) for a function g on the punctured unit disc, this says g(ξe^{−t}) → L as t → 0⁺ with ξ = e^{2πix}: the vertical approach to x is the radial approach to the root of unity ξ from inside the unit disc. The lower version HasRadialLimitBelow G x L means G(x − it/(2π)) → L as t → 0⁺ (functions on the lower half-plane H⁻). The value radialLimit G x is L when a radial limit exists and 0 otherwise. Pinned conventions: q = e^{2πiτ}; the approach parameter is t = 2π·Im τ; x is real (rational x is the case of interest, ξ = e^{2πix} a root of unity).
hypotheses: G is arbitrary; no continuity or boundedness hypothesis is part of the definition.
Limits are taken in 𝓝[>] 0 for t; the approach is vertical, not non-tangential.
proofSteps: Define HasRadialLimit G x L as Tendsto (t ↦ G(x + i t/(2π))) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 L), using Mathlib's Filter.Tendsto with the filter nhdsWithin 0 (Ioi 0).
Define HasRadialLimitBelow G x L as HasRadialLimit (z ↦ G(z̄)) x L, since conj(x + it/(2π)) = x − it/(2π).
Define radialLimit G x by classical choice of L when ∃ L, HasRadialLimit G x L, and 0 otherwise; uniqueness of limits in the Hausdorff space ℂ makes it well defined.
Disc form: for G(τ) = g(e^{2πiτ}), e^{2πi(x + it/(2π))} = e^{2πix}e^{−t}, so the definition is the radial limit g(ξe^{−t}) → L; this identification is the API item hasRadialLimit_iff_disc.
acceptance: The function τ ↦ e^{2πiτ} has radial limit e^{2πix} at every real x.
The function τ ↦ q/(1 − q) has no radial limit at x = 0: its modulus tends to ∞.

A radial limit and a formal evaluation are different objects: HasRadialLimit refers only to the analytic function on ℍ, never to a Habiro-ring evaluation, and the two are compared only by explicit theorems (strange identity, Lawrence–Zagier).

nodes.title: Radial asymptotic expansions at rational points
nodes.statement: For G : ℂ → ℂ, x ∈ ℝ and a formal power series a = Σ a_r t^r ∈ ℂ⟦t⟧, G has radial asymptotic expansion a at x (from above), written HasRadialExpansion G x a, if for every R ∈ ℕ, G(x + it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} a_r t^r = O(t^R) as t → 0⁺. From below: HasRadialExpansionBelow G x a :⟺ G(x − it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} a_r (−t)^r = O(t^R) for every R, so that both are expansions in the same variable 2π·Im τ. Following Bringmann–Rolen, functions f on ℍ and g on H⁻ have agreeing asymptotic expansions at x, RadialExpansionsAgree f g x, if some a satisfies HasRadialExpansion f x a and HasRadialExpansionBelow g x a. The series a is not required to converge.
hypotheses: The expansion is an asymptotic statement for every order R, in Mathlib's big-O sense along 𝓝[>] 0.
proofSteps: Define HasRadialExpansion G x a as ∀ R, (t ↦ G(x + it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} coeff r a · t^r) =O[𝓝[>] 0] (t ↦ t^R), with Asymptotics.IsBigO.
Define HasRadialExpansionBelow G x a as HasRadialExpansion (z ↦ G(z̄)) x (rescale (−1) a).
Define RadialExpansionsAgree f g x as ∃ a, HasRadialExpansion f x a ∧ HasRadialExpansionBelow g x a.
Uniqueness: if a and b are both expansions, the difference of the partial sums is O(t^R) for every R, so the coefficients agree inductively (a polynomial of degree < R that is O(t^R) at 0 is zero).
The constant term: the case R = 1 gives G(x + it/2π) − a₀ = O(t), hence a radial limit a₀.
acceptance: q^m = e^{2πimτ} has expansion e^{2πimx}·exp(−mt) = e^{2πimx} Σ_r (−m)^r t^r/r! at x.
The flat function τ ↦ e^{−2πi/τ} has expansion 0 at x = 0 although it is non-zero on ℍ: the expansion does not determine the function.
An asymptotic expansion is not a Taylor expansion of a Habiro-ring element; the two are compared only by explicit theorems (strange identity, Lawrence–Zagier Theorem 2).

nodes.title: The Hurwitz zeta function at s = 0
nodes.statement: For x ∈ (0, 1], hurwitzZeta x 0 = 1/2 − x, where x is viewed in ℝ/ℤ (so x = 1 gives hurwitzZeta 0 0 = ζ(0) = −1/2).
hypotheses: x ∈ (0, 1]; at x = 0 the formula 1/2 − x is false (the value is ζ(0) = −1/2), which is why the interval is half-open.
proofSteps: Split hurwitzZeta = hurwitzZetaEven + hurwitzZetaOdd (Mathlib's definition).
Even part: hurwitzZetaEven x 0 = −1/2 if x ≡ 0 mod 1 and 0 otherwise (HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZetaEven_apply_zero).
Odd part: the functional equation HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZetaOdd_one_sub at s = 1 gives hurwitzZetaOdd x 0 = (1/π)·sinZeta x 1.

sinZeta x 1 = Σ_{n≥1} sin(2πnx)/n = π(1/2 − x) for 0 < x < 1 (the Fourier series of the sawtooth; its value at the edge s = 1 of the half-plane of absolute convergence is obtained by continuity in s of the analytic continuation and Abel summation of the conditionally convergent series), and sinZeta 0 1 = 0.
Add the two parts: for 0 < x < 1 the value is 0 + (1/2 − x); for x = 1 it is −1/2 + 0 = 1/2 − 1.
acceptance: hurwitzZeta (1/2) 0 = 0.
hurwitzZeta 1 0 = −1/2 = ζ(0).
The pinned Mathlib proves the formula −B_{k+1}(x)/(k+1) only for k ≠ 0 (HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta_neg_nat); this lemma is the k = 0 case on (0, 1].

sources.match: The case r = 0 of (12) is this value −B₁(x) = 1/2 − x of the Hurwitz zeta function, summed against C.
The Hurwitz values ζ(−n, a) at n = 0 are the ones this lemma supplies.

nodes.title: Values of periodic L-functions at non-positive integers
nodes.statement: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ, with L(s, Φ) = ZMod.LFunction Φ s the meromorphic continuation of Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)n^{−s}. For every integer r ≥ 1, L(−r, Φ) = −(M^r/(r+1)) Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n) B_{r+1}(n/M), with B_k the Bernoulli polynomials. If moreover Σ_j Φ(j) = 0, the same formula holds for r = 0: L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M} (n/M − 1/2) Φ(n), and L(s, Φ) is entire.
hypotheses: M ≥ 1; for r = 0 the mean-zero hypothesis Σ Φ = 0 (otherwise the formula still holds but L has a pole at s = 1 that plays no role; the lemma is stated in the form the sources use).
proofSteps: By definition ZMod.LFunction Φ s = M^{−s} Σ_{j ∈ ZMod M} Φ(j) ζ(j/M, s) with ζ(a, s) the Hurwitz zeta function.
For r ≥ 1 insert HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta_neg_nat at x = j.val/M ∈ [0, 1): ζ(x, −r) = −B_{r+1}(x)/(r+1).
Reindex j ∈ {0, …, M−1} by n ∈ {1, …, M}, sending j = 0 to n = M; this is allowed because B_{r+1}(1) = B_{r+1}(0) for r + 1 ≠ 1 (bernoulliFun_eval_one).
For r = 0 use hurwitz-zeta-at-zero with the representatives x = n/M ∈ (0, 1]: L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n)(n/M − 1/2).
Entireness under Σ Φ = 0 is ZMod.differentiable_LFunction_of_sum_zero.
acceptance: For Φ = χ₁₂ (the character (12/·) on ZMod 12), L(−1, χ₁₂) = −(12/2)(B₂(1/12) − B₂(5/12) − B₂(7/12) + B₂(11/12)) = −2, consistent with T₀ = (−1)^{0−1}L(−1, χ)/2 = 1 in Zagier's formula (6).
For even Φ with Σ Φ = 0 the r = 0 formula gives L(0, Φ) = −Φ(0)/2 (the terms n and M − n cancel), in accordance with the Lawrence–Zagier Remark.
For the constant function Φ = 1 on ZMod 1 the r ≥ 1 values are ζ(−r) = −B_{r+1}/(r+1).

sources.match: Formula (12) is this lemma; the mean-zero hypothesis is the Proposition's.

nodes.title: Asymptotics of Σ f((m + a)t) (Euler–Maclaurin)
nodes.statement: Let f : [0, ∞) → ℂ be C^∞ with every derivative of rapid decay at ∞, let b_n = f^{(n)}(0)/n! and I_f = ∫_0^∞ f(x)dx, and let a ∈ (0, 1]. Then, as t → 0⁺, Σ_{m≥0} f((m + a)t) = I_f/t − Σ_{n<N} b_n (B_{n+1}(a)/(n+1)) t^n + O(t^N) for every N. For a = 1 this is Zagier's Proposition 3: Σ_{m≥1} f(mt) ∼ I_f/t + Σ_n b_n (B_{n+1}/(n+1))(−t)^n. Consequently, for Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ Φ = 0: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n) f(nt) ∼ Σ_n b_n L(−n, Φ) t^n.
hypotheses: f smooth on [0, ∞) with f^{(k)}(x) = O(x^{−2}) as x → ∞ for every k (rapid decay suffices).
proofSteps: Apply shifted Euler–Maclaurin on the half-line using the periodised Bernoulli functions with jumps at m+a. Repeated integration by parts, splitting at these lattice points, gives Σ_{m≥0}f((m+a)t)=I_f/t−Σ_{r=1}^{J}B_r(a)f^{(r−1)}(0)t^{r−1}/r! plus a remainder bounded by sup|B̄_J|·t^{J−1}∫₀∞|f^{(J)}|/J!. Use the Bernoulli shift and derivative identities to obtain the boundary coefficients at 0.

For the claimed remainder O(t^N), choose J≥N+1, rather than J=N. Rapid decay makes every derivative integrable and kills the boundary terms at infinity. Absorb the retained terms of degree at least N into O(t^N).

For a=1 use B_r(1)=(−1)^r B_r(0) to match Zagier Proposition3. For the periodic corollary split into the M residue classes n=M m+a, a=1,…,M, at scale Mt; the I_f/(Mt) contributions cancel because ΣΦ=0, and periodic-l-value-bernoulli identifies the remaining coefficients.
acceptance: For f(x) = e^{−λx} and a = 1 the expansion is 1/(λt) + Σ B_{n+1}(λt)^n/(n+1)!, the expansion of 1/(e^{λt} − 1).

For f(x) = e^{−x} and general a the expansion must reproduce e^{−at}/(1 − e^{−t}) = 1/t + Σ_n (−1)^{n+1}B_{n+1}(a)t^n/(n+1)!; this fixes the sign of the Bernoulli term (the printed eq. (44) of the source has the opposite sign; see the source issues).
With a = 1 the lemma reduces to Zagier's Proposition 3 because B_{n+1}(1) = (−1)^{n+1}B_{n+1}.

sources.match: The a = 1 case; its proof by Euler–Maclaurin (printed pp. 12–13) is the proof of this node.
The shifted and periodic forms; the node uses the corrected sign of the Bernoulli term in (44).

nodes.title: Expansion of Σ Φ(n)e^{−nt} for mean-zero periodic Φ
nodes.statement: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0. Then Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−nt} = Σ_{r≥0} L(−r, Φ)(−t)^r/r! as a convergent power series for 0 < t < 2π/M; in particular the left side has the asymptotic expansion Σ L(−r, Φ)(−t)^r/r! as t → 0⁺ and the limit L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M}(n/M − 1/2)Φ(n).
hypotheses: Σ Φ = 0 (mean value zero); without it the sum has a pole (ΣΦ/M)/t at t = 0.
proofSteps: Sum the geometric series: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−nt} = Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n)e^{−nt}/(1 − e^{−Mt}).

For complex t the quotient t·Σ_{n=1}^M Φ(n)e^{−nt}/(1−e^{−Mt}) has a removable value at 0 and is holomorphic for |t|<2π/M; the denominator has no further zeros there. The mean-zero numerator makes the original quotient removable as well. Compare Taylor coefficients after clearing the denominator with Polynomial.bernoulli_generating_function, which is a formal identity; coefficient recurrence uniqueness identifies them. Analytic Taylor convergence on this disc supplies the asserted HasSum. Do not evaluate a formal series in ℂ merely using PowerSeries.eval₂.
The r = −1 term is Σ_n Φ(n)/(Mt), which vanishes by the mean-zero hypothesis.
The coefficient of (−t)^r/r! is −M^r/(r+1) Σ_n Φ(n)B_{r+1}(n/M) = L(−r, Φ) by periodic-l-value-bernoulli.
acceptance: For Φ = χ₁₂ the sum is Σ χ₁₂(m)e^{−mt} = sinh(2t)/cosh(3t) = 2t − (23/3)t³ + …, whose coefficients are the Glaisher numbers (Zagier's (5)).
The Lawrence–Zagier Remark: for odd Φ the expansion is even in t, for even Φ with Φ(0)=0 it is odd; in general the even-Φ exponential sum plus Φ(0)/2 is odd.

sources.locator: §3, Proposition and its proof, printed pp. 98–99
sources.match: The first expansion of the Proposition and the geometric-series proof this node records.

nodes.title: Asymptotic expansion of Σ n^ν Φ(n)e^{−n²t} for mean-zero periodic Φ
nodes.statement: Let M ≥ 1, Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0, and ν ∈ {0, 1}. As t → 0⁺, Σ_{n≥1} n^ν Φ(n) e^{−n²t} ∼ Σ_{r≥0} L(−2r − ν, Φ)(−t)^r/r!. In particular Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−n²t} → L(0, Φ) and Σ_{n≥1} nΦ(n)e^{−n²t} → L(−1, Φ).
hypotheses: Σ Φ = 0.
ν ∈ {0, 1} (the two cases the sources use: weight-1/2 and weight-3/2 unary theta series).
proofSteps: Apply euler-maclaurin-asymptotic to f(x) = x^ν e^{−x²} (smooth, all derivatives of rapid decay) at scale s = √t: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)f(ns) ∼ Σ_n b_n L(−n, Φ) s^n, the I_f/s term cancelling since Σ Φ = 0.
For ν = 0 only even n contribute, b_{2r} = (−1)^r/r!, and s^{2r} = t^r.
For ν = 1, Σ nΦ(n)e^{−n²t} = s^{−1}Σ Φ(n)f(ns), only odd n = 2r + 1 contribute with b_{2r+1} = (−1)^r/r!, giving Σ L(−2r−1, Φ)(−t)^r/r!.
acceptance: For Φ = χ₁₂ and ν = 1, Σ mχ₁₂(m)e^{−m²t/24} ∼ Σ L(−2n−1, χ₁₂)(−t/24)^n/n! (Zagier (25)), whose leading term is L(−1, χ₁₂) = −2.
For even Φ and ν = 0 all coefficients with r > 0 vanish (Lawrence–Zagier Remark: the sum is then O(e^{−A/t}) minus ½Φ(0)).

sources.match: The ν = 0 case and the route (Euler–Maclaurin) this node follows.
The ν = 1 case for Φ = χ₁₂ (and, in Theorem 6, its twists).

nodes.title: The renormalised sum of a mean-zero periodic function
nodes.statement: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0. The three quantities lim_{t→0⁺} Σ_{n≥1}Φ(n)e^{−nt}, lim_{t→0⁺} Σ_{n≥1}Φ(n)e^{−n²t} and L(0, Φ) are equal, and their common value, the renormalised sum Σ*_{n≥1} Φ(n), is −Σ_{n=1}^{M}(n/M − 1/2)Φ(n).
hypotheses: Σ Φ = 0.
proofSteps: The first limit is the constant term of periodic-exponential-sum-asymptotic.
The second is the constant term of periodic-gaussian-sum-asymptotic with ν = 0.
Both equal L(0, Φ), which periodic-l-value-bernoulli evaluates.
acceptance: For Φ(n) = χ₊(n)ξ^{(n²−1)/120} (Lawrence–Zagier, Theorem 1) the renormalised sum is the radial limit A(ξ).
For M = 2, Φ(0) = −1, Φ(1) = 1: the renormalised sum of 1 − 1 + 1 − … is 1/2 (Abel sum).

nodes.title: Quantum modular forms (Zagier's canonical definition)
nodes.statement: Fix a subgroup Γ ≤ SL₂(ℤ), a weight k ∈ ℝ and a multiplier ε : SL₂(ℤ) → ℂ. For γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) and x ∈ ℝ with cx + d ≠ 0, the boundary factor j_k(γ, x) is the limit as y → 0⁺ of the principal power (c(x − iy) + d)^{−k}: it equals |cx + d|^{−k} if cx + d > 0, |cx + d|^{−k}e^{iπk} if cx + d < 0 and c > 0, and |cx + d|^{−k}e^{−iπk} if cx + d < 0 and c ≤ 0 (it is 0 by convention when cx + d = 0). For f : ℚ → ℂ the quantum slash is (f|_{k,ε}γ)(x) = ε(γ)·j_k(γ, x)·f(γx) and the period function is h_γ = f − f|_{k,ε}γ on {x ∈ ℚ : cx + d ≠ 0}. The function f is a quantum modular form of weight k on Γ with multiplier ε if for every γ ∈ Γ there are a finite set S_γ ⊂ ℝ and a function H_γ : ℝ → ℂ, real-analytic on ℝ ∖ S_γ, with H_γ(x) = h_γ(x) for every x ∈ ℚ ∖ S_γ with cx + d ≠ 0. This is Zagier's canonical (weak) definition with P¹(ℝ) replaced by ℝ; the boundary factor is the one of the lower half-plane, which is the branch in which the half-integral weight examples (Eichler integrals of theta series, Kontsevich's function) have constant multipliers.
hypotheses: Γ is any subgroup of SL₂(ℤ); in all examples it has finite index.
ε is an arbitrary function on SL₂(ℤ); no cocycle condition is imposed in the definition (it enters only through quantum-modular-cocycle).
Real-analytic means AnalyticOnNhd ℝ H_γ on the open set ℝ ∖ S_γ, for H_γ : ℝ → ℂ.
proofSteps: Define boundaryFactor k γ x by the three cases above; prove it equals lim_{y→0⁺} (c(x − iy) + d)^{−k} for Mathlib's principal cpow (API boundaryFactor_eq_limit).
Define quantumSlash k ε γ f x := ε γ * boundaryFactor k γ x * f (γ • x), where γ acts on ℚ by Möbius transformation (0 off the domain).
Define quantumPeriodFunction k ε γ f := f − quantumSlash k ε γ f.
Define IsQuantumModularForm Γ k ε f := ∀ γ ∈ Γ, ∃ S : Finset ℝ, ∃ H : ℝ → ℂ, AnalyticOnNhd ℝ H (↑S)ᶜ ∧ ∀ x : ℚ, (x:ℝ) ∉ S → c x + d ≠ 0 → H x = quantumPeriodFunction k ε γ f x.
The quantum modular forms of fixed (Γ, k, ε) form a ℂ-subspace: sums and scalar multiples of period functions are period functions, with S the union of the exceptional sets.
acceptance: The restriction to ℚ of a real-analytic function is a quantum modular form of every weight k ∈ ℤ on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1 (its period functions are real-analytic off {−d/c}); the notion is deliberately weak.

The indicator function of ℤ on ℚ is not a quantum modular form of weight 0 on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1: its S-period function is −1 at the points 1/m, which accumulate only at 0, and 0 at the other rationals near them.

Kontsevich's φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}) is one of weight 3/2 on SL₂(ℤ) with ε(T) = e^{−2πi/24}, ε(S) = e^{2πi/8} (kontsevich-quantum-modular). Its extension to all SL₂(ℤ) includes the negative-real-cut sign correction recorded in QM.5/kontsevich-quantum-modular.

uses.how: each example is a function on ℚ whose period functions are real-analytic off finitely many points
Eichler integrals of half-integral weight cusp forms are quantum modular forms of weight 2 − k
Kontsevich's φ is quantum modular of weight 3/2 with an η-type multiplier
the WRT values of Σ(2,3,5) are quantum modular of weight 1/2

Imports Zagier's canonical weak definition as adapted in this node (ℝ in place of P¹(ℝ), with a multiplier ε) and its lower-boundary slash convention. Knot modularity is a separate theorem or conjecture; a discontinuous knot cocycle does not satisfy this definition merely by being called quantum modular (Zagier, Quantum modular forms, Example 5, p. 12).

nodes.title: The cocycle relation and reduction to generators
nodes.statement: Let k ∈ ℝ and ε : SL₂(ℤ) → ℂ, and suppose ε(1)=1 and the factor J(γ, x) := ε(γ)j_k(γ, x) satisfies J(γ₁γ₂, x) = J(γ₁, γ₂x)J(γ₂, x) for all γ₁, γ₂ ∈ Γ and all x ∈ ℚ outside the finitely many poles involved. Then for f : ℚ → ℂ the period functions satisfy h_{γ₁γ₂} = h_{γ₁}|_{k,ε}γ₂ + h_{γ₂} and h_{γ⁻¹} = −h_γ|_{k,ε}γ⁻¹ (off finitely many points). Consequently, if Γ is generated by a set G and the condition of quantum-modular-form holds for every γ ∈ G, then f is a quantum modular form on Γ.
hypotheses: J satisfies the cocycle condition on Γ (a multiplier system for the lower boundary branch).

Normalise ε(1)=1. Together with the cocycle this implies that J(γ,x) and ε(γ) are nonzero on their domains. Without the normalisation the identically zero factor satisfies the printed cocycle but invalidates the inverse relation and generator reduction (take Γ trivial and the empty generating set).
proofSteps: Expand h_{γ₁γ₂}(x) = f(x) − J(γ₁γ₂, x)f(γ₁γ₂x) and insert J(γ₁γ₂, x) = J(γ₁, γ₂x)J(γ₂, x): the difference from h_{γ₂}(x) is J(γ₂, x)(f(γ₂x) − J(γ₁, γ₂x)f(γ₁γ₂x)) = (h_{γ₁}|γ₂)(x).

The slash of a function real-analytic off a finite set S by γ₂ is real-analytic off γ₂⁻¹(S) ∪ {γ₂⁻¹∞}: Möbius maps and the boundary factor are real-analytic off the pole, where the branch of j_k is locally constant.
Apply to γ₁ = γ, γ₂ = γ⁻¹ for inverses (h_1 = 0 when J(1, x) = 1), and induct on word length in G ∪ G⁻¹.
acceptance: For k ∈ ℤ and ε a character the cocycle condition is automatic.
For Kontsevich's function the check reduces to the two generators T and S of SL₂(ℤ) (Zagier, Topology 40, §6).

nodes.title: Holomorphic Eichler integrals of q-series of real weight
nodes.statement: Let w ∈ ℝ, N ≥ 1 and a : ℕ → ℂ with polynomial growth (|a(n)| ≤ Cn^A). For the q-series f(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} a(n)e^{2πinτ/N} (holomorphic on ℍ, no constant term), the Eichler integral of weight w is f̃(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} (n/N)^{1−w} a(n) e^{2πinτ/N} (τ ∈ ℍ), where (n/N)^{1−w} is the positive real power. Writing D = (2πi)^{−1}d/dτ, one has D f̃_w = f̃_{w−1} and f̃_1 = f, so for integer w = k ≥ 1, D^{k−1} f̃ = f: f̃ is the normalised (k − 1)-fold primitive with no constant term. For a cusp form f = Σ a(n)qⁿ of integral weight k on SL₂(ℤ) this is Σ a(n)n^{1−k}qⁿ, the Eichler integral of Tau Ceti's modular symbols layer; for half-integral w it is the formal Eichler integral of Lawrence–Zagier and Bringmann–Rolen. The function f̃ is an analytic object on ℍ; its radial limits and asymptotic expansions at rational points are separate objects (radial-limit, radial-asymptotic-expansion) and are compared with formal evaluations only by explicit theorems.
hypotheses: a has polynomial growth, so the series converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℍ.
Exponents are n/N ∈ (1/N)ℤ_{>0}; the unary theta series of the sources are the case a supported on squares.
proofSteps: Define eichlerIntegral w N a τ := Σ' n ≥ 1, (n/N : ℝ)^(1−w) • a n • exp(2πi n τ/N).

Convergence: |(n/N)^{1−w}a(n)e^{2πinτ/N}| ≤ C′n^{A+|1−w|}e^{−2πn Im τ/N}, summable locally uniformly in τ ∈ ℍ; holomorphy by the Weierstrass M-test (Mathlib's locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions).
Termwise differentiation: D e^{2πinτ/N} = (n/N)e^{2πinτ/N}, giving D f̃_w = f̃_{w−1}.

Unary theta normalisation: for a(m) = n^ν C(n) when m = n² and 0 otherwise (ν ∈ {0,1}), (n²/N)^{1−w} with w = ν + 1/2 equals N^{ν−1/2}n^{1−2ν}, so f̃ = N^{ν−1/2}Σ n^{1−ν}C(n)q^{n²/N}; the sources drop the scalar N^{ν−1/2}.
acceptance: For Δ (w = 12, N = 1) the coefficient of q² in Δ̃ is τ(2)/2^{11} = −24/2048 = −3/256.
For η (w = 1/2, N = 24, a(n²) = χ₁₂(n)) one gets f̃ = 24^{−1/2}Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{n²/24}; Zagier's η̃ is √24 f̃.
f̃ tends to 0 as Im τ → ∞ (no constant term): the Eichler integral is not the formal antiderivative with a constant.

nodes.title: The non-holomorphic Eichler integral on the lower half-plane
nodes.statement: Let k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ and f = Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)qⁿ ∈ S_k(N) a cusp form of half-integral weight on Γ₀(N) (Shimura's multiplier). For τ ∈ H⁻ = {Im τ < 0} define f*(τ) = ((−2πi)^{k−1}/Γ(k − 1)) ∫_{τ̄}^{i∞} f(w)(w − τ)^{k−2} dw, the path running in ℍ from τ̄ to i∞ and (w − τ)^{k−2} the principal branch (w − τ ∈ ℍ). Termwise, f*(τ) = Γ(k − 1)^{−1}Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)n^{1−k}e^{2πinτ}Γ(k − 1, 4πn|Im τ|), with Γ(s, x) = ∫_x^∞ t^{s−1}e^{−t}dt the upper incomplete gamma function. Unlike f̃, f* is real-analytic, not holomorphic, and it has a simple transformation law (nonholomorphic-eichler-transformation).
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N) with k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ (supplied by MetaplecticAutomorphicForms:MP.7).
proofSteps: Convergence: f decays exponentially at i∞, and on the vertical path w = τ̄ + iy the factor |(w − τ)^{k−2}| ≤ (2|Im τ| + y)^{k−2}·e^{π|k−2|} is bounded.
Path independence in ℍ: the integrand is holomorphic in w on ℍ (w − τ ∈ ℍ never vanishes), so Cauchy's theorem for rectangles moves the path.

Termwise integration: ∫_{τ̄}^{i∞} e^{2πinw}(w − τ)^{k−2}dw = i^{k−1}(2πn)^{1−k}e^{2πinτ}Γ(k − 1, 4πn|v|) by the substitution w = τ + iu/(2πn) (BR p. 8), the constants combining because ((−2πi)·i)^{k−1}(2π)^{1−k} = 1 on the principal branches.

Real-analyticity requires normal holomorphic extension in independent variables τ and τ̄ near each point of H⁻. On a small complex polydisc avoiding the path and branch cut, the exponentially decaying q-coefficients dominate the incomplete-gamma terms and every derivative. The extended series converges normally there. Locally uniform convergence of real-analytic terms alone would not suffice.
acceptance: For f = η(24τ) (k = 1/2, N = 576, character χ₁₂) the construction is Zagier's η* up to the scalar of eichler-integral.

For k=3/2 and f=Θ₊(120τ), change variables to the period-120 theta function. To compare the unscaled Θ₊, divide its weight-3/2 Eichler integral by √120. The resulting integral coefficient is (60i)^{−1/2}; the printed LZ coefficient in (17) requires correction E626.
f* is real-analytic but not holomorphic: its τ̄-dependence is through the lower limit, so ∂f*/∂τ̄ = −c_k f(τ̄)(τ̄ − τ)^{k−2}, which is not identically zero.

uses.how: f* carries the transformation law and shares the asymptotic expansion of f̃ at every rational point
Θ*± agree with Θ̃± to infinite order at rationals and are nearly modular of weight 1/2 in H⁻

nodes.title: The period integral r_α of a half-integral weight cusp form
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) as in nonholomorphic-eichler-integral and a cusp α ∈ ℚ, define r_{f,α}(z) = ((−2πi)^{k−1}/Γ(k − 1)) ∫_α^{i∞} f(w)(w − z)^{k−2}dw for z ∈ H⁻ (principal branch, w − z ∈ ℍ), the path running in ℍ from α to i∞. It extends from H⁻ to a real-analytic function on ℝ ∖ {α} (and holomorphically to ℂ minus any path from α to i∞), and it is the half-integral weight analogue of the period polynomial: in integral weight k ≥ 2 the same integral is a polynomial of degree ≤ k − 2.
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ; α ∈ ℚ.
proofSteps: Convergence at α: f(w) decays faster than any power of Im(w) as w → α inside a Stolz angle (α is a cusp and f is cuspidal there), and |(w − z)^{k−2}| is bounded near α for z ∉ {α}.

Holomorphic continuation: for a path L from α to i∞ in ℍ, the integral defines a holomorphic function of z ∈ ℂ ∖ L (the integrand is holomorphic in z off L); choosing L to leave α vertically and deforming it gives the continuation across ℝ ∖ {α}.
Real-analyticity on ℝ ∖ {α} follows by restricting the holomorphic continuation.
acceptance: For integral weight k≥2 this is a polynomial of degree≤k−2. In half-integral weight the kernel is not polynomial; do not claim that every period function is nonpolynomial, since f=0 gives the zero polynomial.
Lawrence–Zagier's r±_α of (16) is this construction for Θ±, up to their factor √(2i/15).

nodes.title: Transformation law of the non-holomorphic Eichler integral (Bringmann–Rolen (2.4))
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) (k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ, trivial character), γ = (a b; c d) ∈ Γ₀(N) and τ ∈ H⁻: f*(τ) − χ₋₄(d)·(f*|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = r_{f,−d/c}(τ), where (g|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = ε_d^{2(2−k)}(c/d)(cτ + d)^{k−2}g(γτ) is Shimura's slash with the principal branch of (cτ + d)^{k−2} on H⁻, ε_d ∈ {1, i} and χ₋₄ = (−4/·).
hypotheses: γ ∈ Γ₀(N); c ≠ 0 (for c = 0 the right side is read as 0 and the statement is the periodicity of f*).
proofSteps: Write f*(γτ) as the integral from γτ̄ to i∞ and substitute w = γu: u runs from τ̄ to γ⁻¹(i∞) = −d/c, dw = du/(cu + d)².
Use the modularity f(γu) = ε_d^{−2k}(c/d)(cu + d)^k f(u) (Shimura's multiplier, supplied by MP.7) and w − γτ = (u − τ)/((cu + d)(cτ + d)).

Branch bookkeeping: for c > 0, cu + d ∈ ℍ and cτ + d ∈ H⁻, so the arguments add inside (−π, π) and ((cu + d)(cτ + d))^{2−k} splits; arg(u − τ) − arg((cu + d)(cτ + d)) = arg(w − γτ) because both sides lie in (0, π); the case c < 0 is symmetric.
This gives (f*|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = ε_d^{4−4k}·c_k∫_{τ̄}^{−d/c} f(u)(u − τ)^{k−2}du, and ε_d^{4−4k} = ε_d^{−2} = χ₋₄(d) for k ∈ ½ + ℤ.
Subtract from f*(τ) = c_k∫_{τ̄}^{i∞}: the difference is c_k∫_{−d/c}^{i∞} = r_{f,−d/c}(τ).
acceptance: For γ = T = (1 1; 0 1): χ₋₄(1) = 1 and the statement is f*(τ + 1) = f*(τ).
The right side is independent of τ̄ and extends real-analytically across ℝ ∖ {−d/c}: this is what makes f̃ quantum modular.

sources.match: Equation (2.4), stated without proof (‘We easily compute’); the node supplies the computation.

nodes.title: Non-tangential boundary values of f* at cusps
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) as above and x ∈ ℚ, f*(τ) converges as τ → x within any Stolz angle {τ ∈ H⁻ : |Re τ − x| ≤ C|Im τ|}, and the limit equals the radial limit from below of f* at x.
hypotheses: f cuspidal at every cusp; k∈½+ℕ₀. This does not imply k−2<0.
proofSteps: Split f*(τ) = c_k∫_{τ̄}^{x} + c_k∫_{x}^{i∞}, paths in ℍ, the second taken vertically from x.

For the vertical ray w=x+iv and τ in a fixed small Stolz neighbourhood, |w−τ|≥v and |w−τ|≤v+C₀. Bound the kernel by e^{π|k−2|}v^{min(k−2,0)}(v+C₀)^{max(k−2,0)}. Cuspidal decay at x and at infinity makes this integrable after multiplication by |f(w)|, for every allowed k. Dominated convergence supplies the boundary limit.

Along the segment from τ̄ to x in the Stolz angle, |f(w)|≤C exp(−c/|w−x|). Also |w−τ| is bounded above and below by positive constant multiples of |Im τ|. Thus the integral is O(exp(−c′/|Im τ|)|Im τ|^{k−1})→0, for every k.
Hence the limit exists within the Stolz angle and equals c_k∫_x^{i∞}f(w)(w − x)^{k−2}dw, which is also the vertical limit.
acceptance: The image under γ ∈ Γ₀(N) of the vertical ray below x approaches γx tangentially to the vertical (γ(x − iy) − γx = −iy/(cx + d)² + O(y²)), so it lies eventually in every Stolz angle at γx; this is the use in half-integral-eichler-quantum-modular.
The statement fails for tangential approach along a horocycle, which the sources never need.

sources.match: The passage from (2.4) on H⁻ to values at rationals, which uses the limit of f*(γτ) along a non-vertical curve; this node supplies it (see the source issues).

nodes.title: Twisted L-functions of half-integral weight cusp forms (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 2.2)
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ, and d/c ∈ ℚ in lowest terms. The twisted L-function L_f(ζ_c^d; s) = Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)ζ_c^{dn}n^{−s} (Re s ≫ 0, ζ_c^d = e^{2πid/c}) extends to an entire function of s, and L_f(ζ_c^d; −m) = 0 for every m ∈ ℕ₀.
hypotheses: f cuspidal; the twisted series converges absolutely for Re s > k/2 + 1 by the Hecke bound a_f(n) = O(n^{k/2}).
proofSteps: f_{d/c}(τ) := Σ a_f(n)ζ_c^{dn}qⁿ = f(τ + d/c) is modular of weight k on the conjugate group, and lies in S_k(Γ₁(Nc²)) (conjugation by (1 d/c; 0 1)).
Decompose S_k(Γ₁(Nc²)) = ⊕_χ S_k(Nc², χ) (character decomposition, supplied by MetaplecticAutomorphicForms:MP.7), so it suffices to treat g ∈ S_k(M, χ), 4 | M.
Hecke's integral: Λ_g(s) = ∫_0^∞ g(iv/√M)v^{s−1}dv = (√M/2π)^sΓ(s)L_g(s) (mellin of the q-expansion, Mathlib's mellin and Complex.Gamma).

Split at v = 1, substitute v ↦ 1/v in ∫_0^1 and apply the Fricke involution g|_kW_M ∈ S_k(M, χ(M/·)) (MP.7): Λ_g(s) = ∫_1^∞ (g|W_M)(iv/√M)v^{k−s−1}dv + ∫_1^∞ g(iv/√M)v^{s−1}dv, entire because both integrands decay exponentially.
L_g(s) = (2π/√M)^sΛ_g(s)/Γ(s) is entire since 1/Γ is entire, and vanishes at s = −m because 1/Γ(−m) = 0 while Λ_g(−m) is finite.
acceptance: The values L_f(ζ; −m) vanish, while the Taylor coefficients of f̃ at d/c are the values at k − 1 − n, which for k ∈ ½ + ℤ are half-integers and in general non-zero.
The vanishing at non-positive integers is what makes f̃ and f* have the same expansion (the odd powers of √t in f* drop out).

sources.match: The cited statement supplies the target, and its proof on pp.6–7 gives the indicated argument.

nodes.title: Exponential decay of Γ on vertical lines (Stirling's estimate)
nodes.statement: For every compact interval [x₁, x₂] ⊂ ℝ there is C such that |Γ(x + iy)| ≤ C|y|^{x−1/2}e^{−π|y|/2} for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and |y| ≥ 1; more precisely |Γ(x + iy)| = √(2π)|y|^{x−1/2}e^{−π|y|/2}(1 + O(1/|y|)) uniformly for x in compact sets.
hypotheses: x in a fixed compact interval; |y| ≥ 1 (away from the poles on the real axis).
proofSteps: Base cases from the reflection formula (Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub): |Γ(iy)|² = π/(|y| sinh π|y|) and |Γ(1/2 + iy)|² = π/cosh(πy).
Recurrence Γ(s + 1) = sΓ(s) (Complex.Gamma_add_one) shifts x by integers, multiplying by |s| ≍ |y|.

A uniform two-sided complex Stirling estimate on finite vertical strips gives the asserted leading constant and relative O(1/|y|) error. DLMF 5.11.9 states the modulus asymptotic and 5.11(ii) records remainder bounds, but the exact complex-parameter proof is not supplied by the pinned baseline. PhragmenLindelof.vertical_strip alone provides an upper bound and cannot establish this asymptotic or the reciprocal-gamma lower bound; this remains the quantitative Stirling gap.
acceptance: The pinned Mathlib has Complex.Gamma, its recurrence and reflection formula but no Stirling estimate in vertical strips.

sources.match: The estimate (3.2), quoted from DLMF 5.11.9.

nodes.title: Polynomial growth of twisted L-functions in vertical strips (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 2.3)
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) and d/c ∈ ℚ as in twisted-cusp-form-l-function, and every compact interval [x₁, x₂], there are C, A with |L_f(ζ_c^d; x + it)| ≤ C(1 + |t|)^A for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and t ∈ ℝ.
hypotheses: As in twisted-cusp-form-l-function.
proofSteps: Right of absolute convergence (x ≥ k/2 + 2) the Dirichlet series is bounded.

Left of the critical strip use the functional equation Λ_g(s) = Λ_{g|W}(k − s) of each nebentypus component and gamma-vertical-decay: L_g(s) = (2π/√M)^{2s−k}Γ(k − s)/Γ(s)·L_{g|W}(k − s), and |Γ(k − s)/Γ(s)| grows polynomially in |t|. Use the two-sided asymptotic, in particular an eventual positive lower bound for |Γ(s)| after normalization. An upper bound alone cannot bound the quotient.

In between, Λ_g is bounded in vertical strips (the integral representation), so L_g(s) = Λ_g(s)(2π/√M)^s/Γ(s) is at most e^{π|t|/2}|t|^B; Phragmén–Lindelöf (PhragmenLindelof.vertical_strip) applied to L_g·(s + B)^{−A}, choosing real B > −x₁ + 1 so that the normalizing denominator has no zero in the closed strip interpolates the polynomial bounds on the two edges.
acceptance: The lemma is exactly what makes Γ(s)L_f(ζ; k − 1 + s) decay rapidly in vertical strips, the hypothesis of mellin-asymptotic-transfer.
The source states the lemma and omits the proof as standard (see the source issues).

sources.match: Supplies the statement; the packet explicitly records uniformity in x, as needed in the proof of Proposition2.1.

nodes.title: Asymptotic expansions from poles of Mellin transforms (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 3.1)
nodes.statement: Let F : (0, ∞) → ℂ be continuous with Mellin transform M(F)(s) = ∫_0^∞ F(x)x^{s−1}dx converging for Re s > α. Suppose M(F) continues meromorphically to a neighbourhood of Re s ≥ β (β < α) with finitely many poles a₀, …, a_M in Re s > β, all simple with residues α₀, …, α_M, is analytic on the line Re s = β, and satisfies M(F)(s) = O(|s|^{−r}) as |Im s| → ∞ in every finite vertical strip β ≤ Re s ≤ c for some r > 1. Then F(x) = Σ_j α_j x^{−a_j} + O(x^{−β}) as x → 0⁺. If the hypotheses hold for every β, F has the asymptotic expansion Σ_j α_j x^{−a_j} (all orders).
hypotheses: F continuous; absolutely convergent Mellin integral on some right half-plane; uniform O(|Im s|^{−r}), r>1, on each finite contour strip β≤Re s≤c, and integrability on the boundary line. No uniform bound as Re s→+∞ is required.
proofSteps: Mellin inversion on the line Re s = c > α: F(x) = (2πi)^{−1}∫_{c−i∞}^{c+i∞} M(F)(s)x^{−s}ds (mellinInv_mellin_eq, using the decay for vertical integrability).

Move the line to Re s = β: integrate over rectangles [β, c] × [−T, T] (Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_differentiableOn after subtracting the principal parts α_j/(s − a_j)), let T → ∞ using the O(|s|^{−r}) decay on the horizontal sides.
The residues contribute α_j x^{−a_j}; the remaining integral on Re s = β is bounded by x^{−β}∫|M(F)(β + it)|dt = O(x^{−β}).
acceptance: For F(x) = e^{−x}, M(F) = Γ(s) with residues (−1)^n/n! at −n: the lemma recovers e^{−x} = Σ (−x)^n/n! to every order.
Without the decay hypothesis the conclusion fails: the Mellin transform of a function with an oscillating term like sin(1/x) has the same poles but no such expansion.

sources.match: The statement of Lemma 3.1, quoted from Flajolet–Gourdon–Dumas; the proof steps are the standard contour shift (the source gives none).
The correspondence between poles of the Mellin transform and terms of the asymptotic expansion.

nodes.title: Radial expansion of f̃ at rational points (Bringmann–Rolen (3.1)–(3.3))
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) (k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ) and d/c ∈ ℚ: f̃(d/c + it/(2π)) ∼ Σ_{n≥0} ((−1)^n/n!)L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1 − n)t^n as t → 0⁺. In particular f̃ has radial limit L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1) at d/c.
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N).
proofSteps: Termwise Mellin transform: M(t ↦ f̃(d/c + it/2π))(s) = Σ n^{1−k}a_f(n)ζ^{nd}∫_0^∞ e^{−nt}t^{s−1}dt = Γ(s)L_f(ζ; k − 1 + s) for Re s ≫ 0.
By twisted-cusp-form-l-function the right side is meromorphic on ℂ with poles only at s = −n (from Γ), simple, residue (−1)^n/n!·L_f(ζ; k − 1 − n).
By twisted-l-function-vertical-growth and gamma-vertical-decay it decays faster than any power of |s| in every vertical strip.
Apply mellin-asymptotic-transfer for every β.
acceptance: For f = η(24τ) this recovers Zagier's expansion of H(ξe^{−t}) in Theorem 6 (after the normalisations of eichler-integral).
The constant term L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1) is Bringmann–Rolen's Q_f(d/c).

nodes.title: Poles and residues of the Mellin transform of e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t) (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 3.2 core)
nodes.statement: Let k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀ and G_k(s) = M(t ↦ e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t))(s). For Re s > 0 and Re(k − 1 + s) > 0, G_k(s) = β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s)Γ(k − 1 + s) with β(z; a, b) = ∫_0^z t^{a−1}(1 − t)^{b−1}dt the incomplete beta function; equivalently G_k(s) = 2^{k−1}Γ(s + k − 1)·₂F₁(1, s + k − 1; 1 + s; −1)/s. G_k continues meromorphically to ℂ; its poles lie in −ℕ₀ ∪ {1 − k − m : m ∈ ℕ₀}, are simple, and at s = −n (n ∈ ℕ₀) the residue is Γ(k − 1)/n!. Moreover β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s) is bounded on vertical lines for |Im s| large. Consequently, for an entire function L with L(k − 1 + s) = 0 at the points s = 1 − k − m, Γ(k − 1)^{−1}L(k − 1 + s)G_k(s) has simple poles only at s = −n, with residue L(k − 1 − n)/n!.
hypotheses: k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀; the regularized incomplete beta function I(z; a, b) = β(z; a, b)/B(a, b).
The incomplete beta integral at1/2 initially needs only Re(s)>0; its second parameter is unrestricted there. All boundary hypergeometric displays refer to analytic continuation.
proofSteps: Derive G_k(s)=Γ(s+k−1)β(1/2;s,2−k−s) by absolute Fubini in Re s>0, Re(s+k−1)>0: reverse 0<t<x/2 in ∫t^{s−1}e^t∫_{2t}∞x^{k−2}e^{−x}dx dt and set t=xu. The x-integral is Γ(s+k−1)(1−u)^{−(s+k−1)}.

Put v=u/(1−u), giving β=∫₀¹v^{s−1}(1+v)^{k−2}dv. Subtract J Taylor terms of (1+v)^{k−2} at0, integrate them as binomial(k−2,j)/(s+j), and let J grow. This gives meromorphic continuation with simple possible poles s=−j; on any finite vertical strip choose J large enough to make the residual integral absolutely bounded. The finitely many rational terms are bounded for |Im s|≥1.

At s=−n, multiply its residue binomial(k−2,n) by Γ(k−1−n); repeated Gamma recurrence gives Γ(k−1)/n!. The other possible poles come from Γ(s+k−1), at s=1−k−m; these are simple and are cancelled by L(k−1+s)=0. Distinct half-integral k keeps the two sets disjoint.

The hypergeometric displays follow by expanding the integral at the interior point1/2 and applying the Pfaff continuation formula; the value at−1 means analytic continuation of ₂F₁, not the totalised pinned ordinaryHypergeometric evaluated outside its convergence disc.
acceptance: For k = 3/2 and n = 0 the residue formula gives L(1/2)/0! = L(k − 1), the radial limit value.

The incomplete gamma and beta functions with complex parameters and the Gauss hypergeometric function at the boundary point −1 are not in the pinned libraries (Tau Ceti's incomplete gamma and beta are for positive real parameters); this node owns the identities it needs.

nodes.title: Radial expansion of f* from below (Bringmann–Rolen (3.19))
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) and d/c ∈ ℚ: f*(d/c − it/(2π)) ∼ Σ_{n≥0} (1/n!)L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1 − n)t^n as t → 0⁺.
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ.
proofSteps: Termwise Mellin transform of (3.4): M(f*(d/c − it/2π))(s) = Γ(k − 1)^{−1}L_f(ζ; k − 1 + s)·M(e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t))(s).

Poles and residues: incomplete-gamma-mellin-poles together with the vanishing L_f(ζ; −m) = 0 (twisted-cusp-form-l-function) at the half-integers s ≤ 1 − k give simple poles only at s = −n with residue L_f(ζ; k − 1 − n)/n!.

Decay in vertical strips: β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s) is bounded for |Im s| large (from (3.9), (3.17) and gamma-vertical-decay), and twisted-l-function-vertical-growth bounds L; Γ(k − 1 + s) decays exponentially.
Apply mellin-asymptotic-transfer for every β.
acceptance: The expansion of f* has no half-integral powers of t although the incomplete gamma factor contributes an odd power series in √t: they cancel against the zeros of L_f(ζ; ·) at non-positive integers.
Compared with eichler-integral-asymptotic-expansion the n-th coefficients differ by (−1)^n, which is the change of variable t ↦ −t between the two half-planes.

nodes.title: f̃ and f* have agreeing expansions at every rational point (Bringmann–Rolen Proposition 2.1)
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) (k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ) and every x ∈ ℚ, RadialExpansionsAgree f̃ f* x: with β(n) = ((−1)^n/n!)L_f(ζ_x; k − 1 − n) (ζ_x = e^{2πix}), f̃(x + it/2π) ∼ Σ β(n)t^n and f*(x − it/2π) ∼ Σ β(n)(−t)^n. In particular the radial limit of f̃ from above and of f* from below at x are both L_f(e^{2πix}; k − 1).
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N).
proofSteps: Combine eichler-integral-asymptotic-expansion and nonholomorphic-eichler-asymptotic-expansion: (1/n!)L_f(ζ; k − 1 − n)t^n = β(n)(−t)^n.
acceptance: The strange identity is the case f = η(24τ) (after the character extension, see half-integral-eichler-quantum-modular) combined with Zagier's Theorem 2.
The same asymptotic expansion is obtained by approaching the rational boundary from above and from below.

nodes.title: Eichler integrals of half-integral weight cusp forms are quantum modular (Bringmann–Rolen Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ S_k(N) with k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀ and N ∈ 4ℕ. Define f̃ : ℚ → ℂ by f̃(x) = radial limit of the Eichler integral f̃ at x (which exists by eichler-integral-asymptotic-expansion). Then f̃ is a quantum modular form of weight 2 − k on Γ₀(N) with multiplier ε(γ) = χ₋₄(d)ε_d^{2(2−k)}(c/d) for d>0, extended to d<0 by requiring J(−γ,x)=J(γ,x) for J=ε·j_{2−k}; explicitly ε(γ)=ε(−γ)e^{−iπ(2−k)} if c>0 and ε(γ)=ε(−γ)e^{iπ(2−k)} if c≤0, and for every γ ∈ Γ₀(N) its period function extends to the real-analytic function r_{f,−d/c} on ℝ ∖ {−d/c}.
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N) with trivial character (the character case is recorded in the source issues and in kontsevich-quantum-modular).
Weight 2 − k, multiplier as stated, lower-boundary branch of quantum-modular-form.
For negative d, use the stated extension from −γ with positive d; the local positive-denominator Jacobi formula with |d| is not an extended negative-denominator formula. In particular J(−I,x)=1.
proofSteps: By eichler-asymptotic-agreement the radial limit of f̃ at x equals the radial limit of f* from below at x.
Take x ∈ ℚ with cx + d ≠ 0 and let τ = x − iy, y → 0⁺, in nonholomorphic-eichler-transformation.

f*(τ) → f̃(x); (cτ + d)^{k−2} → the boundary factor j_{2−k}(γ, x) of quantum-modular-form (lower branch); f*(γτ) → f̃(γx) by nonholomorphic-eichler-nontangential-limit, since γτ approaches γx tangentially to the vertical.
The right side r_{f,−d/c}(τ) → r_{f,−d/c}(x), real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {−d/c} (eichler-period-integral).
Hence h_γ(x) = r_{f,−d/c}(x) on ℚ ∖ {−d/c}, which is the definition with S_γ = {−d/c}.

First prove the law for d>0, as in the native Shimura stand-in. For d<0 apply it to −γ, which acts by the same Möbius transformation, and use the constant ratio of lower boundary factors just stated. This gives the full subgroup law and its trivial central action.
acceptance: For f = Θ₊(120τ) (k = 3/2, after the character extension) this is Lawrence–Zagier's quantum modularity of the Poincaré-sphere WRT values.
The half-integral-weight kernel is not polynomial; this does not exclude zero period functions or accidental polynomial examples.
The theorem concerns radial limits of f̃; it says nothing about formal (Habiro) evaluations, which are compared separately (strange-identity).

nodes.title: Twisted central-type L-values as quantum modular forms (Bringmann–Rolen Corollary 1.2)
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) (k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ) define Q_f : ℚ → ℂ by Q_f(d/c) = L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1) (analytic continuation). Then Q_f is a quantum modular form of weight 2 − k on Γ₀(N) whose period functions are real-analytic except at γ⁻¹∞; indeed Q_f is the function x ↦ radial limit of f̃ at x.
hypotheses: As in half-integral-eichler-quantum-modular.
proofSteps: The constant term of eichler-integral-asymptotic-expansion identifies Q_f(x) with the radial limit of f̃ at x.
Apply half-integral-eichler-quantum-modular.
acceptance: For f(τ)=η(24τ), the character version gives Q_f(x)=−2φ(24x): eichlerIntegral (1/2) 1 for η(24τ) equals Zagier’s η̃(24τ). For η(τ) at period N=24 the normalized Eichler integral instead has radial value −2φ(x)/√24.

nodes.title: Kontsevich's strange series F(q) = Σ (q;q)_n as an element of the Habiro ring
nodes.statement: Kontsevich's series is F(q) = Σ_{n≥0} (q;q)_n with (q;q)_n = (1 − q)(1 − q²)⋯(1 − qⁿ) the finite q-Pochhammer symbol (QM.0/q-pochhammer). The series does not converge in ℤ⟦q⟧ nor on any open subset of ℂ, but it converges in the Habiro ring ℤ[q]^ = lim_n ℤ[q]/((q;q)_n) (HabiroCyclotomicCompletions:HC.1), where the n-th term lies in the n-th ideal; F denotes that element. Its formal evaluations are the images under the Habiro evaluation and Taylor maps (HC.3): for a root of unity ξ of order N, F(ξ) = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} (ξ;ξ)_n (the terms with n ≥ N vanish), and after the substitution q = ξe^{−t} the Taylor map gives the power series T_ξF = Σ_{n≥0} (ξe^{−t}; ξe^{−t})_n ∈ ℂ⟦t⟧, which converges t-adically because (ξe^{−t}; ξe^{−t})_n ∈ t^{⌊n/N⌋}ℂ⟦t⟧. The normalised function on ℚ is φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}). These are formal evaluations: that they agree with radial limits of a holomorphic q-series is the content of strange-identity, not of this definition.
hypotheses: The Habiro ring, its evaluation maps and Taylor maps are HabiroCyclotomicCompletions:HC.1 and HC.3 (requested).
ξ ranges over roots of unity in ℂ; N ≥ 1 with ξ^N = 1 (any such N gives the same finite sum).
proofSteps: Convergence in the Habiro ring: (q;q)_n ∈ ((q;q)_n), so the partial sums form a compatible system (HC.1).
Evaluation: ev_ξ is continuous and (ξ;ξ)_n = 0 for n ≥ N because the factor 1 − ξ^N vanishes; hence ev_ξ(F) = Σ_{n<N}(ξ;ξ)_n, independent of N with ξ^N = 1.

Taylor map: (ξe^{−t};ξe^{−t})_n contains the ⌊n/N⌋ factors 1 − e^{−jNt} (j ≤ n/N), each in tℂ⟦t⟧, so the sum converges in ℂ⟦t⟧ (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.summable_of_tendsto_order_atTop_nhds_top); it is the image of F under the Taylor map at ξ composed with q ↦ ξe^{−t}.
Constant coefficient of T_ξF is F(ξ) (the constant term of the Taylor map is evaluation, HC.3).
Galois: for σ ∈ Aut(ℂ/ℚ), σ(F(ξ)) = F(σξ) because F(ξ) is a polynomial expression in ξ with integer coefficients.
acceptance: F(1) = 1, F(−1) = 3, F(i) = 8 − 3i, F(e^{2πi/3}) = 5 − e^{2πi/3} (Zagier's table of c₀(ξ)).
The partial sums Σ_{n≤M}(q;q)_n do not converge in ℤ⟦q⟧: their q-coefficient is −M.

uses.how: the Taylor coefficients of F at roots of unity count regular linearized chord diagrams and equal twisted L-values

uses.where: Zagier, Topology 40, §6 Theorem; Quantum modular forms, Example 3
uses.how: φ is a quantum modular form of weight 3/2
F is determined by its values at roots of unity, so it is the unique Habiro element whose values are the radial limits of −½H

Imports the terminating root-of-unity values of F(q) and its formal Habiro interpretation (through the requested HC.1/HC.3 interfaces). No identification with a knot invariant, such as the trefoil's Kashaev invariant, is sourced or supplied here; a consumer that uses one proves its colour, orientation and normalisation comparison.

nodes.title: The sum-of-tails series F₁ = Σ n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ
nodes.statement: F₁(q) = Σ_{n≥1} n (q;q)_{n−1} qⁿ ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧, which also defines a holomorphic function on the unit disc and, since (q;q)_{n−1} ∈ (1 − q)^{n−1}ℤ[q], a formal power series in 1 − q (and in ξ − q for every root of unity ξ). The companion series is F₂(q) = Σ_{n≥0}[(q;q)_n − (q;q)_∞] ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧, the sum of the tails of Euler's product. The Euler product (q;q)_∞ = ∏_{n≥1}(1 − qⁿ) and E(q) = Σ_{n≥1} qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ) = Σ d(n)qⁿ enter the identity of zagier-sum-of-tails-identity.
hypotheses: All series are in ℤ⟦q⟧ with the pi topology; convergence as functions on |q| < 1 is absolute and locally uniform.
proofSteps: F₁ converges in ℤ⟦q⟧ since the n-th term has order n.
F₂ converges in ℤ⟦q⟧ since (q;q)_n − (q;q)_∞ ∈ q^{n+1}ℤ⟦q⟧.
Holomorphy on the disc: |n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ| ≤ n·C(r)|q|ⁿ on |q| ≤ r < 1 with C(r) = ∏(1 + r^j).
acceptance: F₁ = q + 2q² + q³ + ⋯ (and F₂ has the same expansion).
F₁ is not the Habiro element F: F does not lie in ℤ⟦q⟧, while F₁ does; they agree only after expansion at roots of unity (sum-of-tails-agreement).

uses.how: F₁ = −½H + (½ − E)(q)_∞
F₁ agrees with F to all orders at roots of unity, which transfers the identity to F
