nodes.title: F₁ agrees with F to all orders at every root of unity
nodes.statement: (a) For every N ≥ 1, Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}[(q;q)_n − (q;q)_N] = Σ_{n=1}^{N} n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ in ℤ[q]. (b) For every root of unity ξ = e^{2πix}, the function τ ↦ F₁(e^{2πiτ}) has radial asymptotic expansion T_ξF (kontsevich-strange-series) at x: HasRadialExpansion (F₁ ∘ e^{2πi·}) x (kontsevichTaylor ξ). In particular the radial limit of F₁ at ξ is the formal evaluation F(ξ).
hypotheses: ξ a root of unity of order K.
proofSteps: (a) Induction on N (partial summation): passing from N to N + 1 adds (q;q)_N − (N + 1)(q;q)_{N+1} + N(q;q)_N on the left and (N+1)(q;q)_N q^{N+1} on the right, which agree since (q;q)_{N+1} = (q;q)_N(1 − q^{N+1}).
From (a): F₁(q) − Σ_{n<N}(q;q)_n = Σ_{n>N} n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ − N(q;q)_N for |q| < 1.

For q=ξe^{−t}, split the product into K-blocks. Compare block r with ∏_{j=1}^K(1−ξ^j e^{−rKt})=1−e^{−rK²t}. A finite-product telescoping estimate bounds the difference by C_K t e^{−rKt}; hence each block is ≤1+C_K t e^{−rKt}. The product of these bounds is ≤exp(C_K t/(1−e^{−Kt})), uniformly bounded for 0<t≤1. The first m fixed complete blocks each contribute O_m(t), and a last partial block is≤2^K. Therefore |(q;q)_{n−1}|≤C_m t^m uniformly for n>mK. Summing n e^{−nt} gives O(t^{m−2}); choose m as large as needed.
The polynomial Σ_{n<N}(q;q)_n in q = ξe^{−t} has Taylor expansion agreeing with T_ξF modulo t^m (the omitted terms lie in t^m ℂ⟦t⟧).
Letting m grow gives the expansion to every order (HasRadialExpansion), and its constant term gives the radial limit F(ξ).
acceptance: At ξ = 1: F₁(e^{−t}) = 1 + t + (3/2)t² + O(t³), the Taylor series of F at 1.
The formal statement F = F₁ in ℤ[[1 − q]] (which is how the source phrases it) does not by itself give the analytic expansion; the uniform tail estimate is needed (see the source issues).

sources.match: Identity (16), part (a).
Part (b), which the source asserts from the formal agreement; the estimate is supplied here.

nodes.title: The two-variable identity Σ (x;q)_{n+1}xⁿ = Σ χ₁₂(n)x^{(n−1)/2}q^{(n²−1)/24}
nodes.statement: First interpret the sum in (ℤ⟦x⟧)⟦q⟧ with the product topology, where each q-coefficient converges x-adically. Its closed form descends to ℤ[x]⟦q⟧: S(x) := Σ_{n≥0}(x;q)_{n+1}xⁿ = Σ_{n≥1} χ₁₂(n) x^{(n−1)/2} q^{(n²−1)/24}, with (x;q)_{n+1} = (1 − x)(1 − qx)⋯(1 − qⁿx) and χ₁₂ = (12/·) (only n ≡ ±1 mod 6 contribute, so the exponents are integers). Moreover S(x) = (qx;q)_∞ + (1 − x)Σ_{n≥0}[(qx;q)_n − (qx;q)_∞]xⁿ in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧.
hypotheses: The first sum converges coefficientwise x-adically in (ℤ⟦x⟧)⟦q⟧, not q-adically in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧: its summands have nonzero constant q-coefficient (1−x)xⁿ. The recursion proves descent to polynomial q-coefficients; differentiation at x=1 is performed only after this descent.
proofSteps: Form S(a,x)=Σ(a;q)_n xⁿ in the x-adic ring and verify (1−x)S(a,x)=1−axS(a,qx) and S(a,x)=1+(1−a)xS(qa,x) coefficientwise. All rearrangements here are x-adically legitimate.
Deduce S(x) = (1 − x)S(qx, x) satisfies S(x) = 1 − qx² − q²x³S(qx).

The right side R(x) = Σ χ₁₂(n)x^{(n−1)/2}q^{(n²−1)/24} satisfies the same equation: −q²x³R(qx) reindexed by m = n + 6 gives Σ_{m≥7}χ₁₂(m)x^{(m−1)/2}q^{(m²−1)/24}, using χ₁₂(n + 6) = −χ₁₂(n) and (m² − 1)/24 = (n² − 1)/24 + (n + 3)/2.

Uniqueness: the map T ↦ 1 − qx² − q²x³T(qx) raises q-order, so it has a unique fixed point in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧; hence S = R, and in particular each q-coefficient of S is a polynomial (in fact a monomial) in x.
The second expression: split (x;q)_{n+1} = (1 − x)(qx;q)_n and write Σ(qx;q)_n xⁿ(1 − x) = (qx;q)_∞ + (1 − x)Σ[(qx;q)_n − (qx;q)_∞]xⁿ; each q-coefficient involves only n < q-degree.
acceptance: At x = 1: S(1) = (q;q)_∞ = Σ χ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}, Euler's pentagonal number theorem (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.hasProd_one_sub_X_pow).
The first terms are 1 − qx² − q²x³ + q⁵x⁵ + q⁷x⁶ − ⋯ .

sources.locator: §2, proof of Theorem 2, eq. (23), printed p. 951
sources.match: Identity (23) with its recursion S(x) = 1 − qx² − q²x³S(qx); the node proves the closed form from the recursion.

nodes.title: Zagier's identity F₁ = −½H + (½ − E)(q)_∞ (Theorem 2)
nodes.statement: In ℚ⟦q⟧, and hence as holomorphic functions on |q| < 1: F₁(q) = −½H(q) + (½ − E(q))(q;q)_∞, where H(q) = Σ_{n≥1} nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24} (the ‘half-derivative’ of η: q^{1/24}H(q) = η̃, see eichler-integral) and E(q) = Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ) = Σ d(n)qⁿ.
hypotheses: Formal identity in ℚ⟦q⟧; both sides have integer coefficients.
proofSteps: Work in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧, where d/dx at x = 1 is a well-defined derivation followed by evaluation (each q-coefficient is a polynomial in x).
From the closed form of andrews-exercise-identity: S(1) = (q;q)_∞ and (dS/dx)(1) = Σ ((n−1)/2)χ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24} = ½H − ½(q;q)_∞.
From the second expression: (dS/dx)(1) = (d/dx)(qx;q)_∞|_{x=1} − F₂ = −E(q)(q;q)_∞ − F₂, since −(d/dx) log(qx;q)_∞ at x = 1 is E(q).
Equate: F₂ = −½H + ½(q;q)_∞ − E(q)(q;q)_∞, and F₂ = F₁ (sum-of-tails-series).
acceptance: Comparing coefficients: F₁ = q + 2q² + ⋯, −½H = −½ + (5/2)q + (7/2)q² + ⋯ and (½ − E)(q;q)_∞ = ½ − (3/2)q − (3/2)q² + ⋯ .
A consequence (Zagier's Remark): Σ nχ(n)q^{n²/24}/Σ χ(n)q^{n²/24} = 1 − 2Σ qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ)·(1 + 1/((1 − q)⋯(1 − qⁿ))).

sources.match: Theorem 2 (22); its proof compares the ε-coefficients of S(1 − ε), recorded here as the x-derivative at x = 1.

nodes.title: Euler's product vanishes to infinite order at every root of unity
nodes.statement: For every rational x, the function τ ↦ (q;q)_∞ = ∏(1 − e^{2πinτ}) has radial asymptotic expansion 0 at x; more precisely, for x = a/c in lowest terms (c ≥ 1), |(q;q)_∞| ≤ C·y^{−1/2}exp(−π/(12c²y)) for q = e^{2πi(x+iy)}, 0 < y ≤ 1. The same holds for E(q)·(q;q)_∞, since |E(q)| ≤ Σ n|q|ⁿ = O(y^{−2}).
hypotheses: x ∈ ℚ; the constant C depends on x.
proofSteps: Choose γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with γ(∞) = a/c and write τ = x + iy = γτ′; then Im τ′ = 1/(c²y).
The transformation law η(γτ′) = ψ(γ)(cτ′ + d)^{1/2}η(τ′) (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier) gives |η(τ)| = |cτ′ + d|^{1/2}|η(τ′)| with |cτ′ + d| = 1/(cy).
|η(τ′)| ≤ C′e^{−2π Im τ′/24} for Im τ′ ≥ 1, and (q;q)_∞ = e^{−2πiτ/24}η(τ).
Every power y^m dominates exp(−π/(12c²y)), so the expansion is 0 to all orders; multiply by the O(y^{−2}) bound for E.
acceptance: At x=0 and t>0, |(e^{−t};e^{−t})_∞| = √(2π/t)e^{−π²/(6t)}e^{t/24}(e^{−4π²/t};e^{−4π²/t})_∞. In particular it is bounded above by the same expression with the last product omitted, and their ratio tends to 1.

Because the expansion is 0, the mean of m ↦ χ₁₂(m)ξ^{(m²−1)/24} over a period vanishes (otherwise euler-maclaurin-asymptotic would give a term of order t^{−1/2}); this is used in kontsevich-value-formula.

nodes.title: Kontsevich–Zagier strange identity at every root of unity
nodes.statement: Let ξ = e^{2πix} (x ∈ ℚ) and H(q) = Σ_{n≥1} nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}. The holomorphic function τ ↦ H(e^{2πiτ}) on ℍ has radial asymptotic expansion −2·T_ξF at x, where T_ξF = kontsevichTaylor ξ is the formal Taylor expansion of the Habiro element F at ξ in the variable t (q = ξe^{−t}). In particular its radial limit at ξ is −2F(ξ); equivalently, with η̃(τ) = Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{n²/24}, the radial limit of η̃ at x is −2φ(x). This is the exact meaning of the ‘strange identity’ Σ (q;q)_n “=” −½Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}: a comparison between a formal evaluation (left) and the radial limits and asymptotic expansions of a q-series convergent only in the disc (right).
hypotheses: ξ an arbitrary root of unity (all orders, including even and non-prime-power orders).
proofSteps: Theorem 2 (zagier-sum-of-tails-identity) holds as an identity of holomorphic functions on the disc: −½H = F₁ − (½ − E)(q;q)_∞.
F₁ has radial expansion T_ξF at x (sum-of-tails-agreement).
(q;q)_∞ and E(q)(q;q)_∞ have radial expansion 0 at x (eta-infinite-order-vanishing).
Add the expansions (HasRadialExpansion.add); multiply by −2.
acceptance: At ξ = 1: e^{−t/24}F(e^{−t}) = Σ T_n(t/24)ⁿ/n! with the Glaisher numbers T_n = 1, 23, 1681, … (Zagier's Theorem 3; see kontsevich-value-formula).
At ξ = −1 the radial limit of H is −2F(−1) = −6.
The identity is not an identity of power series in q: F has no q-expansion, and H has no values on the unit circle; only their expansions at roots of unity are compared.

sources.match: The statement this node makes precise.

nodes.title: Values and Taylor coefficients of F at roots of unity as twisted L-values
nodes.statement: Let ξ = e^{2πiα} and N a positive multiple of 12 with ξ^{N/12} = 1, and let Φ_ξ(m) = χ₁₂(m)ξ^{(m²−1)/24} (a function on ZMod N, with ξ^{s} := e^{2πiαs}). Define c_n(ξ) by e^{−t/24}F(ξe^{−t}) = Σ c_n(ξ)tⁿ/(24ⁿn!) (the Taylor expansion of kontsevich-strange-series). Then c_n(ξ) = (−1)^{n−1}L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ)/2 = (−1)ⁿN^{2n+1}/(2n + 2)·Σ_{m=1}^{N/2}Φ_ξ(m)B_{2n+2}(m/N); in particular F(ξ) = (1/(4N))Σ_{m=1}^{N} m²Φ_ξ(m), and at ξ = 1 the c_n(1) are the Glaisher numbers T_n given by Σ T_n x^{2n+1}/(2n + 1)! = sin 2x/(2 cos 3x).
hypotheses: N a positive multiple of 12 with ξ^{N/12} = 1 (so Φ_ξ is N-periodic).
proofSteps: Φ_ξ is N-periodic: ((m + N)² − m²)/24 = (N/12)(2m + N)/2 with (2m + N)/2 ∈ ℤ for odd m.

Φ_ξ has mean zero: Σ_{m≥1}Φ_ξ(m)e^{−m²t/24} = e^{−t/24}(q;q)_∞ at q = ξe^{−t}, which tends to 0 (eta-infinite-order-vanishing), while a non-zero mean would contribute a term of order t^{−1/2} by euler-maclaurin-asymptotic.
By periodic-gaussian-sum-asymptotic (ν = 1) applied to Φ_ξ at t/24: e^{−t/24}H(ξe^{−t}) ∼ Σ L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ)(−t/24)ⁿ/n!.
By strange-identity this equals −2e^{−t/24}F(ξe^{−t}) = −2Σ c_n(ξ)tⁿ/(24ⁿn!); compare coefficients.
Evaluate L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ) by periodic-l-value-bernoulli and fold the sum using Φ_ξ(N − m) = Φ_ξ(m) and B_{2n+2}(1 − x) = B_{2n+2}(x).
For n = 0 expand B₂(x) = x² − x + 1/6 and use Σ Φ_ξ = 0 and Σ mΦ_ξ(m) = 0 (from the symmetry m ↔ N − m).
At ξ = 1 (N = 12): Σ_m χ₁₂(m)e^{−mt} = sinh 2t/cosh 3t (partial fractions over one period), whose coefficients give the stated generating function by periodic-exponential-sum-asymptotic.
acceptance: F(−1) = 3 and F(i) = 8 − 3i from the formula with N = 24 and N = 48 respectively (agreeing with kontsevich-strange-series).

nodes.title: Kontsevich's function is a quantum modular form of weight 3/2
nodes.statement: The function φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}) on ℚ satisfies φ(x + 1) = e^{2πi/24}φ(x) and φ(x) + (ix)^{−3/2}φ(−1/x) = g(x) (x ∈ ℚ, x ≠ 0), where (ix)^{−3/2} is the principal branch and g : ℝ → ℂ is C^∞, real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {0}, with g^{(n)}(0) = (−πi/12)ⁿc_n (c_n the Glaisher numbers). Equivalently, φ is a quantum modular form of weight 3/2 on SL₂(ℤ) (quantum-modular-form, lower boundary branch) with multiplier ε determined by ε(T) = e^{−2πi/24} and ε(S) = e^{2πi/8}, ε(γ)=v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c≠0 or d>0, and ε(γ)=−v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c=0,d<0; hence ε(−I)=−i and ε(−I)j_{3/2}(−I,x)=1. For general γ the period function is real-analytic except at γ⁻¹∞.
hypotheses: Use the lower-boundary multiplier ε(γ)=v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c≠0 or d>0, and ε(γ)=−v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c=0,d<0. Its values at T and S are the stated inverse eta values, but its value at −I differs from the naive inverse. The corrected factor satisfies QuantumCocycleCondition and acts trivially at −I.
proofSteps: φ(x) = −½·(radial limit of η̃ at x) by strange-identity, η̃ = √24·(Eichler integral of weight 1/2 of η) (eichler-integral).

Compare upper- and lower-half-plane principal powers by complex conjugation. They differ by a sign precisely for c=0,d<0, where the denominator lies on the negative-real branch cut. Apply this sign to the inverse eta multiplier. Integral weight shifts by 2 leave the cocycle unchanged. This gives the full weight-3/2 lower-boundary factor, including ε(−I)=−i, before propagating the S/T laws.

Transformation of the non-holomorphic Eichler integral η* on H⁻ under S and T: the computation of nonholomorphic-eichler-transformation with the η-multiplier ψ (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier) in place of Shimura's, giving η* − ε(γ)·(η*|γ) = r_{η,−d/c} (eichler-period-integral for η).

Agreement of expansions of η̃ and η* at every rational (eichler-asymptotic-agreement, whose L-function inputs are here the periodic L-functions L(2s − 1, Φ_ξ) of ZMod.LFunction, entire with the required vertical growth, in place of twisted-cusp-form-l-function).
Pass to boundary values as in half-integral-eichler-quantum-modular, using nonholomorphic-eichler-nontangential-limit.

Prove smoothness of the period integral at 0 by differentiating its boundary kernel to every order under the integral: η(w) decays faster than any power as w→0 on the vertical path and exponentially at infinity, furnishing the derivative majorants. Evaluate these integrals by Mellin continuation and kontsevich-value-formula to get g^{(n)}(0)=(−πi/12)ⁿc_n. An asymptotic expansion along the sequence ±1/k alone does not prove smoothness.
acceptance: The factor (ix)^{−3/2} equals e^{−3πi/4}x^{−3/2} for x > 0 and e^{3πi/4}|x|^{−3/2} for x < 0; relative to the lower boundary factor of quantum-modular-form this is the constant −ε(S) = −e^{2πi/8}, which is why the lower branch is pinned.
Consistency check with Kontsevich's asymptotics: φ(1/k) = e^{2πi(3−k)/24}k^{3/2} + Σ c_n(−πi/(12k))ⁿ/n! + o(1) as k → ∞.
Zagier's 2010 account (Quantum modular forms, eq. (26)) prints this law with |x|^{3/2} and ∓i^{1/2}; the correct form is the one here (see the source issues).

sources.match: The theorem (39) and its general-γ form; the source gives only an indication of proof (see the source issues).

nodes.title: Cohen's terminating evaluations of σ and σ* at roots of unity
nodes.statement: For a root of unity ξ define σ(ξ) = 1 + Σ_{n≥0}(−1)ⁿξ^{n+1}(ξ;ξ)_n and σ*(ξ) = −2Σ_{n≥0}ξ^{n+1}(ξ²;ξ²)_n (Andrews' and Cohen's expressions (8) evaluated at q = ξ). Both sums terminate: (ξ;ξ)_n = 0 for n ≥ ord ξ and (ξ²;ξ²)_n = 0 for n ≥ ord(ξ²). These are formal evaluations of Ramanujan's σ(q) = Σ q^{n(n+1)/2}/((1+q)⋯(1+qⁿ)) and its partner σ*(q) = 2Σ(−1)ⁿq^{n²}/((1−q)⋯(1−q^{2n−1})); the latter converge only for |q| < 1, and the agreement of their q-expansions with (8) (Andrews' identity) is not part of this definition.
hypotheses: ξ a root of unity; the finite sums are taken up to any bound past the terminating index.
proofSteps: Define cohenSigma ξ := 1 + Σ_{n<N}(−1)ⁿξ^{n+1}(ξ;ξ)_n and cohenSigmaStar ξ := −2Σ_{n<N}ξ^{n+1}(ξ²;ξ²)_n with N = orderOf ξ.
Independence of the cut-off: the terms with n ≥ N vanish because they contain the factor 1 − ξ^N (resp. 1 − ξ^{2j} with ord(ξ) | 2j ≤ 2n).
acceptance: σ(1) = 2, σ(−1) = −2, σ(ω) = 2ω + 6 for ω² + ω + 1 = 0, σ(±i) = ∓2i − 4 (Zagier's table).

nodes.title: Cohen's telescoping identity (9)
hypotheses: k ≥ 0; the identity is in the Laurent polynomial ring.
proofSteps: The recursion S_{k+1} − S_k = q^{k+1}(S_{k+1} − (1 + q)⋯(1 + q^k)) − q^{−k(k+1)/2}, by comparing the two sums term by term.
Induction on k: the case k = 0 is 0 = 0; the step multiplies the recursion by (1 − q)⋯(1 − q^k) and uses (1 − q^{j})(1 + q^{j}) = 1 − q^{2j}.
acceptance: k = 1: 1 − q = (1 − q)·S₁ with S₁ = 1.

nodes.title: Cohen's duality σ(q) = −σ*(q⁻¹) at roots of unity
nodes.statement: For every root of unity ξ, cohenSigma ξ = −cohenSigmaStar ξ⁻¹.
hypotheses: ξ a root of unity.
proofSteps: Evaluate cohen-telescoping-identity at q = ξ with k ≥ ord ξ: the right side vanishes because (1 − ξ)⋯(1 − ξ^k) contains the factor 1 − ξ^{ord ξ} = 0.

The first sum on the left equals ½σ(ξ⁻¹): with P_n = (ξ^{−1} − 1)⋯(ξ^{−n} − 1) one has ξ^{−n−1}P_n = P_{n+1} + P_n, so ½ + ½Σ_{n<k}ξ^{−n−1}P_n = Σ_{n<k}P_n + ½P_k and P_k = 0; and σ(ξ⁻¹) = 1 + Σ ξ^{−n−1}P_n since (−1)ⁿ(1 − ξ^{−1})⋯(1 − ξ^{−n}) = P_n.
The second sum is −½σ*(ξ) by definition.
Hence σ(ξ⁻¹) + σ*(ξ) = 0; replace ξ by ξ⁻¹.
acceptance: The statement is about formal evaluations only; the quantum modularity of x ↦ e^{2πix/24}σ(e^{2πix}) (Zagier's Proposition) needs Cohen's Maass form and is not decomposed here.

nodes.title: The periodic functions χ₊ and χ₋ of period 60
nodes.statement: χ₊, χ₋ : ℤ → {−1, 0, 1} are the functions of period 60 given by χ₊(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if n² ≡ 1 (mod 120) and 0 otherwise, and χ₋(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if n² ≡ 49 (mod 120) and 0 otherwise (n taken in [0, 60)). They are the real and imaginary parts of the primitive character χ = (12/·)ε of conductor 60, where ε is the character of conductor 5 with ε(1, 2, 3, 4) = (1, −i, i, −1). As functions on ZMod 60, χ₊ takes the value 1 at 1, 11, 19, 29 and −1 at 31, 41, 49, 59.
hypotheses: n is reduced to [0, 60) before ⌊n/30⌋ is taken; equivalently χ₊ is odd and 60-periodic.
proofSteps: Define lzChiPlus, lzChiMinus : ZMod 60 → ℤ by the table, and prove the congruence descriptions by deciding the finitely many cases.
The identification with Re and Im of (12/·)ε is a finite check over ZMod 60.
Oddness χ±(−n) = −χ±(n) and mean zero Σ_{n mod 60} χ±(n) = 0 are finite checks.
acceptance: Zagier's equivalent description: χ₊(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if (n, 6) = 1 and n ≡ ±1 (mod 5), 0 otherwise.

uses.how: χ₊ gives the Eichler integral A(q) and the finite formula for W(ξ)

nodes.title: The Eichler-integral series A(q) of the Poincaré sphere

Θ̃₋ is defined in the same way with χ₋.

Define lzThetaTilde± τ := Σ_{n≥1}χ±(n)e^{2πin²τ/120}.

nodes.title: WRT invariants of the Poincaré sphere as radial limits (Lawrence–Zagier Theorem 1)
nodes.statement: Let W(ξ) = ξ(ξ − 1)Z(ξ), where Z(ξ) is the sl₂ Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of the Poincaré homology sphere Σ(2, 3, 5) at the root of unity ξ (ArithmeticQuantumTopology:QT.4/WRT-invariant-at-a-root, normalised by Z(S³) = 1; W(1) = 0). Then for every root of unity ξ the radial limit of 1 − ½A(q) as q → ξ exists and equals W(ξ). Explicitly W(ξ) = 1 − ½Σ_{n=1}^{30K}χ₊(n)(1 − n/(30K))ξ^{(n²−1)/120} for ξ of order K.
hypotheses: ξ an arbitrary root of unity (all orders); W is extended from ξ = e^{2πi/K} to all primitive K-th roots by Galois equivariance, which agrees with QT.4's invariant at those roots (QT.4/integrality-and-galois).
The orientation of Σ(2, 3, 5) and the normalisation of Z are those of the Lawrence–Rozansky formula requested from ArithmeticQuantumTopology:QT.4.
proofSteps: Radial limit: apply renormalised-sum to Φ(n) = χ₊(n)ξ^{(n²−1)/120}, periodic of period 60K with Φ(60K − n) = −Φ(n), hence of mean zero; A(ξe^{−t}) = e^{t/120}Σ Φ(n)e^{−n²t/120} → L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{60K}(n/(60K) − ½)Φ(n) = Σ_{n=1}^{30K}(1 − n/(30K))Φ(n).
Gauss-sum step (LZ (14)): with ζ a primitive 120K-th root of unity with ζ^{120} = ξ and G = Σ_{β mod 60K}ζ^{−β²}, ξ^{(n²−1)/120} = G^{−1}Σ_β ζ^{−β²−1}ζ^{2nβ}.

nodes.title: Habiro evaluations of the unified invariant of Σ(2,3,5) are radial limits

nodes.title: The SL₂(ℤ)-transformation of the theta pair Θ± (Lawrence–Zagier (15))

nodes.title: The Andrews–Garvan crank of a partition
nodes.statement: For a partition λ of n (Mathlib's Nat.Partition n), let ℓ(λ) be its largest part (0 for the empty partition), ω(λ) the number of parts equal to 1, and μ(λ) the number of parts larger than ω(λ) (counted with multiplicity). The crank is c(λ) = ℓ(λ) if ω(λ) = 0 and c(λ) = μ(λ) − ω(λ) if ω(λ) > 0; it is an integer with |c(λ)| ≤ n.
hypotheses: λ ranges over Nat.Partition n; the empty partition of 0 has crank 0.
proofSteps: Define largestPart λ := λ.parts.sup (0 if empty), numOnes λ := λ.parts.count 1, numPartsAbove λ := (λ.parts.filter (· > numOnes λ)).card.
Define partitionCrank λ := if numOnes λ = 0 then (largestPart λ : ℤ) else numPartsAbove λ − numOnes λ.
The bound |c(λ)| ≤ n: ℓ(λ) ≤ n, and μ, ω ≤ number of parts ≤ n.
acceptance: The crank of (1) is −1 and of the empty partition 0; the generating function of crank-generating-function therefore needs the convention of crank-count at n = 1.

Define crankCountMod t k n := Σ_{m ∈ [−n, n], (m : ZMod t) = k} crankCount m n.
Σ_m M(m, n) = p(n): for n ≠ 1 every partition has exactly one crank; for n = 1, −1 + 1 + 1 = 1 = p(1).

nodes.title: The crank generating function (Andrews–Garvan)
nodes.statement: In the ring of formal power series in q with coefficients Laurent polynomials in z (LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧, pi topology): Σ_{n≥0} (Σ_m M(m, n)z^m) qⁿ = ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿ)/((1 − zqⁿ)(1 − z⁻¹qⁿ)), each factor being invertible (constant coefficient 1).
hypotheses: Formal identity; the infinite product converges q-adically.
proofSteps: Rewrite the product as (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ · (q²;q)_∞/(q/z;q)_∞.

Cauchy's q-binomial theorem Σ_j (a;q)_j t^j/(q;q)_j = (at;q)_∞/(t;q)_∞ (formal, from QM.0) with a = zq, t = q/z gives (q²;q)_∞/(q/z;q)_∞ = Σ_j (zq;q)_j (q/z)^j/(q;q)_j, hence the product is (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ + Σ_{j≥1} q^j z^{−j}/((q²;q)_{j−1}(zq^{j+1};q)_∞).

For j ≥ 1 the j-th term generates the partitions with exactly j ones, the exponent of z being μ(λ) − ω(λ) = c(λ): the ones give q^j z^{−j}, 1/(q²;q)_{j−1} the parts 2, …, j, and 1/(zq^{j+1};q)_∞ the parts > j, each counted by z.

The j = 0 term (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ generates, for n ≥ 2, the partitions without ones weighted by z^{ℓ(λ)} (conjugation: 1/(zq;q)_∞ counts all partitions by largest part, q/(zq;q)_∞ those with a 1, except at n = 1 where adding a 1 changes the largest part).
At n = 1 the coefficient is (z − 1) + z⁻¹, which is the convention of crank-count.
acceptance: Setting z = 1 gives Σ p(n)qⁿ = 1/(q;q)_∞ (Nat.Partition.genFun).
The coefficient of q⁶ is Σ_{λ⊢6} z^{c(λ)} = z⁶ + z⁴ + z³ + z² + z + 1 + z⁻¹ + z⁻² + z⁻³ + z⁻⁴ + z⁻⁶.

nodes.title: Equidistribution from a vanishing sum over a prime-order root of unity
nodes.statement: Let t be a prime, ζ ∈ ℂ a primitive t-th root of unity and c : ZMod t → ℚ. If Σ_{k ∈ ZMod t} c(k)ζ^k = 0 then c is constant; hence if Σ_k c(k) = P then c(k) = P/t for every k.
hypotheses: t prime (for composite t the conclusion fails: 1 + ζ² = 0 for t = 4).
proofSteps: The minimal polynomial of ζ over ℚ is the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_t (Polynomial.cyclotomic_eq_minpoly_rat), which for t prime is 1 + X + ⋯ + X^{t−1} (Polynomial.cyclotomic_prime).
P(X) = Σ_{k=0}^{t−1} c(k)X^k has degree ≤ t − 1 and P(ζ) = 0, so Φ_t ∣ P and P = c·Φ_t for a constant c.

For t = 4, c = (1, 0, 1, 0) gives Σ c(k)i^k = 0 but c is not constant: primality is needed.

nodes.title: The crank explains p(5n + 4) ≡ 0 (mod 5)
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 0 and k ∈ ZMod 5, M(k, 5, 5n + 4) = p(5n + 4)/5.
proofSteps: Substitute z = ζ = e^{2πi/5} in crank-generating-function: Σ_k M(k, 5, N)ζ^k is the coefficient of q^N in C(ζ; q) = (q;q)_∞/((ζq;q)_∞(ζ⁻¹q;q)_∞).

Jacobi's triple product (QM.0/jacobi-triple-product) gives (ζ²;q)_∞(ζ⁻²q;q)_∞(q;q)_∞ = Σ_m (−1)^m ζ^{2m}q^{m(m−1)/2}, and Euler's pentagonal theorem (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.hasProd_one_sub_X_pow) gives (q;q)_∞ = Σ_n (−1)ⁿq^{n(3n−1)/2}.
Mod 5, m(m−1)/2 takes the values 0, 0, 1, 3, 1 and n(3n−1)/2 the values 0, 1, 0, 2, 2 (m, n ≡ 0, …, 4); the sum is ≡ 4 only for m ≡ 3, n ≡ 1, where ζ^{2m} = ζ is constant.
The involution m ↦ 1 − m preserves m ≡ 3 (mod 5) and m(m − 1)/2 and changes (−1)^m, so the q^{5N+4}-part of the product vanishes; dividing by the q⁵-series (q⁵;q⁵)_∞ preserves this.
Hence Σ_k M(k, 5, 5n + 4)ζ^k = 0; apply equal-classes-from-root-of-unity with Σ_k M(k, 5, 5n + 4) = p(5n + 4) (sum_crankCountMod).

As a corollary p(5n + 4) ≡ 0 (mod 5), Ramanujan's congruence (QM.0/ramanujan-congruences).

The product T(ζ²)T(ζ³) = Σ_{m,n}(−1)^{m+n}ζ^{2m+3n}q^{m(m−1)/2 + n(n−1)/2}; mod 7, m(m−1)/2 takes the values 0, 0, 1, 3, 6, 3, 1, and the sum of two such values is ≡ 5 only when m ≡ n ≡ 4, where ζ^{2m+3n} = ζ⁶ is constant.
The involution m ↦ 1 − m preserves m ≡ 4 (mod 7) and m(m − 1)/2 and changes the sign, so the q^{7N+5}-part vanishes.
Conclude with equal-classes-from-root-of-unity as for crank-mod-five.

nodes.title: Dyson's rank and the rank counts N(m, n)
nodes.statement: The rank of a partition λ is ℓ(λ) − #parts(λ) (largest part minus number of parts; 0 for the empty partition). N(m, n) is the number of partitions of n with rank m (so N(0, 0) = 1, the convention of Folsom–Ono–Rhoades (1.4); Atkin–Swinnerton-Dyer and Garvan set N(0, 0) = 0), and N(k, t, n) = Σ_{m ≡ k (mod t)} N(m, n).
hypotheses: The two conventions for N(0, 0) differ only in the constant term of the generating function.
proofSteps: Define dysonRank λ := (largestPart λ : ℤ) − card λ.parts, dysonRankCount m n := #{λ ⊢ n | dysonRank λ = m}, dysonRankCountMod t k n := Σ_{m ≡ k} dysonRankCount m n.
Conjugation (Tau Ceti's TauCeti.conjugate, an involution by TauCeti.conjugate_conjugate) exchanges largest part and number of parts, so rank(λ′) = −rank(λ) and N(−m, n) = N(m, n).
acceptance: The rank of 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 is 4 − 7 = −3 (Garvan's example).

The ranks of the five partitions of 4 are 3, 1, 0, −1, −3, one in each class mod 5; the ranks of the partitions of 6 are 5, 3, 2, 1, 1, 0, −1, −1, −2, −3, −5, not equidistributed mod 11 (Dyson's observation that led to the crank).

R(−1; q) is Ramanujan's third-order mock theta function f(q)

nodes.title: The rank generating function R(z; q) (Durfee square)
nodes.statement: In LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧: Σ_{n≥0}Σ_m N(m, n)z^m qⁿ = 1 + Σ_{n≥1} q^{n²}/((zq;q)_n(z⁻¹q;q)_n) =: R(z; q). In particular R(−1; q) = Σ_{n≥0} q^{n²}/(−q;q)_n² is Ramanujan's third-order mock theta function f(q), whose coefficient of qⁿ is N(0, 2, n) − N(1, 2, n).
hypotheses: Formal identity; the series converges q-adically since the n-th term has order n².
proofSteps: Decompose a non-empty partition by its Durfee square, the largest n × n square in its Young diagram: the square contributes q^{n²}.
The part to the right of the square is a partition with at most n parts; by conjugation its generating function with z marking its largest part is 1/(zq;q)_n.
The part below the square is a partition with parts ≤ n; with z⁻¹ marking its number of parts its generating function is 1/(z⁻¹q;q)_n.
The rank is (n + largest part of the right piece) − (n + number of parts of the lower piece), matching the exponent of z; the empty partition gives the constant 1.
acceptance: At z = 1: 1 + Σ q^{n²}/(q;q)_n² = 1/(q;q)_∞ (the Durfee-square identity).
R(−1; q) = 1 + q − 2q² + 3q³ − 3q⁴ + 3q⁵ − 5q⁶ + ⋯ (the coefficients of f(q)).

sources.locator: §4, proof of Theorem 4, eq. (4.28), printed p. 40

nodes.title: The rank explains the congruences mod 5 and 7 (Atkin–Swinnerton-Dyer)

proofSteps: By rank-generating-function at z = ζ₅: Σ_k N(k, 5, N)ζ₅^k is the coefficient of q^N in R(ζ₅; q).
The 5-dissection of R(ζ₅; q) (Ramanujan's lost-notebook identity, Garvan's (4.4), equivalent to Atkin–Swinnerton-Dyer's Theorem 1 by Garvan's Theorem 4) has no q^{5N+4} terms.
Conclude with equal-classes-from-root-of-unity; the mod 7 case uses the corresponding 7-dissection.
The dissection identities themselves (Atkin–Swinnerton-Dyer 1954) are not in a read source; see the coverage.

nodes.title: Uniform bounds for q-Pochhammer symbols near roots of unity
nodes.statement: Let ξ = e^{2πih/k} with gcd(h, k) = 1 and let w ∈ ℂ with w^k = 1 and w ∈ ⟨ξ⟩. For q = ξe^{−t} (0 < t ≤ 1): (i) |(wq;q)_n| ≤ C_k for all n; (ii) for every m ≥ 1 there is C_{k,m} with |(wq;q)_n| ≤ C_{k,m}t^m for all n ≥ (m + 1)k. The constants do not depend on n or t.
hypotheses: w a root of unity lying in the cyclic group generated by ξ (for w = 1 this covers (q;q)_n itself).
proofSteps: Group the factors 1 − wq^j into blocks of k consecutive indices j = rk + 1, …, rk + k; with x_r = e^{−rkt} a block equals ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − wξ^i x_r e^{−it}).
Unperturbed, ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − wξ^i x) = 1 − w^kx^k = 1 − x^k because {wξ^i} is the full group of k-th roots of unity; the perturbation e^{−it} changes the block by at most C′_k x_r t.
Hence |block_r| ≤ min(1, (r + 1)k²t) + C′_k x_r t; the product over r ≥ m of (1 + C′_k x_r t) is at most exp(C′_k t Σ_r e^{−rkt}) ≤ exp(C′_k(1+1/k)) since t/(1−e^{−kt})≤t+1/k≤1+1/k, bounded.
The first m blocks give O(t^m); the last incomplete block is bounded by 2^k. Combine.
acceptance: For w = 1 and ξ = 1: |(e^{−t};e^{−t})_n| ≤ n!tⁿ from 1 − e^{−jt} ≤ jt.
Termwise bounds by ∏(1 + |q|^j) are useless here (they grow like e^{c/t}); the block cancellation is essential.

sources.match: The analytic agreement this bound makes rigorous (with w = 1); the estimate itself is supplied by this blueprint.
The radial limit of U(ζ_b^a; q) at ζ_k^h, which follows from this bound (b | k gives w = ζ_b^a ∈ ⟨ζ_k^h⟩).

nodes.title: The unimodal-sequence series U(w; q) and its values at roots of unity
nodes.statement: U(w; q) = Σ_{n≥0}(wq;q)_n(w⁻¹q;q)_n q^{n+1} ∈ LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧, the generating function Σ u(m, n)(−w)^m qⁿ of strongly unimodal sequences of size n and rank m. For a root of unity w = ζ_b^a and ζ = ζ_k^h with b | k, gcd(a, b) = gcd(h, k) = 1, the formal value U(w; ζ) = Σ_{n=0}^{k−1}(wζ;ζ)_n(w⁻¹ζ;ζ)_nζ^{n+1} is a finite sum (the terms with n ≥ k vanish, since some factor 1 − wζ^j is 0). This formal value is distinct from the radial limit of U(w; q) as q → ζ; they are equal by pochhammer-root-of-unity-bound, which is a theorem and not part of the definition.
hypotheses: b | k for the formal value; for b ∤ k the series does not terminate (e.g. U(−1; e^{2πi/3}), where no factor 1 + ζ^j vanishes).
proofSteps: Define unimodalSeries w as Σ_n (wq;q)_n(w⁻¹q;q)_n q^{n+1}, convergent q-adically (the n-th term has order n + 1).
Define unimodalValue a b h k := Σ_{n<k}(ζ_b^aζ_k^h;ζ_k^h)_n(ζ_b^{−a}ζ_k^h;ζ_k^h)_nζ_k^{h(n+1)}.
Termination: since b | k, ζ_b^a = ζ_k^{ha′} for some a′, so 1 − ζ_b^{−a}ζ_k^{hj} = 0 for j ≡ a′ (mod k), which occurs among j ≤ k.
Relation: Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ(w;q)_n(w⁻¹;q)_n = (1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; q), from (w;q)_{n} = (1 − w)(wq;q)_{n−1}.
acceptance: U(−1; q) = q + q² + 3q³ + ⋯ (1, 1, 3 strongly unimodal sequences of sizes 1, 2, 3).
U(−1; −1) = −1 and U(−1; i) = −i, so −4U(−1; ζ) = 4 and 4i: the constants in Ramanujan's claim (ramanujan-radial-limit-claim).

uses.how: −(1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; ζ) is the radial limit of R(w; q) − c·C(w; q)
U(w; q) is the second sum in Choi's identity

nodes.title: Choi's identity relating the rank function to an Appell–Lerch sum
nodes.statement: For q = e^{2πiz} (z ∈ ℍ) and α = e^{2πiu}, β = e^{2πiv} with u, v ∉ ℤz + ℤ: Σ_{n≥0}(αβ)ⁿq^{n²}/((αq;q)_n(βq;q)_n) + Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ(α⁻¹;q)_n(β⁻¹;q)_n = iq^{1/8}(1 − α)(βα⁻¹)^{1/2}(qα⁻¹;q)_∞(β⁻¹;q)_∞µ(u, v; z), with µ Zwegers' Appell–Lerch sum (QM.4/appell-lerch-sum). With α = ζ_b^{−a}, β = ζ_b^a it reads R(ζ_b^a; q) + (1 − ζ_b^a)(1 − ζ_b^{−a})U(ζ_b^a; q) = m(a, b; z)µ(−a/b, a/b; z).
hypotheses: The branch of (βα⁻¹)^{1/2} as in the source; generic u, v (the specialisation used has αβ = 1).
proofSteps: The identity is quoted by Folsom–Ono–Rhoades from Choi and from Ramanujan's lost notebook (Entry 3.4.7 in Andrews–Berndt); its proof is not in a read source.
The specialisation: the first sum is R(w; q) with w = β (rank-generating-function), the second is (1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; q) (unimodal-rank-series relation).
acceptance: At α = β⁻¹ the left side is exactly R(w; q) + (1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; q), which ties the rank mock theta function to U.
The identity involves the non-modular µ; its modular completion enters only through rank-mixed-mock-asymptotic.

nodes.title: Radial asymptotics of the mixed mock modular form m·µ (Folsom–Ono–Rhoades Theorem 3.2)
nodes.statement: Let b | k, gcd(a, b) = gcd(h, k) = 1, bb′ = k, hh′ ≡ −1 (mod k), q = e^{(2πi/k)(h+iz)}, q₁ = e^{(2πi/k)(h′+i/z)}. As z → 0⁺ (z > 0): m(a, b; (h + iz)/k)µ(−a/b, a/b; (h + iz)/k) = (i/z)^{1/2}ψ(γ)^{−1}q^{1/24}q₁^{−1/24}(−1)^{ab′}ζ_{2b}^{ah′−a}ζ_{2b²}^{−3a²kh′}(ζ_b^a − 1)/(1 − ζ_b^{ah′})·(1 + O(q₁^α)) for some α > 1/24, with γ = (h, −(hh′+1)/k; k, −h′) and ψ the η-multiplier.
hypotheses: As stated; z real and positive.
proofSteps: Write m·µ = q^{1/24}ζ_{2b}^{−a}(ζ_b^a − 1)A(−a/b, a/b; Z)/η(Z) with A = ϑµ (FOR (3.15)).
Transform the completion Â = A + (i/2)ϑR (QM.4/zwegers-completion) by (3.10) and (3.11) under γ, Z = γZ′.
Dissect R(−2a/b; Z) into k pieces with the Bringmann–Folsom dissection (FOR Lemma 3.4) and the transformations (3.8)–(3.9) of R and the Mordell integral h.
Show that two of the resulting sums cancel (FOR Lemma 3.5) and bound the others (Lemmas 3.6–3.7), using the η and ϑ transformations (QM.1).
acceptance: The leading term depends only on the cusp h/k through h′ and on a/b; the error is exponentially small in 1/z.
The dissection of R used in Lemma 3.4 is from Bringmann–Folsom, not read here.

sources.match: The statement of Theorem 3.2; its proof occupies §3.3 (pp. 20–25).

nodes.title: Radial asymptotics of the crank function (Folsom–Ono–Rhoades Proposition 3.3)
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of rank-mixed-mock-asymptotic, as z → 0⁺: C(ζ_b^a; (h + iz)/k) = (i/z)^{1/2}ψ(γ)^{−1}q^{1/24}q₁^{−1/24}(−1)^{ab′}ζ_{2b}^{ah′−a}ζ_{2b²}^{−a²kh′}(ζ_b^a − 1)/(1 − ζ_b^{ah′})·(1 + O(q₁^β)) for some β > 1/24.
hypotheses: As in rank-mixed-mock-asymptotic.
proofSteps: Write C(w; q) = (q;q)_∞/((wq;q)_∞(w⁻¹q;q)_∞) as an explicit multiple of η(z)³/ϑ(a/b; z) (Jacobi's product (3.4), QM.0/jacobi-triple-product), equivalently via the Klein form t_{(r,s)} of level b.
Apply the transformation laws of η (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier) and of ϑ (QM.1) under γ.
Expand the transformed product at q₁ → 0: the leading term is the displayed constant and the next term is O(q₁^β).
acceptance: For a/b = 1/2 and h/k = 1/2 this gives the growth of b(q) = C(−1; q) at q = −1 that Ramanujan's claim cancels.
The multiplicative constants of Theorem 3.2 and Proposition 3.3 differ exactly by ζ_{b²}^{−a²h′k}, the constant in Theorem 1.2.

nodes.title: Radial limits of rank minus crank are unimodal values (Folsom–Ono–Rhoades Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement: Let 1 ≤ a < b and 1 ≤ h < k be integers with gcd(a, b) = gcd(h, k) = 1 and b | k, and h′ with hh′ ≡ −1 (mod k). As q → ζ_k^h radially within the unit disc, R(ζ_b^a; q) − ζ_{b²}^{−a²h′k}C(ζ_b^a; q) → −(1 − ζ_b^a)(1 − ζ_b^{−a})U(ζ_b^a; ζ_k^h), where U(ζ_b^a; ζ_k^h) is the terminating formal value of unimodal-rank-series. Here R is the rank generating function (a mock modular form for these w) and C the crank generating function (a modular form).
hypotheses: b | k (otherwise U does not terminate and the statement changes); radial approach.
proofSteps: By choi-identity, R(w; q) − cC(w; q) = [m·µ − cC(w; q)] − (1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; q) with w = ζ_b^a, c = ζ_{b²}^{−a²h′k}.
m·µ − cC → 0: rank-mixed-mock-asymptotic and crank-radial-asymptotic have the same main term, and the error terms are O(z^{−1/2}|q₁|^{min(α,β)−1/24}) → 0.

For U, choose N≥(m+1)k. The terms n≥N have both Pochhammer factors O(t^m) uniformly by pochhammer-root-of-unity-bound, so their sum is O(t^{2m−1}). The finitely many terms k≤n<N tend to 0 since they contain a factor vanishing at the limiting root. The terms n<k tend to the terminating value. A tail beginning at the fixed index k is not uniformly O(t^m) for arbitrary m.
acceptance: a/b = 1/2 gives ramanujan-radial-limit-claim.
The limit is a formal root-of-unity value (a finite sum), while R and C are only defined inside the disc: this is an explicit comparison of the two, not an equality of q-series.

nodes.title: Ramanujan's radial limit claim for f(q) (Folsom–Ono–Rhoades Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: Let f(q) = Σ_{n≥0}q^{n²}/(−q;q)_n² (Ramanujan's third-order mock theta function, = R(−1; q)) and b(q) = (q;q)_∞/(−q;q)_∞² = C(−1; q). If ζ is a primitive root of unity of even order 2k, then as q → ζ radially within the unit disc, f(q) − (−1)^k b(q) → −4Σ_{n=0}^{k−1}(1 + ζ)²(1 + ζ²)²⋯(1 + ζⁿ)²ζ^{n+1} = −4U(−1; ζ).
hypotheses: ζ primitive of even order 2k.
proofSteps: Apply rank-crank-radial-limit with a = 1, b = 2 and ζ = ζ_{2k}^h: R(−1; q) = f(q) (rank-generating-function), C(−1; q) = b(q) (crank-generating-function at z = −1), and ζ_4^{−h′·2k} = (−1)^{k} since h′ is odd.
(1 − ζ₂)(1 − ζ₂⁻¹) = 4 and U(−1; ζ) = Σ_{n<k}(−ζ;ζ)_n²ζ^{n+1} (unimodal-rank-series).
acceptance: ζ = i: f(q) − b(q) → 4i.
At odd-order roots of unity f itself has a finite value; the claim concerns the even orders where f grows exponentially.

nodes.title: Positive definite forms of discriminant −d, their CM points and weights
nodes.statement: For an integer d > 0 with d ≡ 0 or 3 (mod 4), Q_d is the set of positive definite integral binary quadratic forms Q = [a, b, c] = aX² + bXY + cY² (a > 0) with b² − 4ac = −d, primitive or not, with the action of Γ = PSL₂(ℤ) by (Q∘γ)(X, Y) = Q(aX + bY, cX + dY). Its CM point is the unique root α_Q = (−b + i√d)/(2a) ∈ ℍ of Q(X, 1), and w_Q = |Γ_Q| is the order of its stabiliser in PSL₂(ℤ): w_Q = 2 if Q ∼ [a, 0, a], 3 if Q ∼ [a, a, a], 1 otherwise. Q_d/Γ is finite (every class contains a unique reduced form |b| ≤ a ≤ c, with b ≥ 0 if |b| = a or a = c), and the weighted count Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ}1/w_Q is the Hurwitz–Kronecker class number H(d).
hypotheses: d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4); for d ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4), Q_d is empty.
The class number H(d) of Tau Ceti's ModularForms layer 11 (reduced forms, weights 1/2 and 1/3) is the same weighted count.
proofSteps: Define heegnerForms d as {Q : Fin 3 → ℤ | Q 0 > 0 ∧ Q 1² − 4·Q 0·Q 2 = −d} with the right action of SL₂(ℤ) through its image in PSL₂(ℤ).
cmPoint Q := (−b + i√d)/(2a) ∈ ℍ; it satisfies α_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹α_Q (Möbius action), so it depends only on the orbit up to the action.

Import the reduced-form representatives and reduction theory from Tau Ceti ModularForms layer11 rather than replanning it. Add the CM-point/action comparison to that existing representation; reduction gives a≤√(d/3) and the finite orbit representatives.
stabiliserOrder Q := card of the stabiliser of Q in PSL₂(ℤ), equal to the stabiliser of α_Q, which is trivial except at the orbits of i and ρ = e^{2πi/3}.

the points α_Q are the fixed points of integral matrices of determinant n and trace r with r² − 4n = −d
the Hurwitz class numbers H(D) are the weighted counts of the same classes

nodes.statement: With J(τ) = j(τ) − 744 = q⁻¹ + 196884q + ⋯ the normalised Hauptmodul of PSL₂(ℤ) (j = E₄³/Δ, Tau Ceti ModularForms layer 0), t(d) = Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ} J(α_Q)/w_Q for d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4), and t(d) = 0 otherwise. The sum runs over all forms, primitive or not.
hypotheses: j is the normalised modular invariant E₄³/Δ (requested from Tau Ceti ModularForms layer 0); J(α_Q) depends only on the class of Q.
proofSteps: Define modularTrace d := Σ_{Q ∈ heegnerClasses d} (j(α_Q) − 744)/w_Q.
Independence of representatives: j is PSL₂(ℤ)-invariant and α_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹α_Q.

nodes.title: Zagier's weight-3/2 form g = θ₁E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶
nodes.statement: g(τ) = θ₁(τ)E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶ on ℍ, with θ₁(τ) = Σ_{n∈ℤ}(−1)ⁿq^{n²} (= jacobiTheta₂(1/2, 2τ)), E₄ the normalised Eisenstein series of weight 4 and η the Dedekind eta function. It is a weakly holomorphic modular form of weight 3/2 on Γ₀(4) in Kohnen's plus space, with Fourier expansion g(τ) = Σ_{d≥−1}B(d)q^d = q⁻¹ − 2 + 248q³ − 492q⁴ + 4119q⁷ − 7256q⁸ + ⋯, where B(d) = 0 unless d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4).
hypotheses: The half-integral weight structure (Γ₀(4), theta multiplier, plus space) is MetaplecticAutomorphicForms:MP.7's; the definition itself is an explicit quotient.
proofSteps: Define zagierTraceForm τ := jacobiTheta₂ (1/2) (2τ)·E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶ using Mathlib's jacobiTheta₂, ModularForm.E₄ and ModularForm.eta (η(4τ) ≠ 0 by ModularForm.eta_ne_zero).
Its q-expansion: θ₁ = 1 − 2q + 2q⁴ − ⋯, E₄(4τ) = 1 + 240q⁴ + ⋯, η(4τ)^{−6} = q^{−1}(1 + 6q⁴ + ⋯); multiply.
The plus condition B(d) ≠ 0 ⇒ d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4): θ₁ has exponents n² ≡ 0, 1 and E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶ has exponents ≡ −1 (mod 4).

nodes.title: The recursions for the coefficients of g (Zagier §2)
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 0: Σ_{r∈ℤ}B(4n − r²) = 0 and Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²) = 240σ₃(n), with σ₃(0) := 1/240 and B(d) := 0 for d < −1. These determine all B(d) recursively from B(−1) = 1: B(4n − 1) = 240σ₃(n) − Σ_{2≤r≤√(4n+1)}r²B(4n − r²) and B(4n) = −2Σ_{1≤r≤√(4n+1)}B(4n − r²).
proofSteps: gθ, with θ = Σq^{n²}, is a weakly holomorphic form of weight 2 on Γ₀(4) whose U₄-image lies in M^!₂(SL₂(ℤ)) (Kohnen's plus-space lemma, requested from MP.7); its constant term is B(0) + 2B(−1) = 0 and it has no polar terms, so (gθ)|U₄ ∈ M₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 0 (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).

The Rankin–Cohen bracket [g, θ] = g′θ − 3gθ′ (′ = q d/dq) is modular of weight 4 (the first Rankin–Cohen bracket of weights 3/2 and 1/2: the correction terms of the derivatives cancel), and [g, θ]|U₄ ∈ M₄(SL₂(ℤ)) = ℂE₄ (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_four_rank_one).

Its q^{4n}-coefficient is Σ_r(4n − 4r²)B(4n − r²) = −8Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²) (using the first identity); the constant term is −8B(−1) = −8, so [g, θ]|U₄ = −8E₄, and the coefficients 1, 240σ₃(n) of E₄ give Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²) = 240σ₃(n) (with σ₃(0) = 1/240).
Read off Fourier coefficients: the coefficient of qⁿ in (gθ)|U₄ is Σ_r B(4n − r²); in [g, θ]|U₄ it is a multiple of Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²).
Solving the r = 1 and r = 0 terms gives the recursion.
acceptance: The recursion uses only B(−1) and B(0) as initial values.

nodes.title: The weight-two logarithmic derivative Λ_d of the class polynomial
nodes.statement: For d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4): Λ_d(τ) = Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ}(1/w_Q)·j′(τ)/(j(τ) − j(α_Q)), a meromorphic modular form of weight 2 on SL₂(ℤ), holomorphic at ∞, with a simple pole at each α ∈ ℍ satisfying a quadratic equation over ℤ of discriminant −d, of residue 1 as a function on ℍ (Zagier's ‘residue 1/|Γ_α|’ is the residue of Λ_d dτ in the local coordinate of the quotient curve, which differs by the factor |Γ_α| at the elliptic points i and ρ), and with q-expansion −(2πi)⁻¹Λ_d = H(d) + t(d)q + O(q²). It is the logarithmic derivative of H_d(j(τ)) = ∏(j(τ) − j(α_Q))^{1/w_Q}, and it is uniquely characterised among forms with at most simple poles by its poles and residues because M₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 0.
hypotheses: j′ = dj/dτ; Λ_d avoids the fractional powers in H_d.
proofSteps: Define heegnerLogDeriv d τ := Σ_{Q ∈ heegnerClasses d} (1/w_Q)·deriv j τ/(j τ − j α_Q).
Modularity of weight 2: j′ has weight 2 and j is invariant.
Residues: j − j(α_Q) vanishes at α_Q to order |Γ_{α_Q}| = w_Q (to order 2 at i, since j − 1728 = E₆²/Δ, and to order 3 at ρ, since j = E₄³/Δ), so (1/w_Q)j′/(j − j(α_Q)) has residue 1.
Expansion at ∞: −(2πi)^{−1}j′ = q^{−1} − 196884q + ⋯ and j − j(α) = q^{−1} − J(α) + O(q), so each term is 1 + J(α_Q)q + O(q²).
Uniqueness: two meromorphic weight-2 forms with the same principal parts differ by a holomorphic weight-2 form, which is 0 (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).

nodes.title: The logarithmic derivative of Φ_n(j, j) (Zagier (9))
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 not a square let D_n(τ) = ∏_{ad=n, a,d>0}∏_{b=0}^{d−1}(j(τ) − j((aτ + b)/d)) (= Φ_n(j(τ), j(τ)) for the n-th modular polynomial). Then D′_n/D_n = Σ_{|r|<2√n}Λ_{4n−r²} as meromorphic functions on ℍ. For n = m² a square the same holds for D_n/D₁-type quotients: the factor with a = d = m, b = 0 is omitted on the left and Σ_{|r|<2}Λ_{4−r²} is subtracted on the right.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; the square case as stated.
proofSteps: Γ-invariance of D_n: right multiplication by γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) permutes Γ\M_n, whose representatives are the matrices (a b; 0 d), ad = n, 0 ≤ b < d (the coset argument of HeckeRing.GL2.heckeSlashSum_slash_invariant), so D_n is a weakly holomorphic modular function and D′_n/D_n a meromorphic weight-2 form, holomorphic at ∞.

Zeros: D_n(τ) = 0 iff j(τ) = j(Mτ) for some M ∈ M_n iff τ is fixed by some M ∈ M_n (j is injective on Γ\ℍ); the fixed points of M with trace r are the α_Q with disc(Q) = r² − 4n, |r| < 2√n (n not a square excludes scalar M).

Count zeros in local quotient coordinates. At α of stabiliser order w, j−j(α) has order w in τ−α. The determinant-n branches fixing α therefore contribute zeros with the corresponding ramification multiplicities, rather than one simple zero per pair ±M on ℍ. Match these counts with the sum of Λ_{4n−r²}, each of which has residue1 on ℍ; include elliptic stabilisers and omit the scalar branch in the square case. The detailed count must be checked in the source before asserting this equality.
Equality: the difference is a holomorphic weight-2 form on SL₂(ℤ), hence 0 (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).
acceptance: The multiplicity bookkeeping at elliptic points (w_Q = 2, 3) is what the weights 1/w_Q in Λ_d account for.

sources.match: The classical identity (9), in the logarithmic-derivative form that avoids the fractional powers of H_d.

nodes.title: The first recursion for t(d) and the Kronecker–Hurwitz relation (Zagier (5), (7))
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1: Σ_{|r|<2√n} t(4n − r²) = −4 if n is a square, 2 if 4n + 1 is a square, and 0 otherwise; and Σ_{|r|<2√n}H(4n − r²) = Σ_{d|n}max(d, n/d) + (1/6 if n is a square, 0 otherwise).
hypotheses: n ≥ 1 (n and 4n + 1 cannot both be squares).
proofSteps: Expand D_n at ∞ with the representatives (a b; 0 d): j(τ) − j((aτ + b)/d) = q⁻¹ − e^{−2πib/d}q^{−a/d} + O(q^{>0}); the product over b is q^{−d} − q^{−a}(1 + O(q^{>1})) = ±q^{−max(a,d)}(1 − ε_aq + O(q²)) with ε_a = 1 iff |a − d| = 1.
Hence, with A = Σ_{ad=n}max(a, d) and ε the number of factorisations n = ad with |a − d| = 1 (2 if 4n + 1 is a square, else 0): −(2πi)⁻¹D′_n/D_n = −q(d/dq)log D_n = A + εq + O(q²).
By modular-diagonal-log-derivative and heegnerLogDeriv_qExpansion the left side is Σ_r(H(4n − r²) + t(4n − r²)q) + O(q²); compare the q⁰ and q¹ coefficients.

Square n = m²: use the quotient form of modular-diagonal-log-derivative. The factors with a = d = m, b ≠ 0 contribute ∏_{b=1}^{m−1}(1 − ζ_m^{−b})q^{−1}(1 + O(q²)) = m·q^{−(m−1)}(1 + O(q²)), so the q⁰ comparison gives Σ_r H(4n − r²) − (H(4) + 2H(3)) = Σ_{d|n}max(d, n/d) − 1, i.e. the extra term 1/6 = H(4) + 2H(3) − 1, and the q¹ comparison gives Σ_r t(4n − r²) = t(4) + 2t(3) = −4.

sources.match: Recursion (5) and the class number relation (7) proved in §3.

nodes.title: The weight-two identity behind the second recursion (Zagier Proposition (12))
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 not a square and τ ∈ ℍ: (E₄E₆/Δ)(τ)·Σ_{M∈Γ\M_n}(E₄|₄M)(τ)/(j(τ) − j(Mτ)) = (1/(4πi))Σ_{|r|<2√n}(r² − n)Λ_{4n−r²}(τ), where (E₄|₄M)(τ) = n³(cτ + d)^{−4}E₄(Mτ) for M = (a b; c d).
hypotheses: n not a square.
proofSteps: Both sides are meromorphic weight-2 forms on SL₂(ℤ), holomorphic at ∞, with at most simple poles; it suffices to compare residues (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).

At a fixed point α of M with c > 0, λ = cα + d is a quadratic integer of trace r = tr M and norm n, and the residue of the left summand is (2πi)^{−1}·(−λ̄³/(λ − λ̄)), computed from Dj = −E₄²E₆/Δ, E₄(Mα) = E₄(α) and (d/dτ)(Mτ) = n(cτ + d)^{−2} (source p. 5).

Average the summand with its involutive partner nM⁻¹: their residues sum to (2πi)⁻¹(λ³−λ̄³)/(λ−λ̄)=(2πi)⁻¹(r²−n). Thus replacing each summand by the average gives the factor1/2 printed in the proposition. The sum of the pair itself does not carry that factor.
At elliptic points (α a root of E₄ or E₆) the same comparison holds with the stabiliser weights; this case is left to the reader in the source.
acceptance: For non-square n the q⁰ coefficient gives the classical identity Σ_{|r|<2√n}(n − r²)H(4n − r²) = Σ_{d|n}min(d, n/d)³.
The identity is between weight-2 forms, so it is again rigid by M₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 0.

nodes.title: The second recursion for t(d) (Zagier (6))
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1: Σ_{1≤r<2√n} r²t(4n − r²) = −240σ₃(n) + (−8n if n is a square; 4n + 1 if 4n + 1 is a square; 0 otherwise).
proofSteps: Write the left side S_n of weight-two-trace-proposition as Σ_{ad=n}a³S_{a,d} with S_{a,d}(τ) = (E₄E₆/Δ)(τ)·d⁻¹Σ_{0≤b<d}E₄((aτ + b)/d)/(j(τ) − j((aτ + b)/d)).
Expand: for a < d, S_{a,d} = 1 + (240δ_{a,1}σ₃(n) + δ_{a,d−1})q + O(q²); for a > d, S_{a,d} = −δ_{a,d+1}q + O(q²) (only the pairs (l, m) listed in the source contribute).
So the q-coefficient is C₁ = 240σ₃(n) − (3n + 1 if 4n + 1 is a square), while by the proposition and heegnerLogDeriv_qExpansion C₁ = ½Σ_{|r|<2√n}(n − r²)t(4n − r²).
Combine with trace-first-recursion (2·(6) − n·(5)) to obtain (6) for non-square n.
Square n: the same computation including the terms with a = d, which the source leaves to the reader.

nodes.title: Traces of singular moduli are coefficients of a weight-3/2 form (Zagier Theorem 1)
nodes.statement: For every d > 0, t(d) = −B(d), where g(τ) = θ₁(τ)E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶ = Σ_{d≥−1}B(d)q^d (zagier-trace-form) and t(d) is the modular trace of the singular moduli of discriminant −d.
hypotheses: d > 0 (both sides vanish for d ≡ 1, 2 mod 4).
proofSteps: Extend t by t(−1) := −1 and t(0) := 2 (so that −t(−1) = B(−1), −t(0) = B(0)); then (5) and (6) (trace-first-recursion, trace-second-recursion) become Σ_{r∈ℤ}(−t)(4n − r²) = 0 and Σ_{r>0}r²(−t)(4n − r²) = 240σ₃(n) for all n ≥ 1, the boundary terms r² = 4n and r² = 4n + 1 accounting for −4, −8n and 2, 4n + 1.
B satisfies the same identities (zagier-trace-form-recursions), and these identities determine a sequence from its values at −1 and 0 by recursion on d.
Hence −t = B.
acceptance: The theorem is an identity of numbers (traces of algebraic integers) with Fourier coefficients; it involves no Eichler integral or radial limit.

nodes.title: Vertex algebra (Borcherds' axioms)
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring and V an R-module. A vertex algebra structure on V is a pair (Y, 1) with Y : V →ₗ[R] VertexOperator R V (Mathlib's vertex operators: R-linear maps from V to Laurent series in z with coefficients in V, support bounded below) and a vacuum vector 1 ∈ V. Write u_n := VertexOperator.ncoeff (Y u) n ∈ End_R(V), so that Y(u,z) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} u_n z^{−n−1}. The axioms are: (creation) u_n 1 = 0 for n ≥ 0 and u_{−1} 1 = u; (Borcherds identity) for all u, v, w ∈ V and m, n, q ∈ ℤ, Σ_{i≥0} C(m,i) (u_{q+i} v)_{m+n−i} w = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^i C(q,i) ( u_{m+q−i}(v_{n+i} w) − (−1)^q v_{n+q−i}(u_{m+i} w) ), where C(m,i) = m(m−1)⋯(m−i+1)/i! ∈ ℤ is Mathlib's Ring.choose m i. The truncation axiom (for u, v there is N with u_n v = 0 for all n ≥ N) holds automatically because the support of Y(u,z)v is bounded below in z; hence both sums in the Borcherds identity are finite. Convention: index n of u_n is the 'mode' of Borcherds and Matsuo–Nagatomo; (u_n) for n ≥ 0 are the annihilation modes.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring
V is an R-module
proofSteps: Package the data as a structure whose field Y has type V →ₗ[R] VertexOperator R V and whose field vac is the vacuum; the two creation equations and the Borcherds identity are Prop fields stated with VertexOperator.ncoeff and Ring.choose.

Truncation: HVertexOperator.coeff_isPWOsupport gives that the support of the Laurent series Y(u,z)v is partially well ordered, hence bounded below in ℤ; since VertexOperator.ncoeff A n = HVertexOperator.coeff A (−n−1) (VertexOperator.ncoeff_apply), u_n v = 0 for n large.

Finiteness of the sums: the i-th term on the left vanishes once q+i exceeds the truncation bound of (u,v); on the right once n+i and m+i exceed the bounds of (v,w) and (u,w). State the identity with finite sums over ℕ (finsum) and record the finiteness as an API lemma.
acceptance: For a commutative ℚ-algebra A with derivation ∂, u_n v := (∂^{−n−1}u/(−n−1)!)·v for n ≤ −1 and u_n v := 0 for n ≥ 0 is a vertex algebra with vacuum 1 (Borcherds 1992 §3; Matsuo–Nagatomo Note 3.1.3).
The definition agrees with Matsuo–Nagatomo Definition 3.1.1 (B0)–(B2) under (p,q,r) = (m,n,q).

sources.match: Definition, stated over ℝ; here over a commutative ring with the same three axioms.

nodes.title: Vacuum, translation and derivation rules in a vertex algebra
nodes.statement: Let (V, Y, 1) be a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R. Define D : V → V by D v := v_{−2}1 and, for k ≥ 0, D^{(k)} v := v_{−k−1}1. Then: (a) 1_n v = δ_{n,−1} v for all n (Y(1,z) = id); (b) D 1 = 0; (c) (Dv)_n = −n v_{n−1} for all n; (d) [D, v_n] = −n v_{n−1}, i.e. D(v_n w) = (Dv)_n w + v_n(Dw), so D is a derivation of every product; (e) k·D^{(k)} v = D(D^{(k−1)} v) for k ≥ 1, hence k!·D^{(k)} = D^k; (f) u_n 1 = D^{(−n−1)} u for n ≤ −1.
hypotheses: (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra over R
proofSteps: (b): put u = v = w = 1 and m = n = q = −1 in the Borcherds identity (Matsuo–Nagatomo (18)).
(e),(f): put v = w = 1, m = 0, n = −2, q = n; the creation axiom gives (u_n 1)_{−2}1 = −n u_{n−1}1, which is (e) after reindexing (Matsuo–Nagatomo (19)).
(a): put v = w = 1, m = −1, n = q', q = 0 and use (b) (Matsuo–Nagatomo (20)).
(c): put v = 1, m = n', n = 0, q = −2 and use (a) (Matsuo–Nagatomo (21)).
(d): put w = 1, m = 0, n = −2, q = n (Matsuo–Nagatomo (22)); compare with (c).
acceptance: In VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation, D is the given derivation ∂.
Over a ℚ-algebra, Y(u,z)1 = e^{zD}u as formal power series.

sources.match: Each item is one substitution in the Borcherds identity, as listed there.

nodes.title: Commutator and associativity formulas
nodes.statement: In a vertex algebra over a commutative ring, for all u, v ∈ V and m, n, q ∈ ℤ: (commutator formula) [u_m, v_n] = Σ_{i≥0} C(m,i) (u_i v)_{m+n−i}; (associativity formula, applied to each w) (u_q v)_n w = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^i C(q,i) ( u_{q−i}(v_{n+i}w) − (−1)^q v_{n+q−i}(u_iw) ) as a pointwise finite sum in V. The associativity sum need not have finite support as a family of endomorphisms; only its evaluation at each w is finitely supported. In particular [u_0, v_n] = (u_0 v)_n, so u ↦ u_0 acts by derivations of all products.
hypotheses: (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra
proofSteps: Set q = 0 in the Borcherds identity: the right side is u_m v_n w − v_n u_m w since C(0,i) = δ_{i,0} (Matsuo–Nagatomo (25)).

Set m = 0 in the Borcherds identity: the left side is (u_q v)_n w since C(0,i) = δ_{i,0} (Matsuo–Nagatomo (26)). Keep w explicit in the finite sum: truncation bounds depend on w, so finsum in End(V) is not justified.
For m = 0 the commutator formula reads [u_0, v_n] = (u_0 v)_n.
acceptance: For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation all commutators vanish, consistent with u_i v = 0 for i ≥ 0.
Borcherds 1986 §8 states the commutator formula [u_m, v_n] = Σ_j C(m,j)(u_j v)_{m+n−j}.

nodes.title: Skew symmetry
nodes.statement: In a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R, for all u, v ∈ V and n ∈ ℤ: v_n u = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^{n+i+1} D^{(i)}(u_{n+i} v), where D^{(i)}x := x_{−i−1}1 (a finite sum by truncation). In particular v_0 u + u_0 v = Σ_{i≥1} (−1)^{i+1} D^{(i)}(u_i v) lies in the R-span DV_div := Σ_{i≥1} D^{(i)}(V), and, when2 is invertible in R, u_0 u∈DV_div by dividing the self-skew identity by2. The arbitrary-ring alternating conclusion requires a further argument, not this division.
hypotheses: (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra
proofSteps: Put w = 1, m = −1, n = 0, q = n in the Borcherds identity and simplify with the creation axiom and the vacuum-translation lemma (Matsuo–Nagatomo (23)).
For n = 0 separate the i = 0 term: v_0 u = −u_0 v + Σ_{i≥1}(−1)^{i+1}D^{(i)}(u_i v).
acceptance: For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation with n = −1 the identity is v u = u v + (terms with ∂), i.e. commutativity of A.
Borcherds 1986 §4 takes this as axiom (iv).

nodes.title: The Lie algebra V/DV of a vertex algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R and let DV := Σ_{i≥1} D^{(i)}(V) (the R-span of all D^{(i)}w, i ≥ 1; over a ℚ-algebra this is the image of D). Then DV is a two-sided ideal for the product (u, v) ↦ u_0 v, and V/DV is a Lie algebra over R with bracket [u + DV, v + DV] := u_0 v + DV. The map u ↦ u_0 makes V a module over the Lie algebra V/DV (DV acts by 0: (D^{(i)}w)_0 = 0 for i ≥ 1), and each u_0 acts by derivations of all products.
hypotheses: V is a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R
proofSteps: Derive the divided-translation identity (D^{(i)}w)_n=(−1)^i binomial(n,i)w_{n−i} directly from the Borcherds identity; at n=0 and i≥1 the binomial coefficient vanishes. Iterating D alone only shows i! times the claimed identity over an arbitrary ring, which is insufficient when i! is not invertible.

u_0 (D^{(i)} w) = D^{(i)}(u_0 w): u_0 commutes with D by [D, u_n] = −n u_{n−1} at n = 0, and with divided powers by the same identity applied to w_{−i−1}1 and the commutator formula; so DV is a right ideal.

Skew symmetry proves antisymmetry modulo DV. When2 is invertible it also proves alternation u_0u∈DV by dividing the self-skew relation by2. The arbitrary-ring LieRing construction retains an explicit unresolved alternating-bracket obligation; all moonshine consumers are in characteristic0.
Jacobi identity: the commutator formula at m = n = 0 gives u_0(v_0 w) − v_0(u_0 w) = (u_0 v)_0 w.
Package as a LieRing and LieAlgebra R instance on the quotient module V ⧸ DV, and the action as a LieModule.
acceptance: For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation, all 0-products vanish, so V/DV is abelian.
Borcherds 1986 §4: 'If V is any vertex algebra then V/DV is a Lie algebra … [u,v] = u0(v).'

nodes.title: Homomorphisms and automorphisms of vertex algebras
nodes.statement: For vertex algebras (V, Y, 1) and (W, Y', 1') over R, a homomorphism is an R-linear map f : V → W with f(1) = 1' and f(u_n v) = f(u)_n f(v) for all u, v, n (equivalently f ∘ Y(u,z) = Y'(f u, z) ∘ f). The automorphisms of V form a group Aut(V) under composition. If V carries a conformal vector ω (node conformal-vector) the conformal automorphisms are those with g(ω) = ω; if V carries a bilinear form (,) the isometric conformal automorphisms are those with (gu, gv) = (u, v). For a group G, an action of G on V by vertex algebra automorphisms is a group homomorphism G →* Aut(V).
hypotheses: V, W vertex algebras over the same commutative ring R
proofSteps: Define VertexAlgebra.Hom as a structure extending V →ₗ[R] W with the two compatibility fields; composition and identity are immediate.
Define Aut(V) as the group of invertible homomorphisms (bundled as R-linear equivalences satisfying the two conditions); the inverse of a bijective homomorphism is a homomorphism.
Define the subgroups of conformal and of conformal isometric automorphisms as stabilizers.
acceptance: The identity of V is an automorphism; every automorphism commutes with D.

nodes.title: Existence theorem for vertex algebras (locality criterion)
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, V a k-vector space, 1 ∈ V nonzero, T ∈ End_k(V), and S a set of fields on V (formal series A(z) = Σ A_n z^{−n−1} with A_n ∈ End(V) and A(z)w ∈ V((z)) for every w) such that: (S1) the fields in S are pairwise local: for A, B ∈ S there is N with (y−z)^N [A(y), B(z)] = 0; (S2) the vectors A^{λ1}_{−j1−1}⋯A^{λk}_{−jk−1}1 (k ≥ 0, j_i ≥ 0, A^{λi} ∈ S) span V; (S3) each A ∈ S is creative (A_n 1 = 0 for n ≥ 0) and translation covariant: [T, A(z)] = ∂_z A(z), with T1 = 0. Then there is a unique vertex algebra structure on V with vacuum 1 such that Y(A_{−1}1, z) = A(z) for every A ∈ S; its translation operator is T.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
S pairwise local, creative, translation covariant, generating V from 1
proofSteps: Let O be the space of creative fields; the residual products A(z)_{(m)}B(z) of local fields are local (Dong's lemma, Matsuo–Nagatomo Proposition 1.5.5) and creative (Lemma 4.1.2).

The space ⟨S⟩ of fields generated by S under residual products is pairwise local and contains the identity field; by Li's theorem (Matsuo–Nagatomo Theorem 3.3.1, via the Borcherds identity for local fields, Corollary 2.2.2 and Theorem 2.4.1) it is a vertex algebra.
Translation covariance and (S2) make the state map A(z) ↦ A_{−1}1 bijective from ⟨S⟩ onto V (Theorem 5.3.3); transport the structure along it.
Uniqueness: a vertex algebra structure is determined by the fields of a generating set, by the associativity formula (node vertex-algebra-commutator-formula).
acceptance: The vertex algebra structure of VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation is recovered from S = {Y(a, z) : a ∈ A} with T = ∂.
Applied to S = {Y(a⊗1), Y(1⊗b)} it produces the tensor product vertex algebra (node vertex-algebra-tensor-product).

nodes.title: Tensor product of vertex algebras
nodes.statement: Let V, W be vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0. The k-vector space V ⊗_k W carries a unique vertex algebra structure with vacuum 1 ⊗ 1 and (a ⊗ b)_n (c ⊗ d) = Σ_{i∈ℤ} (a_i c) ⊗ (b_{n−1−i} d) (a finite sum by truncation), i.e. Y(a⊗b, z) = Y(a,z) ⊗ Y(b,z). The maps a ↦ a ⊗ 1 and b ↦ 1 ⊗ b are vertex algebra homomorphisms whose images commute: [(a⊗1)_m, (1⊗b)_n] = 0.
hypotheses: V, W vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0
proofSteps: Define the fields Y(a⊗1, z) := Y(a,z) ⊗ id and Y(1⊗b, z) := id ⊗ Y(b,z) on V ⊗ W; they are creative for 1⊗1 and translation covariant for T := D_V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ D_W.
Locality: fields from the same factor are local by locality in V or W (Matsuo–Nagatomo (27)); fields from different factors commute.

The products (a⊗1)_{−1}(1⊗b)_{−1}(1⊗1) = a⊗b span, so the existence theorem gives the vertex algebra; normal ordering identifies Y(a⊗b, z) with Y(a,z)⊗Y(b,z), which yields the displayed formula for the modes.
The two inclusions are homomorphisms by uniqueness in the existence theorem.
acceptance: Borcherds 1992 §3 formula (a ⊗ b)_n(c ⊗ d) = Σ_i (a_i c) ⊗ (b_{n−1−i} d).
V ⊗ k (k the one-dimensional vertex algebra with 1_{−1} = id) is isomorphic to V.

nodes.title: The Virasoro algebra and modules of given central charge
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0. The Virasoro algebra Vir_k is the Lie algebra over k with basis {L_n : n ∈ ℤ} ∪ {C} and bracket [L_m, L_n] = (m − n) L_{m+n} + ((m³ − m)/12) δ_{m+n,0} C, [C, x] = 0 for all x. For c ∈ k, a Virasoro module of central charge c is a Lie module M over Vir_k on which C acts as multiplication by c; equivalently a family of operators L_n ∈ End(M) with [L_m, L_n] = (m−n)L_{m+n} + c(m³−m)/12 δ_{m+n,0}.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0 (the coefficient 1/12 must make sense)
proofSteps: Define Vir_k as the k-module with basis ℤ ⊕ {C} (Finsupp) and the bracket extended bilinearly; check antisymmetry ((m³−m) is odd in m) and the Jacobi identity on basis elements (the cocycle ψ(m,n) = (m³−m)/12 δ_{m+n,0} satisfies the 2-cocycle identity).
Define the module predicate as a LieModule together with the scalar action of C.
acceptance: (L_{−1}, L_0, L_1) span a copy of sl₂: (2L_0, L_{−1}, −L_1) is an sl₂-triple.

nodes.title: Conformal vector of a vertex algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with translation D (node vertex-algebra-vacuum-translation). A conformal vector of central charge c ∈ k is ω ∈ V such that: ω_0 v = Dv for all v; ω_1 ω = 2ω; ω_2 ω = 0; ω_3 ω = (c/2)·1; ω_i ω = 0 for i ≥ 4; and L_0 := ω_1 is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues: V = ⊕_{n∈ℤ} V_n (internal direct sum) with V_n := ker(L_0 − n). Put L_n := ω_{n+1}. The eigenvalue n of v ∈ V_n is its (conformal) weight. Convention (Borcherds): in the moonshine module the space of weight n + 1 is Borcherds' V_n (degree n).
hypotheses: V vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0
c ∈ k
proofSteps: Structure with fields ω, c and the six conditions, the last as DirectSum.IsInternal of the eigenspaces Module.End.eigenspace L_0 (n : k), n ∈ ℤ.
acceptance: For the zero derivation commutative vertex algebra, ω = 0 is a conformal vector of central charge 0.
For the lattice vertex algebra of a nondegenerate even lattice of rank d, ω = ½ Σ_i h_i(−1)h^i(−1)1 (dual bases) is a conformal vector of central charge d (node lattice-vertex-algebra).

nodes.title: Modes of a conformal vector form a Virasoro module

nodes.title: Vertex operator algebra
nodes.statement: A vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 is a vertex algebra V over k with a conformal vector ω of central charge c such that each weight space V_n = ker(L_0 − n) is finite-dimensional and V_n = 0 for all sufficiently negative n (V = ⊕_{n ≥ N} V_n). It is nonnegatively graded when V_n = 0 for n < 0 (Borcherds' definition: all L_0-eigenvalues are nonnegative integers), and of CFT type when moreover 1 ≠ 0 and V_0 = k·1 (a one-dimensional vacuum space). A homomorphism of vertex operator algebras is a vertex algebra homomorphism sending ω to ω; Aut(V, ω) is the group of conformal automorphisms, and each of its elements preserves every V_n.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: Structure extending the vertex algebra by a conformal vector and the two finiteness conditions (FiniteDimensional k (V_n) for all n; ∃ N, ∀ n < N, V_n = ⊥).
Nonnegative grading and CFT type are predicates, not fields.
Conformal automorphisms preserve weight spaces because they commute with L_0 = ω_1.
acceptance: A finite-dimensional commutative k-algebra with the zero derivation and ω = 0 is a vertex operator algebra of central charge 0 concentrated in weight 0.

The lattice vertex algebra of a positive definite even lattice of rank d is a nonnegatively graded vertex operator algebra of CFT type and central charge d; the lattice vertex algebra of II_{1,1} is not a vertex operator algebra.
Agreement with Jurisich 1998 Definition 4 (V1)–(V10) and with Borcherds 1992 §3 (nonnegative case).

nodes.title: Invariant bilinear forms compatible with the conformal vector
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω and locally nilpotent L₁, and θ a vertex algebra automorphism of V with θ² = 1 and θ(ω) = ω (the Cartan involution; θ = id for the moonshine module). A symmetric bilinear form (·,·) on V is θ-invariant (compatible with ω in Borcherds' sense) if for every u ∈ V_i (L_0-weight i), all n ∈ ℤ and all v, w ∈ V: (u_n v, w) = (−1)^i Σ_{j≥0} (1/j!) (v, (L_1^j θ(u))_{2i−j−n−2} w). For θ = id this is the Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky invariance (Y(u,z)v, w) = (v, Y(e^{zL_1}(−z^{−2})^{L_0}u, z^{−1})w). The associated contravariant form is (u, v)_0 := −(u, θ v).
hypotheses: V vertex algebra over k with conformal vector ω
θ ∈ Aut(V), θ² = 1, θω = ω

L₁ is locally nilpotent, so the adjoint sum terminates. This holds for a VOA whose weights are bounded below, and for lattice vertex algebras by the lower bound in each fixed lattice-degree sector; it does not follow merely from integer diagonalisation of L₀ for an arbitrary conformal vertex algebra.
proofSteps: Define the predicate IsInvariantForm θ B by the displayed identity for homogeneous u; extend to all u by linearity using the weight decomposition.
Derived properties: taking u = ω (weight 2, L_1ω = 0, θω = ω) gives L_n* = L_{−n}; taking n = −1, v = 1 gives (V_i, V_j) = 0 for i ≠ j (use L_0* = L_0); for u ∈ P^1 the formula gives u_0* = −θ(u)_0.
acceptance: The zero form is invariant for every θ.

For the lattice vertex algebra of an even unimodular lattice, the Fock-space form with r(i)* = r(−i) and (e^r, e^s) = δ_{r,s} (Borcherds 1986 §2(v)) is invariant for the Cartan involution θ(e^r) = e^{−r} for the normalized bimultiplicative section (or θ(ι(a)) = (−1)^{(r,r)/2}ι(a⁻¹) for an arbitrary double-cover lift), θ(r(i)) = −r(i).

nodes.title: Conformal vector and invariant form of a tensor product
nodes.statement: Let V, W be vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vectors ω_V, ω_W of central charges c_V, c_W, involutions θ_V, θ_W and θ-invariant symmetric forms B_V, B_W. Then ω := ω_V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ ω_W is a conformal vector of V ⊗ W of central charge c_V + c_W, L_n^{V⊗W} = L_n^V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ L_n^W, (V⊗W)_n = ⊕_{a+b=n} V_a ⊗ W_b, θ_V ⊗ θ_W is an involution fixing ω, and B_V ⊗ B_W is a (θ_V ⊗ θ_W)-invariant symmetric form, nondegenerate when B_V and B_W are.
hypotheses: V, W vertex algebras with conformal vectors, involutions and invariant forms
Each factor has locally nilpotent L₁ as required by invariant-bilinear-form; their sum on the tensor product is locally nilpotent on each elementary tensor and finite sum.
proofSteps: Mode formula of the tensor product: (ω_V ⊗ 1)_{n+1} = L_n^V ⊗ 1 and (1 ⊗ ω_W)_{n+1} = 1 ⊗ L_n^W; check the six conformal-vector conditions factorwise (the cross terms vanish because the two factors commute).
Invariance: the adjoint formula is multiplicative for a ⊗ b with a, b homogeneous since L_1 and L_0 act as derivations of the tensor product; check on pure tensors.
acceptance: The central charge of V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} is 24 + 2 = 26 for c_V = 24.
Borcherds 1992 §3 and Jurisich 1998 §6.1 state both parts.

sources.match: Both statements.

nodes.title: Graded trace (graded character) of an endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 and g ∈ End_k(V) with g(V_n) ⊆ V_n for all n (for example g ∈ Aut(V, ω)). The graded trace of g is Z_V(g) := Σ_{n∈ℤ} tr(g|V_n) q^n ∈ k((q)) (a Laurent series because V_n = 0 for n ≪ 0). The graded dimension is Z_V(1) = Σ_n dim(V_n) q^n. Convention: no factor q^{−c/24} is included here (it is added in node mckay-thompson-series for c = 24).
hypotheses: V vertex operator algebra over k
g preserves every weight space
proofSteps: For each n, restrict g to the finite-dimensional V_n (LinearMap.restrict) and take LinearMap.trace; the resulting ℤ-indexed family has support bounded below, so it defines a HahnSeries ℤ k = LaurentSeries k.
acceptance: Z_V(g) depends only on the conjugacy class of g in Aut(V, ω).
Z_{V⊗W}(g ⊗ h) = Z_V(g)·Z_W(h) for the tensor product vertex operator algebra.

nodes.title: McKay–Thompson series
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 and g ∈ Aut(V, ω). The McKay–Thompson series of g is T_g := q^{−1}·Z_V(g) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} tr(g|V_{n+1}) q^n ∈ k((q)), and c_g(n) := tr(g|V_{n+1}) (Borcherds' Thompson series Σ Tr(g|V_n)q^n with Borcherds' V_n = V_{n+1} here). The factor q^{−1} is q^{−c/24} for central charge c = 24, the case used in this stage. For a group G acting on V by conformal automorphisms, T_g for g ∈ G is a class function of g. When V is nonnegatively graded with nonzero vacuum, V_0 = k·1 and V_1 = 0, T_g = q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} c_g(n) q^n.
hypotheses: V vertex operator algebra of central charge 24
g ∈ Aut(V, ω)
proofSteps: Define as HahnSeries.single (−1) 1 * gradedTrace V g in LaurentSeries k.
The normalized shape follows from tr(g|k·1) = 1 (g1 = 1) and V_1 = 0.
acceptance: T_1 is q^{−1} times the graded dimension; for the moonshine module T_1 = J (node moonshine-identity-thompson-series).
For the rank-24 Heisenberg vertex operator algebra, T_1 = q^{−1}Π(1 − q^n)^{−24} = q^{−1} + 24 + 324q + 3200q² + ⋯.

nodes.title: Double cover of an even lattice and its twisted group algebra
nodes.statement: Let (L, ⟨·,·⟩) be an even lattice: a finitely generated free ℤ-module with a symmetric ℤ-valued bilinear form with ⟨α,α⟩ ∈ 2ℤ for all α (in Tau Ceti: the carrier of a TauCeti.IntegralLattice satisfying IsEven). A lattice cocycle is a bimultiplicative map ε : L × L → {±1} with ε(α,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,α⟩/2} for all α; it satisfies ε(α,β)ε(β,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}. Cocycles exist: for a ℤ-basis e_1, …, e_d put ε(e_i,e_j) = (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_j⟩} for i < j, (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_i⟩/2} for i = j, 1 for i > j, and extend bimultiplicatively. For a field k, the twisted group algebra k_ε[L] has k-basis {e^α : α ∈ L} and product e^α e^β = ε(α,β) e^{α+β}; it is associative with unit e^0. Define L̂ abstractly as {±1} × L with multiplication (s,α)(t,β) = (stε(α,β),α+β). This is a central extension 1 → {±1} → L̂ → L → 1 with commutator (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}, unique up to isomorphism; two cocycles give isomorphic twisted group algebras. The realization L̂ = {±e^α} inside k_ε[L] is faithful only if char(k)≠2.
hypotheses: L free of finite rank
⟨·,·⟩ symmetric, ℤ-valued and even
proofSteps: Bimultiplicativity makes ε a 2-cocycle, so k_ε[L] is associative (build it on AddMonoidAlgebra k L with the twisted product).
ε(α,β)ε(β,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}: expand ε(α+β, α+β) = (−1)^{⟨α+β,α+β⟩/2} using bimultiplicativity.
Existence: the displayed values on a basis define a bimultiplicative map with ε(e_i,e_i) = (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_i⟩/2}; the diagonal condition for general α follows from the commutator identity and evenness.

Uniqueness: two cocycles with the same diagonal differ by a symmetric bimultiplicative map η with η(α,α) = 1, which is a coboundary η(α,β) = f(α+β)f(α)^{−1}f(β)^{−1}; rescaling e^α ↦ f(α)e^α gives the isomorphism.
acceptance: For L = ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2, ε(α,α) = −1 and (e^α)² = −e^{2α}.
Borcherds 1986 §2: e^r e^s = ε^{(r,s)} e^s e^r and e^r e^{−r} = ε^{(r,r)/2}.

nodes.title: The vertex algebra of an even lattice
nodes.statement: Let L be an even lattice with cocycle ε, k a field of characteristic 0, h := L ⊗_ℤ k with the k-bilinear extension of ⟨·,·⟩. Put V_L := S(ĥ⁻) ⊗_k k_ε[L], where S(ĥ⁻) is the symmetric algebra of ⊕_{n≥1} h ⊗ t^{−n} (write α(−n) := α ⊗ t^{−n}). For α ∈ h, n ∈ ℤ define α(n) ∈ End(V_L): multiplication by α(n) for n < 0; α(0)(s ⊗ e^γ) = ⟨α,γ⟩ s ⊗ e^γ; for n > 0 the derivation of S(ĥ⁻) with α(n)β(−m) = n⟨α,β⟩δ_{n,m}; so [α(m), β(n)] = m⟨α,β⟩δ_{m+n,0}. Then there is a unique vertex algebra structure on V_L with vacuum 1 := 1 ⊗ e^0 such that Y(α(−1)1, z) = Σ_n α(n) z^{−n−1} and Y(1 ⊗ e^β, z) = exp(Σ_{n≥1} β(−n)z^n/n) exp(−Σ_{n≥1} β(n)z^{−n}/n) e^β z^{β(0)}, where e^β acts by left multiplication in k_ε[L] and z^{β(0)}(s ⊗ e^γ) = z^{⟨β,γ⟩} s ⊗ e^γ. It is L-graded (V_{L,γ} := S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^γ, u_n v ∈ V_{L,α+β} for u ∈ V_{L,α}, v ∈ V_{L,β}). If ⟨·,·⟩ is nondegenerate with dual bases (h_i), (h^i) of h, then ω := ½ Σ_i h_i(−1)h^i(−1)1 is a conformal vector of central charge d = rank L, and L_0(α_1(−n_1)⋯α_k(−n_k) ⊗ e^γ) = (Σ n_i + ⟨γ,γ⟩/2)·(same vector). The Cartan involution θ(α(n)) = −α(n), θ(e^γ) = e^{−γ} for the normalized bimultiplicative cocycle here. Equivalently, on a lift a in L̂ it is θ(ι(a)) = (−1)^{⟨γ,γ⟩/2}ι(a⁻¹); the inverse lift satisfies ι(a⁻¹) = (−1)^{⟨γ,γ⟩/2}e^{−γ} is an automorphism fixing ω. If L is positive definite, V_L is a vertex operator algebra of CFT type.
hypotheses: L even lattice, ε a lattice cocycle
k field of characteristic 0
conformal vector only for nondegenerate ⟨·,·⟩
proofSteps: The operators α(n) form a representation of the Heisenberg Lie algebra ĥ on V_L; α(n)1 = 0 for n ≥ 0.
The fields α(z) and Y(e^β, z) are creative and translation covariant for T(s ⊗ e^γ) := (T_S s) ⊗ e^γ + γ(−1)s ⊗ e^γ with T_S the derivation α(−n) ↦ nα(−n−1).

Locality: [α(z), β(w)] = ⟨α,β⟩∂_wδ(z−w); [α(z), Y(e^β,w)] = ⟨α,β⟩Y(e^β,w)δ(z−w); and Y(e^α,z)Y(e^β,w) = ε(α,β)(z−w)^{⟨α,β⟩} :Y(e^α,z)Y(e^β,w):, so (z−w)^N[Y(e^α,z), Y(e^β,w)] = 0 for N ≥ −⟨α,β⟩, the sign ε(α,β)ε(β,α)(−1)^{⟨α,β⟩} = 1 making the two orders agree.
The vectors α_1(−n_1)⋯α_k(−n_k) ⊗ e^γ are obtained from 1 by the modes of these fields, so the existence theorem gives the vertex algebra; the grading statement is read off the fields.
Conformal vector: compute ω_{n+1} = ½Σ_i Σ_m :h_i(m)h^i(n−m): (Sugawara/Segal operators) and check the six conditions; the central charge equals the trace of the identity of h, i.e. d.

The normalized bimultiplicative cocycle satisfies ε(−α,−β)=ε(α,β), so θ(e^γ)=e^{−γ} preserves the twisted product. Together with θ(α(n))=−α(n), conjugation preserves the defining fields, hence θ is an automorphism fixing ω. Jurisich1998 p.31 defines θ using the inverse lift a⁻¹, not the chosen lift e^{−γ}; their difference supplies the second sign.
Positive definite L: weights Σn_i + ⟨γ,γ⟩/2 ≥ 0 with finitely many vectors of each weight, and weight 0 only for 1.
acceptance: For L = ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2, (e^α)_0 e^{−α} = ε(α,−α) α(−1)1 and V_1 (with bracket u_0 v) is isomorphic to sl₂ (Borcherds 1986 §5).
For positive definite L of rank d, the graded dimension is Σ_{γ∈L} q^{⟨γ,γ⟩/2} / Π_{n≥1}(1−q^n)^d.

nodes.title: Invariant form on the vertex algebra of an even unimodular lattice
nodes.statement: Let L be an even unimodular lattice (for example II_{1,1}) and V_L its vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω and Cartan involution θ. Then V_L carries a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form (·,·), invariant in the Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky sense (θ = id in node invariant-bilinear-form), unique up to a nonzero scalar; it satisfies (V_{L,r}, V_{L,s}) = 0 unless r + s = 0, (α(n)u, v) = −(u, α(−n)v), θ preserves it, and with the normalization (1,1) = −1 one has (e^r, θ(e^r)) = −1 for every r ∈ L. Consequently, for a vertex algebra V with id-invariant form (·,·)_V, the product form on V ⊗ V_L satisfies (u ⊗ e^r, θ(u ⊗ e^r)) = −(u,u)_V.
hypotheses: L even unimodular
k field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: V_L is an irreducible module over itself and every irreducible V_L-module is isomorphic to V_L (Dong 1993, cited in Jurisich 1998 Lemma 6.1); the contragredient module V_L' (restricted dual with respect to the L × ℤ grading) is irreducible, hence isomorphic to V_L; an isomorphism V_L ≅ V_L' is a nondegenerate invariant form, and symmetry holds by Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky Remark 5.3.3 (Jurisich 1998 Lemma 6.1).
Orthogonality of degrees: invariance with u = α(−1)1 gives (α(0)x, y) = −(x, α(0)y), so (x,y) = 0 unless the degrees add to 0.

For q=⟨r,r⟩/2, θ(e^r)=e^{−r}. The primary-vector adjoint formula gives (e^r,e^{−r})=(−1)^q(1,(e^r)_{2q−1}e^{−r})=(−1)^qε(r,−r)(1,1)=(1,1). Exactly two signs cancel. Jurisich1998 p.33 uses an inverse lift with product ι(a)ι(a⁻¹)=1 and writes θ(ι(a))=(−1)^qι(a⁻¹); these are equivalent normalizations, not an extra sign on e^{−r}.
The product-form statement is the tensor-product lemma applied to V ⊗ V_L.
acceptance: The form restricted to the weight-one degree-zero space span{α(−1)1} is ±⟨·,·⟩, of signature (1,1) for II_{1,1}.

nodes.title: Physical spaces P^i of a vertex algebra with conformal vector
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω and L_n = ω_{n+1}. For i ∈ ℤ the physical space of weight i is P^i := {v ∈ V : L_0 v = i v and L_n v = 0 for all n ≥ 1} (the lowest-weight vectors of the Virasoro action of weight i). If V is graded by an abelian group Λ compatibly with the vertex algebra structure and with L_0 ∈ End of degree 0, then P^i = ⊕_{r∈Λ} P^i_r.
hypotheses: V vertex algebra with conformal vector ω over a field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: Define P^i as the intersection of the L_0-eigenspace of eigenvalue i with the kernels of L_n, n ≥ 1 (a k-submodule); since L_n for n ≥ 3 lies in the Lie algebra generated by L_1 and L_2, it suffices to impose L_1 v = L_2 v = 0.
u, v ∈ P^1 ⇒ u_0 v ∈ P^1: by the Virasoro-representation theorem (c), [L_m, u_0] = 0 for u ∈ P^1, and u_0 commutes with L_0.
acceptance: 1 ∈ P^0; when the vacuum is nonzero, ω ∈ P^2 exactly when c = 0, since L_2ω = (c/2)1.
For the lattice vertex algebra of ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2: e^α, e^{−α}, α(−1)1 ∈ P^1.
