nodes.title: The Lie algebra of physical states
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω, an involution θ ∈ Aut(V) fixing ω, and a symmetric bilinear form (·,·) that is invariant (Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky sense, node invariant-bilinear-form with θ = id) and θ-stable. Let N := {p ∈ P^1 : (p, P^1) = 0}. Then g(V) := P^1/N is a Lie algebra over k with bracket [u + N, v + N] := u_0 v + N; (·,·) induces on g(V) a nondegenerate symmetric invariant form ([x,y],z) = −(y,[x,z]); θ induces a Lie algebra involution; the contravariant form is (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy). P^1 ∩ DV ⊆ N, so g(V) is a quotient of the Lie subalgebra P^1/(P^1 ∩ DV) of V/DV. If V is graded by an abelian group Λ (compatibly with products, L_0 of degree 0, (V_r, V_s) = 0 unless r + s = 0, θ(V_r) = V_{−r}), then g(V) = ⊕_{r∈Λ} g(V)_r is a Λ-graded Lie algebra. Every g ∈ Aut(V) fixing ω, commuting with θ and preserving (·,·) induces an automorphism of g(V) preserving both forms. It preserves each graded piece if g also preserves the Λ-grading; this does not follow from the other conditions.
hypotheses: V vertex algebra with conformal vector ω over a field of characteristic 0
θ involutive automorphism fixing ω
(·,·) symmetric, invariant, θ-stable
proofSteps: P^1 is closed under u_0 (physical-space API).
P^1 ∩ DV ⊆ N: for p = Dv ∈ P^1 and q ∈ P^1, (Dv, q) = (L_{−1}v, q) = (v, L_1 q) = 0 using L_n* = L_{−n}.

N is an ideal: for u ∈ P^1, r ∈ N, q ∈ P^1: (u_0 r, q) = −(r, u_0 q) = 0 by the adjoint formula for weight-one primaries (u_0* = −u_0); r_0 u = −u_0 r + (element of DV) by skew symmetry, and this element lies in P^1 ∩ DV ⊆ N.
Antisymmetry: u_0 u ∈ DV ∩ P^1 ⊆ N by skew symmetry. Jacobi identity: commutator formula (u_0 v)_0 = [u_0, v_0].
Invariance of the induced form is (u_0 v, w) = −(v, u_0 w); nondegeneracy holds by construction; θ-stability of (·,·) and θω = ω give the involution.
Grading: each P^1_r is stable under the construction and N = ⊕_r N_r because the form pairs degree r with −r.
Functoriality: automorphisms preserve P^1, N and the bracket.
acceptance: For a vertex operator algebra of CFT type with nondegenerate invariant form, g(V) = V_1 with bracket u_0 v (for the A_1 lattice: sl₂).
Jurisich 2009 Lemma 3.2 and Jurisich 1998 §6.1 prove the Lie algebra structure on P^1/L_{−1}P^0.

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 1: adjoints, commutators and nondegeneracy
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: (a) with respect to (·,·)_0, L_i* = L_{−i} and K_i* = K_{−i} for all i; (b) [L_i, K_j] = −j K_{i+j} and [K_i, K_j] = 0; (c) (·,·)_0 restricted to H is nondegenerate; (d) H = ⊕_{n ≥ ⟨r,r⟩/2} H_n with each L_0-weight space H_n finite-dimensional.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
proofSteps: (a): apply the adjoint formula to ω (weight 2, L_1ω = 0, θω = ω) and to 1 ⊗ w(−1)1 (weight 1, L_1 = 0, θ = −1).
(b): [L_m, w(n)] = −n w(m+n) in V_L and w(i), w(j) commute because ⟨w,w⟩ = 0.
(c): the form on W is nondegenerate and pairs degree r with degree r only (for the contravariant form), so its radical on H lies in the radical on W.
(d): weights of v ⊗ α_1(−n_1)⋯ ⊗ e^r are wt(v) + Σn_i + ⟨r,r⟩/2 with wt(v) ≥ 0; finitely many vectors of each weight because V has finite-dimensional weight spaces and the partitions are finite.
acceptance: For r = (1,1), H has lowest weight ⟨r,r⟩/2 = −1 with H_{−1} = V_0 ⊗ e^r one-dimensional.

sources.match: Parts (a), (c); (b) is displayed before Lemma A.1.

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 2: H is generated by transverse states
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: H = U(𝒜)T, i.e. every vector of H is obtained from vectors annihilated by all L_i, K_i (i > 0) by applying the operators L_i, K_i.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
proofSteps: The inherited proof, following Jurisich1998 Lemma A.3, infers H_n=M_n⊕M_n⊥ for M=U(𝒜)T solely from nondegeneracy of H_n. This is not valid for an indefinite form: it also requires nondegeneracy on M_n. Establish that restriction or give a triangular/PBW generation argument before using this decomposition. This is an explicit unresolved proof obligation.

Once the missing direct-complement argument is established, the adjoint-stable orthogonal complement is a graded 𝒜-submodule. Its lowest nonzero weight would lie in T⊆M, contradicting directness. Without the missing argument, a vector may lie in M∩M⊥ and there is no contradiction.
acceptance: For V = V♮ and r = (1,1), the lowest weight space H_{−1} = V_0 ⊗ e^r lies in T.

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 3: the transverse space is isomorphic to V ⊗ e^r
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: (a) K = T ⊕ rad(K) with (·,·)_0 nondegenerate on T; (b) K = (V ⊗ e^r) ⊕ rad(K), and K is exactly the space of lowest-weight vectors of the abelian Lie algebra 𝒴 in H; (c) consequently the projections give a G-equivariant isometric isomorphism V ⊗ e^r ≅ T respecting L_0-weights, so T_1 ≅ V_{1−⟨r,r⟩/2} as G-modules with forms, where (u ⊗ e^r, u ⊗ e^r)_0 = (u,u)_V.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
PBW theorem for U(𝒴) and U(𝒜)
proofSteps: (a): by PBW, K = U(𝒴⁻)U(𝒴⁺)U(𝒴⁰)T = U(𝒴⁻)T = T ⊕ 𝒴⁻U(𝒴⁻)T; the second summand is orthogonal to K (adjoints K_i* = K_{−i}), hence in rad(K); T ∩ rad = 0 by step 1 (c) and step 2.

(b): H = U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T by PBW and step 2, and no nonzero vector of 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T is a 𝒴-lowest-weight vector, so K is the space of 𝒴-lowest-weight vectors. Since ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, (w, r) is a basis of ℝ²; writing S(ĥ⁻) = ℝ[x_i] ⊗ ℝ[z_i] with x_i = w(−i), z_i = r(−i), K_k = 1 ⊗ w(k) acts on ℝ[z_i] as k⟨r,w⟩∂/∂z_k (k > 0) and commutes with ℝ[x_i]; ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0 forces the lowest-weight vectors to be V ⊗ ℝ[x_i] ⊗ e^r, of which the part of positive x-degree is null.
(c): both V ⊗ e^r and T map isomorphically onto K/rad(K); the maps commute with G (G acts trivially on V_L) and with L_0 on the weight-one parts.
acceptance: For r = (1,−1) (norm 2), T_1 ≅ V_0 is one-dimensional: the root space of the real simple root.

sources.match: Parts (a), (b); their proofs use PBW and the differential-operator description of K_k.

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 4: spurious states in critical dimension
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: H = S ⊕ K, and the operators L_1 and L_2 + (3/2)L_1², which generate the associative algebra generated by all L_i with i > 0, map S_1 into S. This uses that the central charge of W is 26.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
central charge of V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} equal to 26
proofSteps: H = S ⊕ K from H = U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T (PBW) and K = U(𝒴⁻)T.
Every s ∈ S_1 can be written s = L_{−1}f_1 + L_{−2}f_2 with L_0 f_1 = 0 and L_0 f_2 = −f_2, since every L_{−m} (m > 0) is a polynomial in L_{−1}, L_{−2}.

Compute with the Virasoro relations of central charge c: L_1 s = L_{−1}(L_1f_1 + 3f_2) + L_{−2}L_1f_2 and (L_2 + (3/2)L_1²)s = L_{−1}(L_2 + (3/2)L_1²)f_1 + L_{−2}(L_2 + (3/2)L_1²)f_2 + 9L_{−1}L_1f_2 + (c/2 − 13)f_2. Since S = L_{−1}H + L_{−2}H, both lie in S exactly because c = 26 kills the last term.
L_1 and L_2 + (3/2)L_1² generate the associative algebra generated by the L_i, i > 0 (L_2 is obtained, then L_{i+1} = [L_i, L_1]/(i−1) for i ≥ 2).
acceptance: For c ≠ 26 the computation leaves the term (c/2 − 13)f_2 and the lemma fails (the no-ghost theorem needs central charge 24 for V).

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 5: physical states are transverse plus null
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: P_1 = T_1 ⊕ N_1, where N_1 = rad((·,·)_0|_{P_1}) = S_1 ∩ P_1.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
proofSteps: Write p ∈ P_1 as p = k + s with k ∈ K_1, s ∈ S_1 (step 4).

For a generator u ∈ {L_1, L_2 + (3/2)L_1²}: 0 = up = uk + us with uk ∈ K (K is stable under L_i, i > 0, being U(𝒴)T with [L_i, K_j] ∈ 𝒴) and us ∈ S (step 4); directness of H = S ⊕ K gives uk = us = 0.
Hence k ∈ K ∩ P = T and s ∈ S ∩ P; S is orthogonal to P (adjoints: (L_{−m}f, p) = (f, L_m p) = 0), so s ∈ N_1; T_1 ∩ N_1 = 0 by step 3 (a).
acceptance: For r = (1,1) and V = V♮: P_1 = T_1 ⊕ N_1 with T_1 ≅ V_2 of dimension 196884.

nodes.title: The no-ghost theorem (Goddard–Thorn, Borcherds)
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex operator algebra over ℝ of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form, and let G be a group acting on V by automorphisms preserving ω and the form. Let W := V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} with its conformal vector (central charge 26), involution θ = id ⊗ θ_{II_{1,1}}, product form and contravariant form (x,y)_0 = −(x,θy); let P^1_r ⊆ W be the physical space of weight 1 and degree r ∈ II_{1,1}, with G acting through V. Then the quotient of P^1_r by the radical of (·,·)_0 restricted to P^1_r is isomorphic, as a G-module with invariant bilinear form, to V_{1−⟨r,r⟩/2} if r ≠ 0, and to V_1 ⊕ ℝ², with the form of II_{1,1} on the second summand (G acting trivially on ℝ²) if r = 0. In particular, if (·,·)_V is positive definite then the induced contravariant form on P^1_r/rad is positive definite for r ≠ 0.
hypotheses: V vertex operator algebra over ℝ, c = 24
V nonnegatively graded, dim V_0 = 1
nondegenerate symmetric invariant form on V
G acts by automorphisms preserving ω and the form
proofSteps: r ≠ 0: combine step 3 (V_{1−⟨r,r⟩/2} ⊗ e^r ≅ T_1, weights: wt(v ⊗ e^r) = wt(v) + ⟨r,r⟩/2 = 1) with step 5 (P^1_r/N_1 ≅ T_1); all maps are G-equivariant and preserve the forms.
Positivity: for x = u ⊗ e^r, (x, θx) = −(u,u)_V (lattice invariant-form lemma), so (x,x)_0 = (u,u)_V > 0 for u ≠ 0.

r = 0: the weight-one degree-zero space of W is V_1 ⊗ 1 ⊕ V_0 ⊗ span{α(−1)1 : α ∈ ℝ²}; since dim V_0 = 1, L_1V_1 ⊆ V_0 = ℝ1 and (L_1v, 1) = (v, L_{−1}1) = 0 give L_1V_1 = 0, and L_n (n ≥ 2) kills it by weight; the form on this space is nondegenerate, so P^1_0/rad ≅ V_1 ⊕ ℝ².
acceptance: For V = V♮ (moonshine module) and r = (a,b) ≠ 0: P^1_r/rad ≅ V♮_{1+ab}, of dimension c(ab).
Without the hypothesis dim V_0 = 1 the r = 0 case fails (for V♮ × V♮ the quotient is V_1 ⊕ ℝ⁴); see sourceIssues E705.

nodes.title: Borcherds' axioms for a moonshine module
nodes.statement: A moonshine module (Borcherds' properties (1)–(2)) is a vertex operator algebra V over ℝ such that: (1) the central charge is 24 and V carries a positive definite symmetric bilinear form that is invariant in the Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky sense (θ = id in node invariant-bilinear-form); (2) V is nonnegatively graded and q^{−1}·gradedDimension(V) = J, the Laurent series q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} c(n)qⁿ of j − 744 (node j-laurent-series); equivalently dim V_{n+1} = c(n) for all n ≥ −1, so V_0 = ℝ·1, V_1 = 0, dim V_2 = 196884. A moonshine module with symmetry group G is moreover a group homomorphism ρ : G →* Aut(V, ω, (·,·)) into the conformal automorphisms preserving the form (Borcherds' property (3) for G the Monster).
hypotheses: V vertex operator algebra over ℝ
proofSteps: Structure (Prop-valued) on a vertex operator algebra with a bilinear form: centralCharge = 24, form symmetric, invariant, positive definite, IsNonnegGraded, and mckayThompsonSeries V 1 = J.
Derived: dim V_0 = c(−1) = 1 and 1 ∈ V_0 is nonzero (positive definiteness and (1,1) > 0 once V ≠ 0), so V_0 = ℝ1; dim V_1 = c(0) = 0.
The no-ghost hypotheses (dim V_0 = 1, c = 24, nondegenerate invariant form, group action) follow.
acceptance: For the Frenkel–Lepowsky–Meurman module V♮ these properties are FLM's theorems (recorded as the gap 'FLM moonshine module').
The Leech lattice vertex operator algebra has q^{−1} times its graded dimension equal to q^{−1}+24+196884q+⋯ and is not a moonshine module.

nodes.title: The Monster Lie algebra m(V)
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module (node moonshine-module-axioms) and G ≤ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)). Let W := V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ = id ⊗ θ_{II_{1,1}} and product form (normalized (1,1)_{V_{II_{1,1}}} = −1). The Monster Lie algebra is m(V) := g(W), the physical Lie algebra of W (P^1 modulo the radical of the form). It satisfies: (1) m = ⊕_{r∈II_{1,1}} m_r is II_{1,1}-graded; (2) θ maps m_r onto m_{−r} and the contravariant form (x,y)_0 = −(x,θy) is positive definite on m_r for r ≠ 0; (3) G acts on m by graded Lie algebra automorphisms, and m_{(a,b)} ≅ V_{ab+1} as G-modules for (a,b) ≠ (0,0) (so dim m_{(a,b)} = c(ab)), while m_{(0,0)} = span{1 ⊗ α(−1)1 : α ∈ ℝ²} ≅ ℝ² with trivial G-action; (4) m_{(0,0)} is abelian and 1 ⊗ α(−1)1 acts on m_r by the scalar ⟨α, r⟩.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: W is a vertex algebra with conformal vector (tensor-product lemma) and invariant product form; it is II_{1,1}-graded through V_{II_{1,1}}.
Apply the physical Lie algebra construction; the grading and G-action are its API.
No-ghost theorem with r = (a,b): 1 − ⟨r,r⟩/2 = 1 + ab gives m_{(a,b)} ≅ V_{ab+1}; r = 0 gives V_1 ⊕ ℝ² = ℝ² since V_1 = 0.
Positivity: for x = u ⊗ e^r, (x,x)_0 = (u,u)_V > 0 (lattice invariant-form lemma).
acceptance: m_{(a,b)} = 0 whenever ab < −1.

nodes.title: Borcherds (generalized Kac–Moody) algebra of a matrix
nodes.statement: Let I be a countable set and A = (a_ij)_{i,j∈I} a real matrix with (C1) A symmetric, (C2) a_ij ≤ 0 for i ≠ j, (C3) 2a_ij/a_ii ∈ ℤ whenever a_ii > 0. The Borcherds algebra g(A) is the real Lie algebra generated by h_i, e_i, f_i (i ∈ I) with relations [h_i,h_j] = 0, [h_i,e_k] = a_ik e_k, [h_i,f_k] = −a_ik f_k, [e_i,f_j] = δ_ij h_i, (ad e_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii} e_j = 0 = (ad f_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii} f_j for i ≠ j with a_ii > 0, and [e_i,e_j] = [f_i,f_j] = 0 whenever a_ij = 0. It is graded by the root lattice Q := ⊕_{i∈I} ℤα_i ((α_i,α_j) := a_ij; deg e_i = α_i, deg f_i = −α_i, deg h_i = 0). A simple root α_i is real if a_ii > 0 and imaginary otherwise. The Chevalley involution η acts as −1 on span{h_i} and maps e_i ↦ −f_i, f_i ↦ −e_i. When A is a symmetrized generalized Cartan matrix, g(A) is the (derived) Kac–Moody algebra.
hypotheses: I countable
A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
proofSteps: Define g(A) as the quotient of Mathlib's FreeLieAlgebra ℝ (I ⊕ I ⊕ I) by the Lie ideal generated by the relations (the pattern of Mathlib's Matrix.ToLieAlgebra).
The Q-grading exists because every relation is homogeneous; η is well defined because the relations are stable under it.
acceptance: For A = (2): g(A) ≅ sl₂(ℝ). For A = (0): g(A) is the three-dimensional Heisenberg algebra.
For A a Cartan matrix of finite type (a_ii = 2, integer entries) g(A) agrees with Matrix.ToLieAlgebra.

nodes.title: Triangular and root space decomposition of a Borcherds algebra
nodes.statement: For A satisfying (C1)–(C3): g(A) = n⁻ ⊕ h ⊕ n⁺ as vector spaces, where h = span{h_i} is abelian with basis {h_i}_{i∈I}, n⁺ (resp. n⁻) is the subalgebra generated by the e_i (resp. f_i) and is the quotient of the free Lie algebra on {e_i} (resp. {f_i}) by the ideal generated by the relations of degree > 0 (resp. < 0). Every root space g_α (α ∈ Q∖{0}) is finite-dimensional and nonzero only for α ∈ Q_+ ∪ (−Q_+) (Q_+ = ⊕ℕα_i); g_{α_i} = ℝe_i. There is a unique symmetric invariant bilinear form with (e_i, f_j) = δ_ij, (h_i,h_j) = a_ij; it pairs g_α with g_{−α} nondegenerately for α ≠ 0.
hypotheses: A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
proofSteps: For the algebra g_0 (relations without the Serre-type ones) construct the module X (free associative algebra on symbols x_i) of Jurisich 1998 Proposition 3.1 to prove g_0 = n_0⁻ ⊕ h ⊕ n_0⁺ with n_0^± free and {h_i} independent.
The Serre-type relations generate an ideal k_0 = k_0⁺ ⊕ k_0⁻ contained in n_0^+ ⊕ n_0^− (Jurisich 1998 Propositions 3.2–3.3), so the decomposition descends to g(A).
Finite-dimensionality: g_α ⊆ image of the degree-α part of the free Lie algebra, finite-dimensional for α ∈ Q_+.

Construct the invariant form inductively on root height, normalized by (e_i,f_j)=δ_ij and (h_i,h_j)=a_ij. Its nondegeneracy between nonzero root degrees for arbitrary matrices requires the generalized Serre-presentation/radical theorem cited in Jurisich1998 pp.6–7. Corollary5.3 in that paper covers the restricted no-orthogonal-imaginary-roots case, not all matrices in the statement. The general dependency remains open here.
acceptance: For A = (2) the decomposition is sl₂ = ℝf ⊕ ℝh ⊕ ℝe.

nodes.title: The canonical central extension ĝ(A)
nodes.statement: For A satisfying (C1)–(C3), ĝ(A) is the real Lie algebra with generators e_i, f_i, h_ij (i, j ∈ I) and relations [h_ij, h_kl] = 0, [h_ij, e_k] = δ_ij a_ik e_k, [h_ij, f_k] = −δ_ij a_ik f_k, [e_i, f_j] = h_ij, (ad e_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii}e_j = 0 = (ad f_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii}f_j (i ≠ j, a_ii > 0), [e_i,e_j] = [f_i,f_j] = 0 when a_ij = 0 (Borcherds' universal generalized Kac–Moody algebra). Then h_ij = 0 unless the i-th and j-th columns of A are equal; the h_ij with equal columns form a basis of an abelian subalgebra ĥ; ĝ = n⁻ ⊕ ĥ ⊕ n⁺ with n^± as in g(A); c := span{h_ij : i ≠ j} is central, and ĝ(A)/c ≅ g(A).
hypotheses: A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
proofSteps: Lemma: h_ij acts on e_k by δ_ij a_ik and on f_k by −δ_ij a_ik; applying the Jacobi identity to [e_i, f_j] with e_k, f_k shows h_ij = 0 unless columns i and j agree (Jurisich 1998 Lemma 3.1).
Triangular decomposition via the module X with λ vanishing on h_ij for unequal columns (Jurisich 1998 Proposition 3.1); the relations of degree ≠ 0 generate ideals k^± (Propositions 3.2–3.3).
The map ĝ → g(A), h_ij ↦ δ_ij h_i, is surjective with kernel c (Theorem 3.1).
acceptance: For a Kac–Moody matrix (all a_ii > 0) no two columns agree, c = 0 and ĝ = g(A).
For Jurisich's matrix M of the Monster Lie algebra, the c(n) columns of block n agree, so c contains h_ij for all i ≠ j in one block and is infinite-dimensional (c(n) ≥ 2 for n ≥ 1).

nodes.title: Borcherds' characterisation of generalized Kac–Moody algebras
nodes.statement: Let g be a real Lie algebra such that: (1) g = ⊕_{i∈ℤ} g_i is ℤ-graded with g_i finite-dimensional for i ≠ 0, and g is diagonalizable with respect to g_0; (2) g has an involution ω with ω(g_i) = g_{−i} acting as −1 on the noncentral elements of g_0 (so g_0 is abelian); (3) g has an ω-invariant symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·) with (g_i, g_j) = 0 unless i + j = 0, such that (x,y)_0 := −(x, ω(y)) is positive definite on g_m for every m ≠ 0; (4) g_0 ⊆ [g,g]. Then there is a matrix A satisfying (C1)–(C3) and a surjective Lie algebra homomorphism π : ĝ(A) → g whose kernel is central. If moreover (·,·) is nondegenerate, then g ≅ l/c for a Borcherds algebra l = g(A) with c the centre of l. The generators e_i can be chosen as g_0-weight vectors forming orthonormal bases (for (·,·)_0) of the orthogonal complements e_m of the subalgebra generated by ⊕_{0<n<m} g_n in g_m, with f_i = −ω(e_i).
hypotheses: g real Lie algebra with (1)–(4)
proofSteps: For m > 0 let l_m be the subalgebra generated by the g_n, 0 < n < m, and e_m := (l_m ∩ g_m)^⊥ in g_m for (·,·)_0; e_m is g_0-stable and has an orthonormal basis of g_0-weight vectors; their union {e_i} generates ⊕_{n>0} g_n; put f_i := −ω(e_i), h_ij := [e_i, f_j].
h_ij ∈ g_0 and h_ij = 0 unless deg e_i = deg e_j (contravariance and positivity); by (4) g_0 is spanned by the h_ij.
The radical of (·,·) is central; for i ≠ j, h_ij lies in the radical.

[h, e_i] = (h, h_ii)e_i, and (x,y)_0-positivity gives a_ij := (h_ii,h_jj) ≤ 0 for i ≠ j, with [e_i, e_j] = 0 iff a_ij = 0 (Jurisich 1998 equation (10)); for a_ii > 0 the sl₂-representation theory gives 2a_ij/a_ii ∈ ℤ and the Serre relations (using Jurisich 1998 Proposition 3.2 and positivity).
Hence the generators satisfy the relations of ĝ(A) and π exists; the form pulls back and nondegeneracy on ĝ_n ⊕ ĝ_{−n} shows the kernel lies in ĥ and is central.
If the form is nondegenerate then all h_ij (i ≠ j) vanish and Jurisich 1998 Corollary 4.1 gives g ≅ l/c.
acceptance: For g = sl₂(ℝ) with the grading by the h-eigenvalue/2, ω the Cartan involution and the trace form, the theorem returns A = (2).
Borcherds 1988 Theorem 3.1 and Borcherds 1992 Theorem 4.1 are versions of this statement.

nodes.title: Lazard elimination for free Lie algebras
nodes.statement: Let X be a set, S ⊆ X, and L(X) the free Lie algebra on X over a field (Mathlib FreeLieAlgebra). Then (a) L(X) = L(S) ⊕ 𝔞 as vector spaces, where L(S) is the subalgebra generated by S and 𝔞 is the ideal generated by X ∖ S; (b) 𝔞 is a free Lie algebra: the map (s_1, …, s_n, x) ↦ (ad s_1 ⋯ ad s_n)(x), for n ≥ 0, s_i ∈ S, x ∈ X ∖ S, extends to an isomorphism L(T) ≅ 𝔞 from the free Lie algebra on the set T of such sequences. All statements are compatible with gradings in which X is homogeneous.
hypotheses: X a set, S ⊆ X
proofSteps: Define the Lie algebra map L(X) → L(S) killing X ∖ S (a retraction onto L(S)); its kernel is 𝔞, giving (a).

Construct L(S) ⋉ L(T) with L(S) acting on L(T) by derivations extending s · (s_1,…,s_n,x) = (s, s_1, …, s_n, x); the universal property of L(X) gives a map L(X) → L(S) ⋉ L(T), inverse to the map induced by (ad s_1⋯ad s_n)(x); restrict to 𝔞 (Bourbaki, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras II §2.9).
acceptance: For X = {s, x}, S = {s}: the ideal generated by x is free on {x, [s,x], [s,[s,x]], …}.

sources.match: Statement (from Bourbaki).

nodes.title: Traces on exterior, symmetric and tensor powers (Adams operations)
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0. (a) For a finite-dimensional k-vector space U and g ∈ End(U), in k[[t]]: Σ_{n≥0} (−1)ⁿ tr(g|Λⁿ U) tⁿ = det(1 − tg) = exp(−Σ_{m≥1} tr(g^m) t^m/m), Σ_{n≥0} tr(g|Sⁿ U) tⁿ = det(1 − tg)^{−1} = exp(Σ_{m≥1} tr(g^m) t^m/m), and Σ_{n≥0} tr(g|U^{⊗n}) tⁿ = (1 − tr(g) t)^{−1}. (b) Let Γ be a finitely generated free abelian group with a homomorphism deg : Γ → ℤ, U = ⊕_{γ∈Γ} U_γ with U_γ finite-dimensional and U_γ = 0 unless deg γ > 0, finitely many γ of each degree, and g a graded endomorphism. In the completed group ring k[[Γ_{>0}]] (series supported in deg γ > 0 together with 0, with finite support below each degree bound, so coefficient convolution is finite), with ch_g(U) := Σ_γ tr(g|U_γ)e^γ and the Adams operation ψ^m(Σ a_γ e^γ)[g] := Σ tr(g^m|U_γ) e^{mγ}: ch_g Λ_{−1}(U) := Σ_n (−1)ⁿ ch_g(Λⁿ U) = exp(−Σ_{m≥1} ψ^m ch_g(U)/m), ch_g S(U) = exp(Σ_m ψ^m ch_g(U)/m), ch_g T(U) = (1 − ch_g U)^{−1}.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
U finite-dimensional, or graded with finite-dimensional pieces of positive degree
proofSteps: (a) Extend scalars to an algebraic closure and triangularize g with eigenvalues λ_1, …, λ_d: tr(g|Λⁿ) = e_n(λ), tr(g|Sⁿ) = h_n(λ), and Π(1 − λ_i t) = exp(Σ_i log(1 − λ_i t)) = exp(−Σ_m p_m(λ)t^m/m) with p_m(λ) = tr(g^m); the tensor power statement is tr(g^{⊗n}) = tr(g)ⁿ.

(b) Truncate to degrees ≤ N: finitely many U_γ contribute; Λ(⊕U_γ) = ⊗Λ(U_γ) as graded g-modules, so characters multiply; apply (a) to each U_γ with t replaced by e^γ (the splitting principle of Borcherds 1992 §8).
Traces on Λⁿ, Sⁿ use Mathlib's exteriorPower.map, SymmetricAlgebra and LinearMap.trace; exp and log of series in the maximal ideal via PowerSeries.exp and PowerSeries.subst.
acceptance: For U = k and g = λ: Σ(−1)ⁿ tr(Λⁿ)tⁿ = 1 − λt = exp(−Σ λ^m t^m/m).
For g = 1 and graded U, (b) gives Π_γ (1 − e^γ)^{dim U_γ} = exp(−Σ_m ψ^m ch(U)/m).

sources.match: Part (a) for Λ and its graded extension (b).
Adams operations through exterior powers; extended to graded series in (29).

nodes.title: Character formula for graded free Lie algebras (Witt's formula)
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, Γ, deg as in node graded-trace-exterior-symmetric-power, W = ⊕_γ W_γ a Γ-graded vector space with W_γ finite-dimensional, zero unless deg γ > 0, finitely many γ of each degree, and g a graded linear automorphism of W. Let L(W) be the free Lie algebra on W (graded, with g acting by the induced Lie algebra automorphism). Then each L(W)_γ is finite-dimensional and, in k[[Γ_{>0}]], exp(−Σ_{m≥1} ψ^m ch_g(L(W))/m) = 1 − ch_g(W); for g = 1: Π_{γ} (1 − e^γ)^{dim L(W)_γ} = 1 − Σ_γ dim(W_γ) e^γ, and by Möbius inversion dim L(W)_β = Σ_{mγ=β} (μ(m)/m) Σ_{a∈P(γ)} ((|a|−1)!/a!) Π_α (dim W_α)^{a_α}, where P(γ) is the set of multi-indices a = (a_α) with Σ a_α α = γ.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
W graded as stated, g graded automorphism
proofSteps: U(L(W)) ≅ T(W) as graded algebras with g-action: Mathlib's FreeLieAlgebra.universalEnvelopingEquivFreeAlgebra and FreeAlgebra ≅ TensorAlgebra on a basis (the equivalences are natural, hence g-equivariant).

PBW: the associated graded of U(L) for the PBW filtration is Sym(L), naturally in Lie algebra automorphisms; since traces of a filtered endomorphism on a finite-dimensional space equal those on the associated graded, ch_g U(L(W)) = ch_g Sym(L(W)) (request to LieHighestWeight Layer 3).
By the trace lemma, ch_g Sym(L) = exp(Σ_m ψ^m ch_g(L)/m) and ch_g T(W) = (1 − ch_g W)^{−1}; equate and invert.
g = 1 case and Möbius inversion: take logarithms, compare coefficients of e^β and invert the divisor sum (Jurisich 1998 Propositions 5.1–5.2).
acceptance: For W = k·x in degree 1: L(W) = kx, and 1 − e = (1 − e)^1.
For W with two generators of degree 1 (Γ = ℤ): dim L_n = (1/n)Σ_{d|n} μ(d)2^{n/d} (Witt), e.g. dim L_2 = 1, dim L_3 = 2.

sources.match: The case g = 1; Proposition 5.2 is the Möbius-inverted form.
The equivariant version via homology and the Euler–Poincaré identity (an alternative proof route).

nodes.title: Free subalgebras of Borcherds algebras (Jurisich)
nodes.statement: Let A satisfy (C1)–(C3), J := {i ∈ I : a_ii > 0} (real simple roots) and g_J the Kac–Moody subalgebra generated by e_i, f_i (i ∈ J), g_J = n_J⁺ ⊕ h_J ⊕ n_J⁻. Assume that a_ij < 0 for all distinct i, j ∈ I ∖ J (no two imaginary simple roots are orthogonal). Then g(A) = u⁺ ⊕ (g_J + h) ⊕ u⁻, where u⁻ is the free Lie algebra on ⊕_{j∈I∖J} U(n_J⁻)·f_j and u⁺ the free Lie algebra on ⊕_{j∈I∖J} U(n_J⁺)·e_j; each U(n_J⁻)·f_j is an integrable highest-weight g_J-module and each U(n_J⁺)·e_j an integrable lowest-weight g_J-module (quotients of U(n_J^±)e_j by the Serre relations (ad e_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii}e_j, i ∈ J). u^± are g_J-stable ideals of n^±.
hypotheses: A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
a_ij < 0 for i ≠ j in I ∖ J
proofSteps: n⁺ = L({e_i}_{i∈I})/k_0⁺ with k_0⁺ generated by the Serre elements with i ∈ J (no relations of type [e_i,e_j] = 0 occur among imaginary indices by hypothesis).
Eliminate S = {e_i}_{i∈J} (Lazard): L({e_i}) = L({e_i}_{i∈J}) ⋉ L(W), W = ⊕_{j∉J} U(l)e_j with l = L({e_i}_{i∈J}).
Split W = ⊕_j (U(l)e_j/R_j ⊕ R_j) with R_j generated by the Serre elements, and eliminate again twice (the ideals b, c generated by R_j and K e_j lie in k_0⁺).
Conclude n⁺ = n_J⁺ ⋉ L(⊕_j U(n_J⁺)·e_j) and similarly for n⁻ (apply η).
acceptance: With one real simple root i, the free generators are (ad e_i)^l e_j with 0≤l≤−2a_ij/a_ii, j imaginary (Jurisich1998 Corollary5.1). For a direct-sum matrix whose real-imaginary cross entries vanish, only l=0 occurs.

For these matrices the largest graded ideal meeting the Cartan subalgebra trivially is zero (Jurisich 1998 Corollary 5.3). This presentation radical is not the nullspace of the invariant form on the Cartan subalgebra.

sources.match: Statement.
Module structure of the generating spaces.

nodes.title: The Monster Lie algebra is a Borcherds algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module and m = m(V). Grade m by i := 2a + b on m_{(a,b)} and let θ be the induced involution. Then m satisfies hypotheses (1)–(4) of Borcherds' characterisation with nondegenerate form, hence m ≅ g(A)/c for a matrix A satisfying (C1)–(C3), c the centre of g(A); under this isomorphism m_{(0,0)} is the image of the Cartan subalgebra, the II_{1,1}-grading of m is the root grading, and the simple roots have degrees (a,b) with 2a + b > 0.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: (1): m_{(a,b)} ≠ 0 forces ab ≥ −1, so for i ≠ 0 only finitely many (a,b) with 2a + b = i contribute, each finite-dimensional; i = 0 forces (a,b) = (0,0). m is diagonalizable for m_{(0,0)} by the scalar action ⟨α, r⟩ (Monster Lie algebra API (4)), which separates degrees.
(2),(3): θ maps m_r to m_{−r}, is −1 on m_{(0,0)}, preserves the form; the contravariant form is positive definite off degree 0 (Monster Lie algebra API).

The two brackets in independent Cartan directions (1,1) and (1,−1) are nonzero. When written with inverse lifts ι(a⁻¹) they have Jurisich1998 formulas (25)–(26); with the normalized section e^{−r} each includes ε(r,−r)=(−1)^{⟨r,r⟩/2}. For u,v∈V₂ choose (u,v)≠0 so u₃v is a nonzero scalar vacuum; the resulting two Cartan vectors span m_(0,0), establishing (4).
The radical of the form on m is zero by construction; apply the nondegenerate case of the characterisation theorem.
acceptance: Borcherds 1992 Theorem 6.2, p.22: the physical-state Monster Lie algebra satisfies the generalized Kac–Moody characterization.

sources.match: Statement and grading.
Same statement; proof checks conditions (i)–(iv) as in the proof steps.

nodes.title: Simple roots and denominator formula of the Monster Lie algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module. The Monster Lie algebra m = m(V) is isomorphic to g(M)/c, where M is Jurisich's matrix indexed by pairs (j,k) with j ∈ {−1} ∪ ℤ_{≥1}, 1 ≤ k ≤ c(j), with entries −(j + j') (so the simple roots are (1,−1), real of norm 2, and (1,n) for n ≥ 1, imaginary of norm −2n, each with multiplicity c(n)); the isomorphism matches root spaces with II_{1,1}-graded pieces. Its denominator formula is p·(J(p) − J(q)) = Π_{m≥1, n≥−1} (1 − p^m q^n)^{c(mn)}, where p, q stand for e^{(1,0)}, e^{(0,1)} and J = Σ c(n)qⁿ.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: By the previous theorem m ≅ g(A)/c with simple roots in degrees of positive 2a + b. Real roots have norm −2ab > 0 and m_{(a,b)} ≠ 0 needs ab ≥ −1, so the only positive real root is (1,−1), which is simple; imaginary simple roots have degrees (a,b) with a, b ≥ 1 (m_{(a,0)} ≅ V_1 = 0), and two of them have inner product −(ab' + a'b) < 0.

Hence the free-subalgebra theorem applies with g_J = sl₂: u⁺ = L(W) with W = ⊕_j U(n_J⁺)e_j, the sl₂-string of a simple root (a,b) (b ≥ a, since ⟨(1,−1),(a,b)⟩ = a − b ≤ 0) consisting of the degrees (a+k, b−k), 0 ≤ k ≤ b − a.
Free Lie character formula for u⁺ = ⊕_{a,b≥1} m_{(a,b)} with dim m_{(a,b)} = c(ab) (no-ghost): 1 − ch W = Π_{a,b≥1}(1 − p^a q^b)^{c(ab)}.

The j product formula p(J(p) − J(q)) = (1 − pq^{−1})·Π_{a,b≥1}(1 − p^aq^b)^{c(ab)} (the only factor with n = −1 is 1 − pq^{−1}, and the factors with n = 0 have exponent c(0) = 0) together with the telescoping identity p(J(p) − J(q)) = (1 − pq^{−1})(1 − Σ_{a,b≥1} c(a+b−1)p^aq^b) gives ch W = Σ_{a,b≥1} c(a+b−1)p^aq^b.

Induction on a: the coefficient at (1,n) comes only from strings starting at (1,n), so the multiplicity of the simple root (1,n) is c(n); the string from (1, a+b−1) already accounts for (a,b), so there are no simple roots with a ≥ 2.
The denominator formula is the j product formula with (1 − p/q) = the factor of the real simple root.
acceptance: The matrix M has first row 2, 0 (c(1) times), −1 (c(2) times), −2, …; the simple root spaces sum to V (Borcherds 1992 §1).
The coefficient of p q^1 in the denominator formula gives −c(1) on both sides.

sources.match: Statement (Borcherds proves it through the generalized Kac–Moody denominator formula).
Denominator formula of g(M) via the free Lie algebra and identification with m.

nodes.title: m = u⁺ ⊕ gl₂ ⊕ u⁻ with u⁻ free, equivariantly
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module, G ≤ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)) and m = m(V). Then m = u⁺ ⊕ gl₂ ⊕ u⁻ where gl₂ = m_{(−1,1)} ⊕ m_{(0,0)} ⊕ m_{(1,−1)} and u⁻ = ⊕_{a,b≥1} m_{(−a,−b)}, u⁺ = ⊕_{a,b≥1} m_{(a,b)} are free Lie algebras. Let W ⊆ u⁻ be the orthogonal complement of [u⁻,u⁻] for the contravariant form, degree by degree. Then W is G-stable, the inclusion induces a G-equivariant Lie algebra isomorphism L(W) ≅ u⁻ (G acting on L(W) through W), W is stable under gl₂, and for all a, b ≥ 1 there is a G-equivariant linear isomorphism W_{−(a,b)} ≅ V_{a+b} (VOA weight a + b), while W_{−(a,b)} = 0 unless a, b ≥ 1.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: By the simple-roots theorem and the free-subalgebra theorem (via m ≅ g(M)/c, an isomorphism on n^±) u⁻ is free on ⊕_j U(n_J⁻)f_j, and gl₂ = sl₂ + m_{(0,0)} normalizes u⁻.

A positively graded Lie algebra that is free on some graded subspace is free on every graded complement W of its derived algebra: W generates (induction on degree) and L(W) → u⁻ is injective by comparing graded dimensions through the free Lie character formula (g = 1).

The contravariant form is positive definite and G-invariant on each finite-dimensional m_r, r ≠ 0, and [u⁻,u⁻] is G-stable, so the orthogonal complement W is G-stable; hence L(W) ≅ u⁻ is G-equivariant.
W ≅ u⁻/[u⁻,u⁻] as G × gl₂-modules. For n ≥ 1, W_{−(1,n)} = u⁻_{−(1,n)} = m_{−(1,n)} ≅ V_{n+1} (no bracket of two elements of u⁻ has first coordinate −1).

By the free Lie character formula and the j product formula (as in the simple-roots proof) dim W_{−(a,b)} = c(a+b−1) for a,b ≥ 1. As an sl₂-module (raising operator f_{(−1,1)} of degree (−1,1)), W is finite-dimensional in each string {−(a,b) : a + b = s} with constant multiplicity c(s−1) from weight a − b = −(s−2) to s−2, so it is c(s−1) copies of the s−1-dimensional irreducible, and the powers of the lowering operator give isomorphisms W_{−(1,s−1)} ≅ W_{−(a,s−a)} (sl₂ theory, request to LieHighestWeight Layer 0).
These isomorphisms commute with G because G fixes the one-dimensional spaces m_{±(1,−1)} ≅ V_0 = ℝ1 pointwise.
acceptance: Jurisich 2009 §4: U = ∐_{i>0} W_i ⊗ V♮_{i+1} as gl₂ × M-modules.

sources.match: Decomposition.
The generating space as gl₂ × M-module.

nodes.title: Borcherds' twisted denominator identity
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module and g ∈ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)); write c_h(n) := tr(h|V_{n+1}) for h = g^i (so c_h(−1) = 1, c_h(0) = 0 and c_h(n) = 0 for n < −1) and T_g = Σ_n c_g(n)qⁿ. Then in the ring ℝ((q))((p)) of formal Laurent series in p with coefficients in ℝ((q)): p^{−1} exp(−Σ_{i≥1} Σ_{m≥1, n∈ℤ} c_{g^i}(mn) p^{mi} q^{ni}/i) = T_g(p) − T_g(q). Equivalently, in ℝ[[p,q]]: exp(−Σ_{i≥1} Σ_{a,b≥1} c_{g^i}(ab) p^{ai}q^{bi}/i) = 1 − Σ_{a,b≥1} c_g(a+b−1) p^a q^b.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
g conformal automorphism preserving the form
proofSteps: Apply the free-decomposition theorem with G = ⟨g⟩: u⁻ ≅ L(W) g-equivariantly with W_{−(a,b)} ≅ V_{a+b}.

The equivariant free Lie character formula (p, q recording the degrees −(1,0), −(0,1)) with ch_g(u⁻) = Σ_{a,b≥1} c_g(ab)p^aq^b (Monster Lie algebra: m_{(−a,−b)} ≅ V_{ab+1} g-equivariantly) and ch_g(W) = Σ c_g(a+b−1)p^aq^b gives the second form (ψ^i ch_g(u⁻) = Σ c_{g^i}(ab)p^{ai}q^{bi}).

Multiply by p^{−1}(1 − p/q) = p^{−1}exp(−Σ_i p^iq^{−i}/i) (the terms with n = −1, m = 1; the terms with n = 0 vanish as c(0) = 0; terms with mn < −1 vanish) and use the telescoping identity (p^{−1} − q^{−1})(1 − Σ c_g(a+b−1)p^aq^b) = T_g(p) − T_g(q).
acceptance: For g = 1 the identity is the j product formula p^{−1}Π(1 − p^mqⁿ)^{c(mn)} = J(p) − J(q).
Comparing coefficients of p²q^2 gives c_g(4) = c_g(3) + (c_g(1)² − c_{g²}(1))/2.

sources.match: Statement in Borcherds' indexing.
The derivation from the free Lie algebra u⁻ (Euler–Poincaré form).
Same identity in Gannon's notation.

nodes.title: Completely replicable functions and replication families
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0. A normalized q-series is f ∈ k((q)) with f = q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} a(n)qⁿ (coefficient 1 at q^{−1}, 0 at q^0, and no other negative powers); write a(−1) = 1, a(0) = 0, a(n) = 0 for n < −1. A replication family is a map F : ℕ_{≥1} → k((q)) with each F(s) normalized, coefficients a_s(n), such that for every s ≥ 1, in k((q))((p)): p^{−1} exp(−Σ_{i≥1} Σ_{m≥1, n∈ℤ} a_{si}(mn) p^{mi} q^{ni}/i) = F(s)(p) − F(s)(q). A normalized f is completely replicable if f = F(1) for some replication family F (its replicates are f^{(s)} := F(s)); Norton's definition via the identities Σ_{ad=n, 0≤b<d} f^{(a)}((aτ+b)/d) = Q_n(f(τ)) is equivalent (Borcherds 1992 §8).
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: Define IsNormalizedQSeries f, the replication identity for a family at index s (a statement in LaurentSeries (LaurentSeries k) using PowerSeries.subst for exp), IsReplicationFamily F and IsCompletelyReplicable f := ∃ F, IsReplicationFamily F ∧ F 1 = f.
The exponential is well defined because the exponent lies in p·k((q))[[p]] after removing the single term with n = −1, m = 1, which contributes the factor 1 − p/q.
acceptance: The constant family F(s) = J is a replication family (j product formula).
For a moonshine module V and g ∈ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)), s ↦ T_{g^s} is a replication family (twisted denominator identity).

sources.match: Definition adopted here.

api.name: ReplicationIdentity

api.name: IsReplicationFamily
api.statement: Every F(s) is normalized and the replication identity holds at every s.

nodes.title: Recursion formulas and determination of replication families
nodes.statement: Let F be a replication family over a field of characteristic 0 with coefficients a_s(n). (a) For all s ≥ 1 and k ≥ 1 (writing a = a_s, a' = a_{2s}): a(4k) = a(2k+1) + (a(k)² − a'(k))/2 + Σ_{1≤j<k} a(j)a(2k−j); a(4k+1) = a(2k+3) − a(2)a(2k) + (a(2k)² + a'(2k))/2 + (a(k+1)² − a'(k+1))/2 + Σ_{1≤j≤k} a(j)a(2k−j+2) + Σ_{1≤j<k} a'(j)a(4k−4j) + Σ_{1≤j<2k} (−1)^j a(j)a(4k−j); a(4k+2) = a(2k+2) + Σ_{1≤j≤k} a(j)a(2k−j+1); a(4k+3) = a(2k+4) − a(2)a(2k+1) − (a(2k+1)² − a'(2k+1))/2 + Σ_{1≤j≤k+1} a(j)a(2k−j+3) + Σ_{1≤j≤k} a'(j)a(4k−4j+2) + Σ_{1≤j≤2k} (−1)^j a(j)a(4k−j+2). (b) Consequently, for n = 4 or n ≥ 6, a_s(n) is determined by the a_s(j) and a_{2s}(j) with j < n; hence two replication families F, F' with a_s(n) = a'_s(n) for all s ≥ 1 and n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5} are equal.
hypotheses: F replication family
proofSteps: Compare the coefficients of p² and p⁴ of both sides of the replication identity at index s (Borcherds 1992 §9) and solve for the coefficient of highest index.
(b): strong induction on n, simultaneously for all s; the right sides of (a) involve only indices < n when n = 4 or n ≥ 6 (for n = 5 the formula for a(4·1+1) degenerates to a(5) = a(5)).
Alternative: Möbius inversion of the p^iq^j coefficients shows a_s(ij) = a_s(i+j−1) + (terms of level ≤ i+j−3) (Jurisich–Lepowsky–Wilson (37)–(38)).
acceptance: Checked numerically for J (a_s = c for all s) for k = 1, …, 4 and for the 2B series with a' = c (a(4) = −49152, a(6) = −614400, …).

sources.match: Part (b); the displayed formulas (9.1) are part (a).
Part (b) by the level argument.

nodes.title: McKay–Thompson series of a moonshine module are completely replicable
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module (Borcherds' properties (1)–(2)) and g ∈ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)). Then s ↦ T_{g^s} is a replication family; in particular T_g is completely replicable with replicates T_{g^s}, and T_g is determined by the numbers c_{g^s}(n), s ≥ 1, n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5}. This holds for every automorphism, without reference to the Monster.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
g conformal automorphism preserving the form
proofSteps: Each T_{g^s} is normalized: V_0 = ℝ1 with g^s·1 = 1 and V_1 = 0.
The replication identity at index s is the twisted denominator identity for g^s (since (g^s)^i = g^{si}).
Determination by the listed coefficients is the recursion theorem.
acceptance: For g = 1 this recovers the complete replicability of J.
Borcherds 1992 §3: properties (1)–(2) imply that Σ Tr(g|V_i)q^i is completely replicable for any automorphism g.

sources.match: Statement.

nodes.title: The Laurent series J = j − 744

nodes.title: Level-one modular functions holomorphic on ℍ
nodes.statement: M^!_0 is the weight-0, level-one case of the weakly holomorphic modular forms of QM.3 (QM.3/weakly-holomorphic-modular-form with Γ = SL₂(ℤ) and k = 0): the set of f : ℍ → ℂ that are holomorphic on ℍ, invariant under SL₂(ℤ) (f(γτ) = f(τ) for all γ), and meromorphic at i∞: τ ↦ e^{2πiNτ}f(τ) is bounded as Im τ → ∞ for some N ∈ ℕ (for level one, exponential growth at the single cusp is equivalent to this). This node adds the ring structure used by the moonshine chain. It is a ℂ-subalgebra of the functions ℍ → ℂ; each f ∈ M^!_0 has a Laurent q-expansion with coefficients zero below −N; f is bounded at i∞ if and only if its Laurent expansion has no negative powers, and then f is a level-one modular form of weight 0, hence constant.

nodes.title: Holomorphic level-one modular functions are polynomials in j
nodes.statement: Every f ∈ M^!_0 whose Laurent q-expansion has no powers below q^{−N} is P(j) for a unique polynomial P ∈ ℂ[X] of degree ≤ N; P is determined by the coefficients of f at q^{−N}, …, q^0. Hence M^!_0 = ℂ[j] and evaluation at j is an isomorphism of ℂ-algebras ℂ[X] ≅ M^!_0.

N > 0: j ∈ M^!_0 has Laurent expansion q^{−1} + 744 + O(q) (ModularForms Layer 0), so j^N = q^{−N} + (higher powers); f − a_{−N} j^N ∈ M^!_0 has no powers below q^{−(N−1)}; apply the induction hypothesis.
Uniqueness: j^n has leading term q^{−n}, so the j^n are linearly independent and a nonzero P(j) has leading term (lead P)·q^{−deg P}.

nodes.title: Formal weight-zero Hecke operators on Laurent series
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0 and m ≥ 1. The formal Hecke operator T_m : k((q)) → k((q)) is the k-linear map with (T_m f)_n := Σ_{a ≥ 1, a | m, a | n} a^{−1} f_{mn/a²} for n ∈ ℤ (for n = 0 the sum is over all a | m). It is the q-expansion of the weight-zero Hecke operator (1/m)Σ_{ad=m, 0≤b<d} f((aτ+b)/d). If f = q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} f_n qⁿ is normalized then T_m f = (1/m)q^{−m} + Σ_{n≥1}(T_m f)_n qⁿ.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: The sum is finite (a | m); the support of T_m f is bounded below by m·(order of f) when the order is negative, and by 0 otherwise, so T_m f is a Laurent series.
Normalized f: a coefficient at n < 0 needs mn/a² ≥ −1 with a | gcd(m,n); a² = m|n| with a ≤ m, a ≤ |n| forces a = m = |n|, giving (T_m f)_{−m} = f_{−1}/m; the constant term is σ_{−1}(m) f_0 = 0.
acceptance: T_1 = id.

nodes.title: Logarithm of the j product
nodes.statement: In the ring ℚ((q))[[p]] (formal power series in p over Laurent series in q), the product Π_{m≥1, n≥−1}(1 − p^m q^n)^{c(mn)} = (1 − pq^{−1})·Π_{m,n≥1}(1 − p^mq^n)^{c(mn)} converges (the second factor in ℚ[[p,q]] in the (p,q)-adic topology; factors with n ≤ −2 or n = 0 have exponent 0 and the only factor with n = −1 is 1 − pq^{−1}), and it equals exp(−Σ_{M≥1} (formalHecke M J)(q)·p^M).

nodes.title: The product formula for j (Koike–Norton–Zagier; Borcherds' Lemma 7.1)
nodes.statement: In ℤ((q))((p)) (formal Laurent series in p over ℤ((q))): p^{−1} Π_{m≥1, n∈ℤ} (1 − p^m q^n)^{c(mn)} = J(p) − J(q), where J = Σ_{n≥−1} c(n)qⁿ is the Laurent series of j − 744 (equivalently j(p) − j(q)). Equivalently, in ℤ[[p,q]]: Π_{m,n≥1}(1 − p^mq^n)^{c(mn)} = 1 − Σ_{m,n≥1} c(m+n−1)p^mq^n.
hypotheses: none
proofSteps: By the logarithm lemma, p·LHS = exp(−Σ_M T_M(J) p^M); each T_M J = P_M(J) ∈ ℂ[J] (hecke-transform-of-j), and the coefficient of p^M in exp(−Σ T_M(J)p^M) is a polynomial with rational coefficients in the T_{M'}J, M' ≤ M, hence lies in ℂ[J].
p·RHS = 1 − pJ(q) + Σ_{M≥2} c(M−1)p^M also has all p-coefficients in ℂ[J].

Coefficients at q^n, n ≤ 0: p·LHS = (1 − pq^{−1})(1 + q·ℚ[[p,q]]) has q^{−1}-part −p and q^0-part 1 + Σ_{m≥1}c(m)p^{m+1} (the q¹ coefficient of Π_{m,n≥1} is −Σ c(m)p^m); p·RHS has the same q^{−1}- and q^0-parts and no lower terms.
Hence for each M the difference of p^M-coefficients is P(J) with vanishing coefficients at q^n, n ≤ 0, so it is 0 (principal-part lemma); the identity holds over ℂ and therefore over ℤ.
The second form: divide by 1 − pq^{−1} and use the telescoping identity p(J(p) − J(q)) = (1 − pq^{−1})(1 − Σ c(m+n−1)p^mq^n).

nodes.title: Modular groups of moonshine type
nodes.statement: A subgroup Γ ≤ SL₂(ℝ) is of moonshine type if it is discrete, contains the image of Γ₀(N) = {(a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) : N | c} for some N ≥ 1, and for t ∈ ℝ the matrix (1 t; 0 1) lies in Γ if and only if t ∈ ℤ. Such Γ is commensurable with SL₂(ℤ), hence a cofinite Fuchsian group whose cusps are the Γ-orbits of ℚ ∪ {∞}; the cusp ∞ has width 1. Examples: SL₂(ℤ), Γ₀(N), and the Atkin–Lehner extensions Γ₀(N)+ (for N = 2: generated by Γ₀(2) and (0 −1/√2; √2 0)).
hypotheses: Γ ≤ SL₂(ℝ)
proofSteps: Define IsMoonshineType Γ with the three conditions (DiscreteTopology on Γ with the subspace topology; Subgroup.map of Γ₀(N) under Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.map (Int.castRingHom ℝ); the translation condition).

Commensurability: Γ₀(N) has finite index in SL₂(ℤ), and a discrete group containing Γ₀(N) contains it with finite index (both have finite covolume; FuchsianOrbifolds Layer 2); hence Γ is cofinite with cusp set Γ\(ℚ ∪ {∞}).

nodes.title: Normalized Hauptmodul of a genus-zero group
nodes.statement: Let Γ be of moonshine type. A function f : ℍ → ℂ is a normalized Hauptmodul for Γ if: f is holomorphic on ℍ; f(γτ) = f(τ) for all γ ∈ Γ; f(τ) − e^{−2πiτ} → 0 as Im τ → ∞ (so f = q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} a_n qⁿ); and for every A ∈ SL₂(ℤ) such that A·∞ is not Γ-equivalent to ∞ (no γ ∈ Γ has (γ⁻¹A)₁₀ = 0), the function τ ↦ f(Aτ) is bounded as Im τ → ∞. Equivalently (theorem hauptmodul-genus-zero), f descends to a biholomorphism from the compactified quotient X(Γ) to ℙ¹ sending the cusp ∞ to ∞; this is Borcherds' 'isomorphism from the compact Riemann surface H/G to the sphere taking i∞ to ∞' with the normalization e^{−2πiτ} + (a function vanishing at i∞).
hypotheses: Γ of moonshine type
proofSteps: Define IsNormalizedHauptmodul Γ f by the four conditions (MDifferentiable, invariance, IsZeroAtImInfty (f − 1/qParam 1), boundedness at the other cusps through SL₂(ℤ)-translates).
The conditions give a Γ-invariant function with a single simple pole on X(Γ) (at the cusp ∞, of width 1) and no other poles, which is what the genus-zero theorem converts into a degree-one map.
acceptance: J = j − 744 is a normalized Hauptmodul for SL₂(ℤ); Δ(τ)/Δ(2τ) + 24 is one for Γ₀(2).
j is a Hauptmodul for SL₂(ℤ) that is not normalized (constant term 744).

nodes.title: Normalized Hauptmoduln and genus zero
nodes.statement: Let Γ be of moonshine type and X(Γ) its compactified quotient (a compact Riemann surface, FuchsianOrbifolds). (a) If f is a normalized Hauptmodul for Γ, then f descends to a meromorphic function on X(Γ) whose only pole is a simple pole at the cusp ∞; hence the induced holomorphic map X(Γ) → ℙ¹ has degree one and is a biholomorphism, X(Γ) has genus 0, and every Γ-invariant meromorphic function on ℍ that is meromorphic at the cusps is a rational function of f. (b) Conversely, if X(Γ) has genus 0 there is exactly one normalized Hauptmodul for Γ.
hypotheses: Γ of moonshine type
proofSteps: Descent and extension over cusps: f is Γ-invariant, holomorphic, with q-expansion at ∞ in the width-one parameter q (simple pole) and bounded at the other cusps (removable singularities) — FuchsianOrbifolds Layers 3–5.
Degree: the fibre over ∞ ∈ ℙ¹ is the single cusp ∞ with local multiplicity 1; degree-one theorem (FuchsianOrbifolds Layer 5) gives a biholomorphism, so genus X(Γ) = genus ℙ¹ = 0.
Function field: a meromorphic function on X(Γ) ≅ ℙ¹ is a rational function of the coordinate f.
Uniqueness: the difference of two normalized Hauptmoduln is holomorphic on X(Γ) and vanishes at ∞, hence 0.

Converse: genus 0 gives a biholomorphism X(Γ) ≅ ℙ¹; composing with a Möbius map sending the cusp ∞ to ∞ gives a Hauptmodul, and scaling and translating normalizes it (the pole at ∞ is simple since the degree is one and the width is one).
acceptance: For Γ = SL₂(ℤ), f = J: X(1) ≅ ℙ¹ (FuchsianOrbifolds Layer 6).
For Γ = Γ₀(2), f = Δ(τ)/Δ(2τ) + 24.

nodes.title: The normalized Hauptmodul of Γ₀(2)
nodes.statement: Let Δ be Mathlib's modular discriminant and t_{2B}(τ) := Δ(τ)/Δ(2τ) + 24. Then t_{2B} is a normalized Hauptmodul for Γ₀(2) (so X₀(2) has genus 0), and its Laurent q-expansion is q^{−1}Π_{n≥1}(1 − q^{2n−1})^{24} + 24 = q^{−1} + 276q − 2048q² + 11202q³ − 49152q⁴ + 184024q⁵ + ⋯.
hypotheses: none
proofSteps: Δ(2τ) is a nonzero constant multiple of Δ|₁₂ diag(2,1) is a modular form of weight 12 for Γ₀(2) and never vanishes on ℍ (Mathlib discriminant_ne_zero); so Δ(τ)/Δ(2τ) is holomorphic and Γ₀(2)-invariant (both numerator and denominator have weight 12).

At ∞: Δ(τ)/Δ(2τ) = q^{−1}Π(1 − qⁿ)^{24}(1 − q^{2n})^{−24} = q^{−1}Π(1 + qⁿ)^{−24} = q^{−1}Π(1 − q^{2n−1})^{24} (Euler's identity Π(1 + qⁿ)(1 − q^{2n−1}) = 1), using Mathlib's product formula discriminant_eq_q_prod.
Cusps of Γ₀(2): ∞ and 0 (ModularForms 10A). At 0: Δ(Sτ)/Δ(2Sτ) = τ^{12}Δ(τ)/((τ/2)^{12}Δ(τ/2)) = 2^{12}Δ(τ)/Δ(τ/2) → 0 as Im τ → ∞ (discriminant_S_invariant), so t_{2B}∘S is bounded.
Expand the product to obtain the displayed coefficients (finite computation).
acceptance: t_{2B}(0-cusp value) = 24.

nodes.title: Head characters of the moonshine module
nodes.statement: Let V♮ be the Frenkel–Lepowsky–Meurman moonshine module with its Monster 𝕄 ≤ Aut(V♮, ω, (·,·)), and χ_1, …, χ_7 the irreducible characters of 𝕄 of degrees 1, 196883, 21296876, 842609326, 18538750076, 19360062527, 293553734298. Then as 𝕄-modules V♮_2 ≅ χ_1 + χ_2, V♮_3 ≅ χ_1 + χ_2 + χ_3, V♮_4 ≅ 2χ_1 + 2χ_2 + χ_3 + χ_4, V♮_6 ≅ 4χ_1 + 5χ_2 + 3χ_3 + 2χ_4 + χ_5 + χ_6 + χ_7 (Borcherds' V_1, V_2, V_3, V_5). Consequently, for every g ∈ 𝕄 the coefficients c_g(n), n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5}, of T_g equal the corresponding coefficients of the Conway–Norton function of the class of g.
hypotheses: V♮ the FLM moonshine module (gap)
Monster character table (gap)
proofSteps: The irreducible 𝕄-modules of dimension ≤ dim V♮_6 are exactly those with characters χ_1, …, χ_7 (ATLAS), so the decompositions are determined by the values c_g(n) on seven classes g_1, …, g_7 with det(χ_i(g_j)) ≠ 0.

Take g_1 of class 2B (Thompson series computed by FLM) and six elements of classes 3B, 5B, 7B, 9B, 13B, 15D in the centralizer 2^{1+24}.Co₁ of a 2B element, corresponding to fixed-point-free odd-order automorphisms of the Leech lattice (Co₁ classes 3A, 5A, 7A, 9A, 13A, 15C), for which FLM's formula gives 2Σ_n c_g(n)qⁿ = 1/η_g(q) + η_g(q)/η_g(q²) + η_g(q)/η_g(q^{1/2}) + η_g(q)/η_g(−q^{1/2}).
det(χ_i(g_j)) = 35672555520 = 2^{22}·3^5·5·7 ≠ 0; compare the first coefficients (finite computation) to obtain the decompositions, and read off c_g(n) for all g from the character table.
acceptance: The dimension checks above hold (verified).

nodes.title: The monstrous moonshine theorem (Borcherds)
nodes.statement: Let 𝕄 be the Monster group, presented as TauCeti.SporadicName.Group M (the Y₄₄₃ presentation with Ivanov's central relator). There exist a moonshine module V (Borcherds' axioms: a real vertex operator algebra of central charge 24 with positive definite invariant form and graded dimension J — the Frenkel–Lepowsky–Meurman module V♮) and an injective group homomorphism ρ : 𝕄 →* Aut(V, ω, (·,·)) such that for every g ∈ 𝕄 there are a moonshine-type group Γ_g ≤ SL₂(ℝ) containing Γ₀(N) with N = o(g)·h for some h | gcd(24, o(g)), and a normalized Hauptmodul f_g for Γ_g, whose Laurent q-expansion is the McKay–Thompson series T_{ρ(g)} = Σ_n tr(ρ(g)|V_{n+1}) qⁿ. In particular every Γ_g has genus 0, and T_{ρ(g)} is the function t_g attached to the class of g in Conway–Norton's Table 2.
hypotheses: 𝕄 the Monster (Tau Ceti presentation)
proofSteps: FLM (gap 'FLM moonshine module'): V♮ satisfies the moonshine-module axioms and FLM's Monster acts faithfully by conformal isometries; identify FLM's Monster with the presented group (gap 'Identification of the Monster').

Complete replicability (moonshine-module-complete-replicability): for every g, s ↦ T_{g^s} is a replication family, so T_g is determined by c_{g^s}(n), n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5}, s ≥ 1 (replication-recursion).
Head characters (monster-head-characters): these numbers equal the corresponding coefficients of the Conway–Norton functions t_{g^s}.
The Conway–Norton functions form replication families with t_{g^s} as replicates (Koike; gap 'Conway–Norton functions'): by the recursion theorem T_g = t_g for all g.
Each t_g is the normalized Hauptmodul of the explicit moonshine-type group Γ_g ⊇ Γ₀(o(g)h) of Conway–Norton's Table 2 (gap 'Conway–Norton functions'); by hauptmodul-genus-zero Γ_g has genus 0.
acceptance: g = 1: T_1 = J, Γ_1 = SL₂(ℤ) (moonshine-identity-thompson-series).
g ∈ 2B: T_g = q^{−1}Π(1 − q^{2n−1})^{24} + 24, Γ_g = Γ₀(2) (gamma0-two-hauptmodul).

nodes.statement: For |q|<1, set A=(q;q)∞, B=(q²;q²)∞, C=(-q;q)∞ and D=(-q;q²)∞. The eight definitions are: f0=A⁻¹ Σ_{n≥0,|j|≤n}(-1)^j q^((5n²+n)/2-j²)(1-q^(4n+2)); F0=B⁻¹ Σ_{n≥0,0≤j≤2n}(-1)^n q^(5n²+2n-(j²+j)/2)(1+q^(6n+3)); ψ0=((C/A)[1+2Σ_{n≥1}(-1)^n q^(n²+n)-2Σ_{n≥1,|j|<n}(-1)^j q^((5n²-n-3j²-j)/2)(1-q^n)]-1)/2; φ0=(D/B)Σ_{n≥0,|j|≤n}(-1)^j q^(5n²+2n-3j²-j)(1-q^(6n+3)); f1=A⁻¹Σ_{n≥0,|j|≤n}(-1)^j q^((5n²+3n)/2-j²)(1-q^(2n+1)); F1=B⁻¹Σ_{n≥0,0≤j≤2n}(-1)^n q^(5n²+4n-(j²+j)/2)(1+q^(2n+1)); ψ1=(C/A)Σ_{n≥0,|j|≤n}(-1)^j q^((5n²+3n-3j²-j)/2)(1-q^(2n+1)); φ1=q(D/B)Σ_{n≥0,|j|≤n}(-1)^j q^(5n²+4n-3j²-j)(1-q^(2n+1)). nodes.title: The first six fifth-order functions as sign-difference sums (Zwegers Lemma 4.8)
nodes.statement: Set A to be the diagonal two by two matrix with entries 5 and -2, let Q and B be the associated quadratic and bilinear forms, and set c1 to be the vector with entries 2 and 5 and c2 the vector with entries -2 and 5. Then each of the six functions of the vector F_{5,1}, multiplied by twice the eta function and by its q-power prefactor, equals a sum over the shifted lattice of the difference of the signs of B(nu, c1) and B(nu, c2), times the exponential of 2 pi i Q(nu) tau plus 2 pi i B(nu, b), for the six explicitly listed pairs of characteristics. The six shifts are (1/10, 0), (3/10, 0), (1/5, 1/4), (2/5, 1/4), (1/5, 1/4) and (2/5, 1/4), and the six second characteristics are (0, 1/4), (0, 1/4), (1/2, 1), (1/2, 2), (0, 1/4) and (0, 1/4), with the last two identities carrying an extra factor of the inverse of a primitive eighth root of unity. Moreover B(c1, c2) is -70 and Q(c1) = Q(c2) = -15, so that if the negative cone is chosen to contain c1 it also contains c2, which is the hypothesis the indefinite theta machinery needs.
hypotheses: A is the diagonal matrix with entries 5 and -2, so the form is indefinite of signature (1, 1), which is what the indefinite theta construction requires.
c1 and c2 must lie in the same component of the negative cone; the computation B(c1, c2) = -70 and Q(c1) = Q(c2) = -15 is what guarantees it.
The identities are for the corrected Andrews definitions of the previous node.
proofSteps: Split each double sum by replacing n by -n-1 in the second half, turning the factor 1 minus a power of q into the difference of two lattice sums.
Recognise the resulting difference of sums over the two half-lattices as the sign-difference sum with the stated c1 and c2.

For the functions with the (q^2; q^2)_infinity denominator use the elementary identity rewriting the sum over j from 0 to 2n as a symmetric sum from -n to n, and then argue as before; a term (q^2; q^2)_infinity is split off in the process.
Check the two computations B(c1, c2) = -70 and Q(c1) = Q(c2) = -15 and record the consequence for the negative cone.
acceptance: All six identities are written with their exact characteristics and prefactors.

nodes.title: F_{5,1} = H_{5,1} + G_{5,1}, and the modularity of the completion (Zwegers Prop. 4.10)
nodes.statement: For τ∈ℍ, F₁(τ)=H₁(τ)+G₁(τ), where F₁ is fifthOrderVectorOne and H₁,G₁,M₅,T₅ have the preceding exact coordinates. H₁(τ+1)=T₅H₁(τ) and H₁(−1/τ)=√(−iτ)(2/√5)M₅H₁(τ), using the principal square root. Each coordinate is real-analytic and Δ_(1/2)H₁=0, equivalently Ω_(1/2)H₁=(3/16)H₁ under Ω_(1/2)=Δ_(1/2)+3/16. For each ξ∈ℚ and coordinate i there exist C,δ>0 such that |G₁(ξ+iy)_i|≤C for 0<y<δ. The Eulerian-series comparison is a separate prerequisite gap; these statements use the corrected double-sum definitions.
hypotheses: The vectors are those of the previous node; the characteristics and the cone data come from the lemma.
The T-matrix is not diagonal: it permutes the third and fifth and the fourth and sixth components, because the two half-argument variants are exchanged.
The boundedness of G is towards rationals from above and is what makes the radial-limit statements of the consuming layer possible.
proofSteps: Apply the characteristic translation rules to the six theta components and divide by the eta translation law. The result is exactly T₅, including both exchanged pairs and their phases.

Use the element of the orthogonal group of the form that negates the first coordinate: it exchanges c1 and c2, so the indefinite theta function with characteristics transformed by it is the negative of the original, which is what produces the sign pattern in M_5.
Combine with the S-transformation of the theta functions with characteristics to get the S-transformation of the vector, then divide by the eta transformations to get those of H_{5,1}.

Prove the decomposition by splitting each sign-difference sum into its three parts and applying the splitting proposition, obtaining for each component the identity between the indefinite theta function and twice eta times the mock theta function minus the corresponding unary R combination.
Deduce the Casimir eigenvalue: F_{5,1} is holomorphic so it is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue three sixteenths, and so is G_{5,1} by the property of R, hence so is H_{5,1}.
Deduce the boundedness of G_{5,1} from the corresponding property of the unary R functions.

nodes.title: The remaining four fifth-order functions as sign-difference sums (Zwegers Lemma 4.11)
nodes.statement: With the same matrix A, the same c1 and c2, the four functions psi0, psi1, phi0 and phi1 also become sign-difference sums, after multiplication by twice a root of unity times a quotient of eta functions and by a q-power prefactor: for the two psi functions the quotient is eta of tau squared over eta of two tau, with the shifts (1/10, 1/6) and (3/10, 1/6) and second characteristic (0, 1/6); for the two phi functions, evaluated at minus the square root of q, the quotient is eta of tau squared over eta of tau over two, with the shifts (1/5, 1/6) and (2/5, 1/6) and second characteristic (1/10, 1/6), and the fourth identity carries an overall minus sign. The prefactors are q to the minus one sixtieth, q to the eleven sixtieths, q to the minus one two hundred and fortieth and q to the minus forty-nine two hundred and fortieths respectively, and the roots of unity are inverse twelfth and sixtieth roots.
hypotheses: The same A, c1, c2 as for the first six, so the cone computation carries over unchanged.
The eta quotients are different for the psi and the phi families, and the phi functions are evaluated at minus the square root of q.
One of the four identities carries an overall minus sign, which must not be dropped.
proofSteps: Split each of the four double sums as before, using the re-indexing that turns the factor into a difference of lattice sums.
Identify the resulting sums with sign-difference sums for the same A, c1 and c2, reading off the characteristics.
Record the eta quotients, the prefactors, the roots of unity and the sign of the fourth identity.
Record that the cone computation of the previous lemma applies verbatim.
acceptance: All four identities are written with their characteristics, prefactors, eta quotients and roots of unity.
The overall minus sign in the fourth is recorded.
The reuse of the same A, c1 and c2 is stated.

nodes.title: F_{5,2} = H_{5,2} + G_{5,2}, and the holomorphic sum F_5 (Zwegers Props. 4.13 and 4.14)
nodes.statement: Throughout the fifth-order contracts, q^r means exp(2πirτ), ζ_d means exp(2πi/d), and Θ[a;b] means the indefinite theta function for A=diag(5,−2), c₁=(2,5), c₂=(−2,5), with characteristics a,b. The six coordinates are indexed 0 through 5. F₂=(2q^(−1/60)ψ₀(q), 2q^(11/60)ψ₁(q), q^(−1/240)φ₀(−q^(1/2)), −q^(−49/240)φ₁(−q^(1/2)), q^(−1/240)φ₀(q^(1/2)), q^(−49/240)φ₁(q^(1/2))), with q^(1/2)=exp(πiτ). H₂=(2η(τ)²)⁻¹(2ζ₁₂η(2τ)Θ[(1/10,1/6);(0,1/6)], 2ζ₁₂η(2τ)Θ[(3/10,1/6);(0,1/6)], ζ₆₀⁻¹η(τ/2)Θ[(1/5,1/6);(1/10,1/6)], ζ₆₀^(−7)η(τ/2)Θ[(2/5,1/6);(1/10,1/6)], ζ₁₆η((τ+1)/2)Θ[(1/5,1/6);(0,1/6)], ζ₁₆η((τ+1)/2)Θ[(2/5,1/6);(0,1/6)]). Define G₂=−G₁ coordinatewise. For τ∈ℍ, F₂=H₂+G₂, H₂(τ+1)=T₅H₂(τ), and H₂(−1/τ)=√(−iτ)(2/√5)M₅H₂(τ). Each coordinate of H₂ is real-analytic, Δ_(1/2)H₂=0, and its Ω_(1/2) eigenvalue is 3/16. Each coordinate of G₂ is bounded on ξ+iy for ξ∈ℚ and sufficiently small positive y. Consequently F₅=F₁+F₂=H₁+H₂ is holomorphic and has those same T and S laws. Its coordinates are the six coordinatewise sums of the explicitly specified F₁ and F₂, including q^(71/240)F₁(q^(1/2))−q^(−49/240)φ₁(−q^(1/2)) in position 3. This specifies the generator laws; no unnamed congruence subgroup or congruence-kernel theorem is asserted. Comparison with the classical Eulerian functions still needs the recorded Andrews prerequisite.
hypotheses: The four functions and their identities are those of the previous lemma; the second vector has six components, built from the four functions at both square roots of q.
The cancellation G_{5,2} = -G_{5,1} is what makes the sum holomorphic; it is a computation with the unary R functions and is not a formal consequence of the two decompositions.
The source states modularity on a suitable congruence subgroup, but this contract proves the displayed generator laws. A congruence-kernel supplier remains required for that stronger assertion.
proofSteps: Assemble the six explicitly specified F₂ and H₂ coordinates from Lemma 4.11; set the unary correction to the coordinatewise negative of G₁, as checked from the display on p.80.
Prove the transformation laws of H_{5,2} exactly as for H_{5,1}, obtaining the same T-matrix and the same S-matrix M_5, and the same Casimir eigenvalue.
Prove the boundedness of G_{5,2} towards the rationals from the corresponding property of the unary R functions.
Compute that G_{5,2} equals minus G_{5,1}.
Deduce that F_5 = H_{5,1} + H_{5,2} is holomorphic and read off its transformation laws from those of the two completions.

The six component sums follow by adding the exact F₁ and F₂ coordinates. Watson supplies expressions for the first four (Zwegers p.83, citing Watson pp.299); the other two follow by changing q^(1/2) to −q^(1/2). A congruence-kernel proof is not supplied by the two generator laws alone.
acceptance: The transformation matrices of H_{5,2} are stated and are recorded as the same as those of H_{5,1}.
The cancellation G_{5,2} = -G_{5,1} is stated as the step that makes the sum holomorphic.
The six explicit combinations are written out, and the attribution of the first four to Watson is recorded.
The displayed S and T laws are asserted; the source’s stronger congruence-subgroup assertion remains outside this contract until a congruence-kernel proof is supplied.

nodes.title: The index-13 weight-1 meromorphic Jacobi form and its vector-valued completion (Zwegers Prop. 3.12)
nodes.statement: Define θ[a,b](z,τ)=Σ_{n∈ℤ} exp(πi(n+a)²τ+2πi(n+a)(z+b)) and φ=(θ[0,0]θ[0,1/2]θ[1/2,0])⁹/(Δθ[1/2,1/2]). For Im τ>0, φ obeys the weight-one index-thirteen elliptic and full-group generator laws stated in the API. It has simple lattice poles and residue −128/π at zero. With p=−τ/2−1/2, its coefficient functions are h_l=exp(−πil²τ/26)∫₀¹φ(p+t,τ)exp(−2πil(p+t))dt+256iR_{13,l}(0;τ), for 0≤l≤25. Away from the poles, φ(z,τ)=Σ_{l=0}^{25}h_l(τ)θ_{13,l}(z,τ)+512i f̃₀(z,τ). The h_l obey the explicit T/S laws and unary-theta shadow in the API and are weight-1/2 harmonic functions (Casimir eigenvalue 3/16). Constancy of the residue supplies this last step; the general meromorphic Jacobi decomposition does not assert harmonic coefficient functions.
hypotheses: The quotient is meromorphic in the elliptic variable with simple poles on the lattice; the base point must be chosen so that the singular set is a single point, and the choice minus half tau minus one half does that.
The residue is constant in tau, and that is special to this example.

The transformation of phi like a Jacobi form of weight one and index thirteen is read off from the classical theta transformation table; Zwegers records a misprint in that table, in the fourth formula on the right, which should carry a factor minus i.
proofSteps: Write phi as the stated quotient and record its q-expansion in the elliptic variable.
Read off the weight and index from the theta transformation table, recording the misprint Zwegers corrects.
Locate the poles and choose the base point so that the singular set is the single point zero.
Compute the residue at zero by Jacobi's derivative formula and the identity for the derivative of the odd theta function, obtaining the constant minus one hundred and twenty eight over pi.
Apply the corollary on meromorphic Jacobi forms with simple poles to get the decomposition and the formula for the coefficient functions.

Deduce that the coefficient functions are Casimir eigenfunctions with eigenvalue three sixteenths, since the Fourier coefficients of a holomorphic function are holomorphic and the level-thirteen R at zero is an eigenfunction with the same eigenvalue.
Read off the two transformation laws and the tau-bar derivative.
acceptance: The function is written out and its weight and index are stated with the source of the transformation law.
The residue computation is carried out and its constancy in tau is recorded.
Both transformation laws and the Casimir eigenvalue are stated.
The misprint in the classical table is recorded, with the correction.
For the E₄φ non-example, use the displayed shadow of h₁ and the product rule for Δ_{9/2}; its leading unary-theta term and E₄=1+O(q) show a nonzero value for sufficiently large imaginary τ.

nodes.title: Why the index-13 example is special, and what the general case does not give
nodes.statement: The constant residue of this index-thirteen quotient is a sufficient condition for its completed coefficient functions to have Casimir eigenvalue 3/16. The simple-pole decomposition and residue modularity theorem, without that special condition, do not imply any Casimir eigenfunction property. For example, multiplying by E₄ gives a weight-five index-thirteen form whose coefficient E₄h₁ is not annihilated by Δ_{9/2}. The generic decomposition is retained without an unsupported harmonic conclusion.
hypotheses: The general statement available is the corollary on simple poles together with the modularity of the residue functions.
The constancy of the residues is a property of this particular quotient and is proved by Jacobi's derivative formula.
The generic theorem is a decomposition and residue-modularity statement; the explicit E₄φ non-example is specified and tested at the construction node.
proofSteps: Record what makes the example special: the constancy of the residues.
Record what that buys: the Casimir eigenvalue and hence a real-analytic modular form.
Record what the general case gives instead: the decomposition and the modularity of the residue functions, with no eigenfunction property.
Use the explicit shadow and Laplacian product rule for the E₄φ non-example; ensure no other node applies the special harmonic conclusion to arbitrary meromorphic Jacobi forms.
acceptance: The special hypothesis is named and its consequence identified.
The general statement is named and the gap between the two is explicit.
The boundary is checkable against the other nodes of this layer.

nodes.title: The odd Rademacher quadratic-root sum
nodes.statement: For k ≥ 1 and n ∈ ℤ, let B_k(n) = ∑_{m ∈ ℤ/kℤ, (24m)² = 1−24n} e_k(2m), where e_k is Mathlib's standard additive character. This is a specialized auxiliary of A_k(n), not a new general exponential-sum or character interface. Its definition is meaningful for every positive k; the comparison with A_k below requires gcd(k,6)=1.
hypotheses: k is a positive natural number; n is an integer.
proofSteps: Use the finite carrier ℤ/kℤ, filter by the displayed quadratic equation, and sum the existing standard additive character at 2m. All coefficients are reduced in ℤ/kℤ, so no lift is chosen.
Negation preserves the root set; reindex by m ↦ −m to see the imaginary parts cancel. The convention e_k(2m), rather than e_k(m), matches Whiteman's angle 4πm/k.
acceptance: The singular root set can be nonempty while B_k(n)=0; it is not replaced by its cardinality.
At k=1 the unique residue contributes 1.

nodes.title: Translation of singular Rademacher roots
nodes.statement: Let p>3 be prime, v≥2, and p divide D=1−24n. For every m∈ℤ/p^vℤ, (24(m+p^(v−1)))²=D if and only if (24m)²=D. Thus translation by p^(v−1) permutes the root set used by B_{p^v}(n), without a condition on the p-adic valuation of D.
hypotheses: p is prime and p>3; v≥2; n∈ℤ; p divides 1−24n.
proofSteps: Reduce a root equation modulo p. Since p does not divide 24 and a prime dividing a square divides its base, every root m is divisible by p (use an integer or natural representative).
Expand the change of square as 1152m p^(v−1)+576p^(2v−2). Both terms are divisible by p^v: the first uses p|m, the second uses v≥2.
Apply the same calculation with the negative translation to obtain the reverse implication and inverse permutation. This works for D≡0 modulo p^v and for the empty root set.
acceptance: For p=5,v=2,n=24, translation by 5 cycles all five roots; for n=9 both sets are empty.
Do not assume that a singular root set has two elements.

sources.match: A uniform translation proof of the root grouping used by Whiteman; unlike the printed valuation parametrization, it also covers D≡0 modulo p^v.

nodes.title: Cancellation of singular Rademacher root sums
nodes.statement: For p>3 prime, v≥2, and p | 1−24n, B_{p^v}(n)=0, whether or not roots exist.
hypotheses: p is prime and p>3; v≥2; n∈ℤ; p divides 1−24n.
proofSteps: Reindex the defining finite sum by the permutation supplied by odd-rademacher-root-translation, using Finset.sum_bij.
The standard character's addition law gives B=e_{p^v}(2p^(v−1))B.
The character is injective and maps zero to one. Its displayed multiplier is not one, since 0<2p^(v−1)<p^v for p>3. Translate nonzero residues to divisibility with ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff.
Cancel the nonzero complex scalar 1−e_{p^v}(2p^(v−1)). No root count or finite valuation of D is used.
acceptance: B_25(24)=0 with five roots, B_125(99)=0 with D≡0 mod125, and B_25(9)=0 with no roots.
The first-power case is excluded: B_5(4)=1.

sources.match: The finite-character proof replaces the printed geometric cosine grouping and fills its fully singular subcase.

nodes.title: Whiteman's odd Rademacher root formula
nodes.statement: For k≥1 with gcd(k,6)=1 and n∈ℤ, A_k(n)=(3|k)√k B_k(n), with the positive real square root and the integer Jacobi symbol embedded in ℂ. The original A_k is the Dedekind-sum definition already owned by QM.2.
proofSteps: Apply rademacher-selberg-formula to identify the original Dedekind-defined A_k(n) with the real finite sum S_k(n). This is now the precisely isolated source-dependent input; its Fourier/H-sum proof and the inherited Jacobi multiplier identification remain a recorded gap.

Apply selberg-odd-root-comparison, whose finite proof is decomposed through the half-range identity, the root bijection, the uniform phase congruence and character identity, the Jacobi-three cosine factor and the promoted root-sum conjugation lemma.
No fixed root count or exclusion of the zero root is used. The finite conversion includes k=1. All local A_k endpoints still inherit the source-dependent Selberg equality gap.
acceptance: Recover A_1(n)=1 and A_5(4)=−√5.
A direct finite numerical check is diagnostic only, not a proof or closure of the Selberg bridge.
The formula is restricted to gcd(k,6)=1; exceptional primes have different weights.

sources.match: Whiteman's normalized endpoint, now split into the unresolved Dedekind-to-Selberg equality and the independently decomposed finite conversion (5.1)–(5.3).

nodes.title: The first-prime singular value of Rademacher's sum
nodes.statement: If p>3 is prime and p | 1−24n, then A_p(n)=(3|p)√p in ℂ.
hypotheses: p is prime and p>3; n∈ℤ; p divides 1−24n.
proofSteps: Modulo the prime p, the equation (24m)²=0 forces m=0 because p does not divide 24. Thus the sum B_p(n) consists of the single term e_p(0)=1.
Apply rademacher-odd-root-comparison at k=p. This endpoint retains that comparison's unresolved bridge input.
acceptance: A_5(4)=−√5, not zero; distinguish exponent v=1 from v≥2.
Johansson's printed λ=0 in (2.6) must be λ=1, as his author erratum confirms.

sources.match: The singular first-power branch is separate from the higher-power zero branch.

nodes.title: Higher-prime-power singular vanishing
nodes.statement: If p>3 is prime, v≥2 and p | 1−24n, then A_{p^v}(n)=0. In particular this includes 1−24n≡0 modulo p^v.
hypotheses: p is prime and p>3; v≥2; n∈ℤ; p divides 1−24n.
proofSteps: Apply odd-rademacher-root-singular-cancellation to obtain B_{p^v}(n)=0.
Since gcd(p^v,6)=1, substitute this value in rademacher-odd-root-comparison. The bridge gap remains a transitive input.
acceptance: A_25(24)=0 although the quadratic congruence has five solutions.
A_125(99)=0 in the fully singular case D=−2375, divisible by125.

sources.match: The printed conclusion is retained, with a proof route that includes the omitted D≡0 modulo p^v case.

nodes.title: Nonsquare-discriminant vanishing
nodes.statement: If p>3 is prime, v≥1 and 1−24n is not a square in ℤ/pℤ, then A_{p^v}(n)=0.
hypotheses: p is prime and p>3; v≥1; n∈ℤ; 1−24n is nonsquare modulo p.
proofSteps: Any root (24m)²=1−24n modulo p^v maps under ZMod.castHom to a square root modulo p, a contradiction.
The root sum is therefore empty. Substitute its zero value into rademacher-odd-root-comparison, retaining the bridge gap.
acceptance: A_7(1)=0 because −23≡5 modulo 7 is nonsquare.
This statement does not call zero a nonresidue; the singular branches above handle that case.

sources.match: The stronger mod-p obstruction suffices for empty roots at every positive exponent; no converse or Hensel-lifting theorem is assumed.

nodes.title: The Jacobi heat operator
nodes.statement: Put s=2πi. For m∈ℚ and φ:ℍ×ℂ→ℂ, Lₘφ=4m Dτφ−s⁻²∂²_zφ, where Dτφ(τ,z)=Derivative.normalizedDerivOfComplex (φ(·,z))(τ). The τ derivative uses the existing UpperHalfPlane.ofComplex extension, only at points in ℍ. Derivatives are Mathlib total derivatives; the calculus laws assume holomorphy. On exp(s(aτ+bz)), for arbitrary a,b∈ℂ, Lₘ multiplies by 4ma−b².
proofSteps: Use the native normalized derivative in τ and iteratedDeriv 2 in z. No new E₂ or scalar derivative is defined.
Additivity and complex scalar linearity on holomorphic functions follow from the derivative rules, twice in z; DifferentiableOn.deriv supplies the second derivative on open slices.
Differentiate exp(s(aτ+bz)) once in τ and twice in z. The factors s and s² cancel the prescribed denominators, giving 4ma−b².
acceptance: The discriminant is 4mn−r², with the minus sign fixed by the z derivative.
